News.title: Andy Burnham’s newly appointed Arts Minister was sacked by a French theatre after it ran up huge debts
News.content:
BRITAIN’S new Arts Minister was sacked by a French theatre after it ran up huge debts.

Andy Burnham made arts exec Ruth Mackenzie a peer last month so she could take up the Government role.



The pair were special advisers to former Culture Secretary Chris Smith in Tony Blair’s first Government.

But MPs questioned her appointment after it emerged she was fired from a historic Parisian theatre in 2020.



She served nearly three years as artistic director at the Théâtre du Châtelet before being booted out amid managerial and financial concerns.

It ran up a multi-million-euro deficit due to a series of struggling projects.

They included a loss of more than £855,000 on a production of Singin’ in the Rain and a costly immersive reconstruction of Soviet life.

French audit findings said her appointment produced a governance crisis.

By the time a new director took over in 2023, it had recorded a cumulative deficit since 2017 of £4million.

After she was fired she said: “I can only assume it’s because I’m a woman and foreign.”



Shadow Culture Secretary Nigel Huddleston said last night: “The woman who lost a million euros on Singin’ in the Rain is now deciding how taxpayers’ money is spent.”

She will serve under Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy.

A source close to Ms Nandy said: “She is an asset to the Government, brings a wealth of experience, and her appointment has been rightly welcomed.”

News.title: Somali man arrested over ‘attempted murder’ after stabbing at migrant hotel near Heathrow airport
News.content:
'KNIFE' ARREST Somali man arrested over ‘attempted murder’ after stabbing at migrant hotel near Heathrow airport

A MAN has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after a stabbing at a hotel that has been used to house asylum seekers.

Officers from Surrey Police were called to Stanwell Hotel in Staines at 6.30pm on Saturday to a report of a stabbing, the force said in a Facebook post.

A man in his 20s, who is a Somalian national, has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder.

The victim has been transported to hospital with “serious injuries”, it added.





The force said: “Please can we ask that you do not speculate on this incident and we will continue to provide updates on this channel.”

The hotel was first used to house asylum seekers in 2022.

However, proposals have since been submitted to return the 56-bed hotel back to its former use.

This includes providing lodging for paying guests, as well as respite for passengers at the nearby Heathrow Airport.

News.title: Heart-stopping moment woman dangles from 11th floor window of burning building before daring plunge
News.content:
THIS is the terrifying moment a woman dangles from the 11th floor of a burning building before taking a desperate leap of faith.

Startling footage shows the woman clinging to the side of an apartment building in Berlin.



Her legs can be seen dangling over a 35ft drop as an inferno rages inside.

A firefighter a couple of floors below beckons her towards a ladder, but the gap is too big.



With the ladder only able to reach the ninth floor, the woman is suddenly left with no choice but to jump.

As the flames creep closer, she finally lets go and plummets towards the firefighter with out-stretched arms below.



Miraculously, she landed with a thud in the rescue basket before being lowered safely to the ground.

The extraordinary scenes unfolded in Berlin’s Friedrichshain district.



According to reports, 13 people suffered minor injuries in the blaze.

Firefighters eventually brought the inferno under control in less than three hours.

The incident came months after hundreds of people were forced to flee a German nightclub in March when a fire ripped through and destroyed much of the building.

Around 750 revellers fled K Club, in Kehl, as the blaze spread through the packed building.

The fire broke out at around 3.45am local time and quickly “spread over the whole building”, police said.



Around 750 people were inside the club at the time, but all managed to escape.

Three people were treated by emergency services for shock.

Firefighters battled the inferno as it tore through the nightclub, which is located in an industrial area of the city.

The blaze caused such extensive damage that most of the building was later demolished.

Kehl mayor Wolfram Britz said he was “happy and relieved that nobody was hurt” and praised the nightclub owner for ensuring an orderly evacuation.



The K Club is a popular destination for hip-hop fans and attracts hundreds of revellers each weekend.

German media reported that at least 80 firefighters, police officers and emergency medical personnel attended the scene.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

One reveller told French newspaper DNA: “All of a sudden we heard, ‘There’s a fire!’ There were several announcements in German, French and English.”

An investigation was launched into the blaze, although its cause was not immediately clear.

News.title: John Healey must not increase Britain’s historically high tax rates until mountain of welfare waste is toppled
News.content:
Labour’s forgotten its wallet yet again

WHEN he was a humble Treasury minister in 2006, John Healey arrived at the till in the Commons tea room and realised he had no cash on him.

To save himself embarrassment Mr Healey quickly asked Labour colleagues to bail him out.



Flash forward 20 years. He is now Chancellor and the nation’s coffers are empty thanks to a debt of £3trillion.

So Mr Healey has been tasked with another whipround to save the nation’s blushes, this time from his Labour Cabinet colleagues.



Andy Burnham wants the Chancellor to find savings from existing Whitehall budgets across the board.

Mr Healey is very resourceful, but the kind of spending the new PM wants can’t be funded by passing the hat round to find some shrapnel from the back of the sofa.



It demands deep cuts to ballooning public spending, most notably the £333billion-a-year welfare bill.

For a start Mr Burnham should tackle the staggering £10billion lost to benefit fraud and error every year, which is an insult to every single taxpayer.

There must be no Budget plans to increase Britain’s already historically high tax rates until this mountain of welfare waste is toppled.

The new PM talks a good game when he is attacking private financial scandals. Why doesn’t he apply the same standards to Government waste?



Only last week Mr Burnham blasted rip-off water companies, saying: “Customers can’t be treated as a blank cheque . . . or a bottomless source of funding for other people’s failures.” Spot on, PM.

Now change the word “customers” to “taxpayers” and sort out the mess on your own doorstep.

Creative accounting

ANOTHER clue to Andy Burnham’s business sense can be found in his new appointment as Arts Minister.

The PM went out of his way to make Ruth Mackenzie a peer last month so she could take up the post in his Government.

With that support, most people would imagine she is a much sought-after appointment.



But she was fired from one of her previous jobs in Paris when her ultra woke regime ended up driving a theatre towards a deficit of almost five million euros.

Earlier in her career she was a boss of Scottish Opera when it was brought to the brink of collapse with debts of £2.5million.

Ms Mackenzie may be a titan of culture.

But when it comes to money she doesn’t appear to know her arts from her elbow.

News.title: Farage’s unstoppable march to No10 has stalled despite Clacton win – and made Labour & Lib Dems pact much more likely
News.content:
IT’S not easy to get 22,000 people out to vote in a mid-August by- election, especially when polling day is the hottest of the year.

But Nigel Farage’s gamble that his Clacton base would rally behind him paid off.



Despite the strange circumstances, Farage got more votes than in 2024, showing he can still motivate his supporters to turn up, even when the stakes are low.

In our Clacton focus groups, Farage’s supporters were unmoved by the undeclared £5million gift row. Some saw it as an establishment stitch-up, or no worse than what other politicians do.



Maureen, a retiree, told us: “If someone offered me £5million, I’d take it.”

But another number should worry Farage. Not the votes he received, but vote share.

His 63 per cent was lower than expected, especially since the combined Conservative/Reform vote in Clacton in 2024 was 74 per cent.



That’s a warning many Tory voters still won’t rally behind Reform as the face of the right, even without a Conservative candidate on offer.

Count Binface, meanwhile, won nearly 10,000 votes, or 27 per cent, six times higher than any comedy candidate in a parliamentary election. It is a reminder that Farage’s opponents, who do care about the £5million, are equally motivated to vote against him.

By-elections are unique. It’s difficult to take national lessons from individual local votes.

It’s even harder here because the main opposition is not normally wearing a dustbin on his head.



Yet Clacton still offers us a glimpse of how much the political landscape has changed. Last summer, Reform was on the rise. Their weekly press conferences dominated the news, Farage had the highest approval rating of any party leader.

Our MRP model — a tool for estimating the next election — put Reform within spitting distance of a majority in July. By autumn, it looked like Farage might be our next PM.

What goes up can go down, though. Even before the terminally unpopular Keir Starmer left office, Reform started to dip.



Embracing high-profile ex-Conservatives, such as Suella Braverman and Robert Jenrick, worried some that the party was becoming the Tories 2.0.

Now Andy Burnham has put Labour narrowly ahead — winning back progressives from the Greens, who were disappointed by Starmer’s government.

Reform won many seats in this year’s local elections coming through the middle of a divided Left. If the Left unites, that becomes much harder.

Burnham still has work to do: He is closing the hole on his left flank, but his right remains exposed. He is losing more 2024 Labour voters to Reform than any other party.

As we heard in Clacton, showing he’s serious about stopping Channel crossings and controlling immigration is non-negotiable for many voters.

Reform should also be more worried about the Conservatives today.



HOW SEATS COULD LOOK Labour……………..228

Reform……………..151

Tories………………..130

Lib Dems………..68

SNP…………………..31

Plaid………………..11

Other……………..9

Green…………….3

A year ago, Kemi Badenoch’s challenge was just getting heard. Now, it’s how to turn her growing fanbase into Tory voters.

Badenoch’s popularity has surged in recent months, now second only to Burnham. Farage’s approvals, meanwhile, have declined from -10 to -27, leaving him as unpopular as Green leader Zack Polanski.

But liking Kemi and voting Tory are not the same. Barely half of those who approve of Badenoch would actually vote Conservative.

The Tory brand has further to go if they hope to take on Reform, but they are back on the pitch.



So what does the electoral map look like? Our modelling suggests that Labour could double their seats from their worst projections last year — up from a projection of 100 seats to well over 200 as Burnham squashed Polanski’s Green wave. But still far from a majority.

Meanwhile, the same projections show the Conservatives pulling back from the brink of extinction, coming within 20 seats of Reform, who are estimated to drop back behind Labour.

Which brings us to the party not yet mentioned. Amid a four-way attention war between other party leaders, it is easy to forget that, by seats, the Liberal Democrats are easily the largest third party in British politics.

Yet they could emerge as kingmakers, who would be unlikely to get into bed with either Reform or the Tories.

That suggests an election tomorrow could lead to a left-leaning Labour-Liberal Democrat coalition.



A pact on the right, meanwhile, looks unlikely as the war between Farage, Badenoch and Restore Britain’s Rupert Lowe becomes more brutal.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Last year, Farage’s march on Downing Street looked unstoppable.

A divided Right and united Left mean that a progressive coalition is now much more likely.

News.title: Police gave up on finding phone or bag thief ever SIX minutes over the past year, damning figures reveal
News.content:
COPS gave up on finding a phone or bag thief every six minutes last year.

A Sun on Sunday trawl of police figures found 87,514 of 100,976 recorded “theft from the person” offences ended with no suspect identified.



In 11,932 cases, police were unable to prosecute a suspect, while 92 were given a caution.

Overall, police closed an investigation without finding a suspect 240 times a day — or one every six minutes.



Former Met detective Peter Bleksley said the failure damages public confidence.

He added: “In many cases, police close the investigation without even opening it.

“If people are not caught for these crimes, they will push boundaries further and steal even more.”

The top 23 theft areas in the country were all in London, with Leeds city centre next.

Worst was the West End with 10,579 thefts reported and 10,091 unsolved.

Just 52 suspects were taken to court. The Met said: “Recent figures show theft from the person has fallen 23 per cent in London, more than 23,000 fewer offences.”



Hatton, Stretton and Walton in Cheshire saw all 43 reported thefts unsolved.

Zero out of 32 were solved in Stanmer, East Sussex.

News.title: Reform UK unveils massive £50bn welfare overhaul to scrap PIP and force sick back to work
News.content:
BENEFIT BLITZ Reform UK unveils massive £50bn welfare overhaul to scrap PIP and force sick back to work

REFORM UK has unveiled a massive £50billion overhaul of the welfare system, scrapping PIP and forcing the sick back into work, should it get into power.

The party’s treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick claimed it would introduce the biggest welfare shake-up “in a generation”.



He said the current system was not helping those it was designed to help and it amounted to “suicidal empathy”.

Writing for The Telegraph, Mr Jenrick said Reform would get rid of personal independence payments (PIP) as well as the health part of Universal Credit for working age adults.



He said it would remove or cut benefits for 2.89million people.

To replace PIP, a health security allowance for severe and enduring disability cases would be brought in.

Only those with severe disabilities would get cash support, while other claimants would be given necessary services and support through council-run disability support accounts.

Employers would also have to pay a new form of insurance, called Return to Work Cover, under the new system, which would cover the cost of the first two years after an employee signed off sick.

The policy announcement comes after leader Nigel Farage won the Clacton by-election.

Reform is set to publish a 50-page paper on Monday called Making Welfare Work.



It’s believed that the team behind the paper include some who worked with Sir Iain Duncan Smith on developing Universal Credit, as well as whistleblowers in the Civil Service.

In the article, Mr Jenrick claimed that the policies would “more than double” the £20.5billion in savings made by Sir Iain under the Coalition government, and recent Conservative proposals that they could make savings of £23billion.

Mr Jenrick added that of the welfare reforms, £22billion would take the for of changes to the disability programme.

He claimed the disability support accounts would be used to fund additional disability costs, such as home adjustments, equipment, transport and personal assistance which would be adapted to local needs.

He also said there would be one assessment which would be conducted in person by clinicians instead of what he called a “web of failing tests”.



Any firm with more than five employees would have to take out the new insurance to cover the costs if any of their workers were unwell for longer than statutory sick pay permitted.

In return, companies would get a cut in National Insurance contributions by 0.2 percentage points initially, a move which he claimed would make the scheme “cost neutral”.

Employers would also be encouraged to support employees to return to the workplace more proactively, as this would lead to lower insurance premiums for the company.

Mr Jenrick said the policy was modelled on the Dutch system, where disability benefits applications dropped by 40 per cent.

He also said Reform would also examine children’s benefits and would pledge to reform children’s disability allowance for anxiety, depression and ADHD to align it with the adults’ system.



Those changes though would only apply for future claims and for a subset of mental health conditions.

Mr Jenrick also took aim at the Tories’ proposed welfare reforms, calling them “paper thin” proposals which “could have been written on the back of a fag packet”.

The welfare bill this year is forecast to hit £333billion, according to analysis by the Centre for Social Justice.

Currently, more than four million people claim disability benefits.

The shadow secretary of state for work and pensions Helen Whately called Reform’s criticisms of Conservative policy as a “half-baked attempt to distract from Farage’s fishy £5million” and “his embarrassing underperformance in his pointless by-election”.



After his by-election victory, the parliamentary watchdog will soon reopen its investigation into Mr Farage over a £5m gift given to him by Christopher Harborne, a cryptocurreny billionaire

Ms Whately added: “Reform have been nowhere on the debate on welfare reform.

“They have flip-flopped on restoring the two child benefit cap and claimed they’ll only take benefits away from foreigners, which won’t do enough to bring down the overall bill.

“The Conservatives are on the side of working people and we’re clear about our plans.

“Restore the two-child benefit cap, end benefits for low level mental health conditions, remove benefits from foreign nationals and restore face-to-face assessments.



“Only the Conservatives will get Britain working again.”

A Labour spokesman said Reform’s claim it could save £50billion was “fantasy economics, built on stripping support from disabled people and shifting costs onto employers”.

They added: “Labour is already reforming welfare: narrowing the gap between Universal Credit standard and health rates, restoring face-to-face assessments, and investing £3.5 billion in employment support to end the culture of people being signed off and written off.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We’re putting work and opportunity at the heart of the system, with further reform to follow the Milburn and Timms reports.

“Our reforms deliver credible, independently costed savings, not arbitrary numbers with no credible plan behind them.”

News.title: Kinahan cartel ‘fractured’ with Christy ‘under pressure’ in Dubai & details of gang’s new ‘franchise’ drug plot revealed
News.content:
THE Kinahan cartel still has “significant people” operating across Ireland, The Irish Sun can reveal.

The narco terrorist group’s “principal representative” Ross Browning, 48, remains here, but the transnational crime gang no longer has complete control of the entire drugs market.





Investigators from the Garda National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau believe the Kinahan Organised Crime Group’s leadership in Dubai are working with criminal gangs across Europe to control cocaine supply routes from South America to the continent.

And the Gardai believe the Kinahan network is now operating a “franchise business” focusing on the drug wholesale and importation role.

Many of the Kinahan associates are no longer part of “cell structures” and are no longer taking orders from their HQ in Dubai.

The tight control structures are now regarded by Gardai as “fractured and loose.”

One investigator said: “The criminal organisation just isn’t as powerful as it once was but they still have major associates in Ireland.

“Their cell structures were dismantled when many of their key people were arrested and convicted in the years after the 2016 Kinahan and Hutch feud.





“Their business model is different now because there are other gangs now operating on a transnational scale.

“The Kinahan network will never be allowed to become as powerful as it once was. Their members are now more independent.

“They have their people in Ireland but the leaders with more authority remain in Dubai and Spain.”

We can also reveal that investigations into murders that took place during the feud are ongoing.

One of the biggest probes was into the murder of Gerry ‘The Monk’ Hutch’s brother Eddie, 58, who was shot dead on February 8, 2016, just three days after the infamous Regency Hotel attack.

A huge investigation file on the murder is currently with the Director of Public Prosecutions.

We understand new technology — used to help convict Sean McGovern, 40, of directing the hit teams who murdered Noel Kirwan in December 2016 and the attempted hit on James Gately in April 2017 — has been used in the investigation.

Former Supt Martin Mooney, who was in charge of the probe between 2020 and 2023, hopes a decision will soon be made by the DPP.



Investigators from the Gardai’s North Central Division have already been successful in bringing prosecutions against those responsible for the murders of Michael Barr, 35, and Gareth Hutch, also 35, in 2016.

Mr Mooney told us: “The work that has gone into compiling this massive investigation file has been phenomenal.

“It’s certainly one of the biggest files I ever came across before I retired in 2023.

“The use of new technology when it came to analysing encrypted phones was also utilised in the investigation.

“In my view the investigators have completed a very professional and comprehensive investigation file — just as they did in other investigations.

“I would hope that once analysed the DPP can give a direction to charge a number of individuals in relation to this callous murder.”



He added: “It’s possible there could be a number of serious charges arising out of this investigation.

“All we can do now is await the DPP’s direction.”

At present, cartel founder Christy ‘Dapper Don’ Kinahan, 69, and his son Christopher Jnr, 45 remain in Dubai.

The father and son are the focus of $5million rewards leading to their arrest by the US Treasury Department

The pair stayed on in Dubai despite Daniel Kinahan’s extradition to Ireland from the UAE last week to face a charge of directing the activities of a criminal organisation.

Another investigator told us: “Things aren’t going too well for Christy Kinahan and his son at the moment. They haven’t many options available but they have chosen to remain in Dubai.

“They have been under serious pressure for years but still find time to meet for nice meals. The father and son remain free for the moment but they know they remain the focus of major investigation from European law enforcement agencies and also in America.”

The rewards were issued in 2022 along with sanctions against other members of the group.

They include Ian Dixon, 35 who was identified as “arranging multiple payments” for the cartel, and Bernard Clancy, 45 who was identified as a “key lieutenant.”

Johnny ‘Cash’ Morrissey, 66, is still under investigation in Spain’s Costa del Sol.



Gardai and their international colleagues have targeted money laundering, arms importation and drug smuggling networks as part of their efforts to completely dismantle the gang.

In terms of the cartel’s drugs operations, most shipments

come through Holland and Spain. Once landed in those countries, Kinahan associates arrange transport to Ireland.

After landing here the drugs are then passed to other crime groups for distribution.

Many of the crime gangs in Ireland are also sourcing their own cocaine supply routes from South America.

Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly confirmed on Wednesday that investigations into the Kinahan cartel were ongoing.

He said: “We got Daniel Kinahan back home to court and he’s now in Portlaoise Prison. We are certainly not finished with this. There are other people we are very interested in so we will continue our work.

“We are relentless around this. This isn’t the end of it, certainly not.

“The people I really want to mark out are those people in the Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau who for ten years day in and day out have been working on these cases.

“I want to congratulate these people on the work that they have done.”

News.title: Major incidents across UK putting firefighters under 'incredible pressure', fire chief says
News.content:
Eleven major fires in the past 48 hours and 43 new wildfires since Friday have left services under "incredible pressure", a fire boss has said.

Phil Garrigan from the National Fire Chief's Council (NFCC) said major incidents had been declared across the UK, including in Stourbridge, Sandwell, Pershore and Stoke-on-Trent in the West Midlands, as well as in Hampshire and South Wales.

Many residents forced to flee their homes following the fires are still in the dark about when they can return.

In Stourbridge, where 38 houses have been destroyed or damaged, frustrated residents said they were not getting any answers, although it was hope they may go home later on Saturday.

West Midlands Assistant Chief Fire Officer Simon Barry told residents the fire there was under control and they were just dampening down hot spots.

He said as far as the service was concerned, homes were no longer at risk and he hoped some residents whose homes had been unaffected would be able to move back on Saturday evening.

In a recorded online briefing, Dudley Council chief executive Balvinder Hera stressed residents should not return home until explicitly told they could do so.

She said decisions to reopen roads were being taken on a street-by-street basis, with the council working closely with emergency services.

Police were keen to hear from people with information or video footage that could assist inquiries and had asked the public not to speculate on the fire's cause, she said.

An online fund, external has been set up by the council to allow people to donate to those affected.

News.title: Jason Arday death 'tragedy on so many levels' says PM
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Professor of Black Studies Kehinde Andrews, a friend of Arday, described him as "very down" after resigning from Cambridge.

"He was very upset. He felt that there was no way out. He effectively wasn't leaving the house. He had lost a lot of weight," Andrews said.

"There should be a wakeup call to just how bad black academics actually have it in academia."

Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy also told the programme "the idea that an academic would be dragged through this amount of media scrutiny is unheard of".

On Saturday Scotland's First Minister John Swinney said that people who "made many hard comments must now consider the impact of their words", describing it as a "deeply concerning and very sad case".

Prior to his appointment at Cambridge, Arday had worked as a professor at the University of Glasgow.

Shadow communities secretary Sir James Cleverly said he was angered by the "tragic" death and said "a number of people at a number of academic institutions have serious questions to answer".

When asked by the BBC on Saturday if the University of Cambridge needed to answer questions over its duty of care, Cleverly said the university should "ask themselves how he got into this position, how he ended up being in the eye of the storm, what could and should have happened to prevent this long before it got to this tragic situation".

Arday had denied plagiarism - but admitted errors in his work - and said the recent controversy had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

The row first erupted after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.

Arday said some errors in his early academic work arose because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. Similar scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics, he said.

Questions were also raised about parts of his life story, including that he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised Â£5.5m for charity.

He later said the run was actually completed over a 12-day period to allow for rest days - and that the huge sum was raised with the help of others.

Arday's appointment as Cambridge's youngest ever black professor at the age of 37 in 2023 was hailed at the time.

Announcing his resignation last week, Arday said the "personal cost" of the scrutiny of him had become "too great".

He said: "While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement.

"The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."

He stressed that his resignation should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".

Earlier this week, Cambridge announced an independent investigation around the circumstances of Arday's appointment.

Liverpool John Moores University - which awarded Arday his PhD in 2015 - concluded that he had not plagiarised work.

In a statement on Saturday, a spokesperson for the university said it was "saddened to hear of the tragic loss of Professor Jason Arday".

News.title: Analysis: Arday's death will send shockwaves through a divided academia
News.content:
There was another reason this row had such a high profile. Arday was a celebrity academic known as much for the remarkable life story he told, of an autistic child who didn't speak until 11, or learn to read and write until 18.

Other aspects of his personal narrative came under scrutiny, and he had to clarify that Â£5m raised for charity had been as part of a group effort, and that a 600 mile running challenge had taken twice as long as originally claimed.

Some who had signed a public letter of support quietly removed their names.

By the time he resigned his Cambridge position last week Arday said the "relentless accusations" had taken a "profound toll" on him and his family.

He suggested they had been racially motivated.

There are many unanswered questions which a coroner will no doubt be expected to consider about his circumstances and state of mind in the days before his death.

In the immediate aftermath of his death, his family said Arday had been subjected to a "campaign of misinformation" that was too much for this "gentle man".

Others think that he attracted so much scrutiny because he was a black man in a prominent position.

Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, said Arday had been "the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn't have faced. His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake up call for all of us."

There has been deep unease among some academics of colour who feel the ferocity of the debate was due to Arday being a young black academic.

Professor of Black Studies Kehinde Andrews, a friend of Arday, told Newsnight in the wake of his death: "This is not just something that has happened in the past two weeks, we've seen the stories, this goes back three and a half years.

"The very day he got the position at Cambridge he had a Freedom of Information request asking about his credentials. He had all the right-wing people in America and the UK writing in to see if he was credible.

"Some people didn't believe a black man should be in that position at Cambridge.

"It's been a three-and-a-half-year toll which has come its head now."

What is certain is that Arday had sought to defend his reputation, using a high-profile firm of lawyers to send a letter to a journalist from Times Higher Education who first questioned his work.

The University of Cambridge initially robustly defended Arday then announced an investigation into his appointment and tenure amid growing disquiet.

In 2023, as an elite university which had been criticised for a lack of diversity, Cambridge had been keen to make some high-profile non-white appointments. It had already made a huge effort to ensure admission of students was more diverse.

Whoever was appointed into such a high profile post would have faced scrutiny and Arday had a slighter research track record than some others in the field.

Dr Jo Grady, general secretary of the University and College Union, described Jason Arday's death as "devastating".

"There are so many questions that need to be answered. The level of harassment he suffered and the racism he was subjected to, has been sickening. It must be investigated."

For the University of Cambridge now there will be the difficult task of holding together an academic community divided and shocked by the controversy and now the death of Jason Arday.

It had announced an investigation into his appointment and tenure at the university and a review of how senior staff are chosen.

Now all of that has been overtaken by his sudden and shocking death.

News.title: Met Police apologises for data breach involving alleged Al Fayed victims
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has apologised after it inadvertently disclosed email addresses of around 140 people who say they were sexually abused by the late Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed.

Scotland Yard confirmed to the BBC it copied in all those who had signed up to receive a monthly email update for victims instead of blind copying them.

The update revealed a further three suspects in their 70s and 80s had been interviewed under caution, bringing the total number interviewed to seven.

The force said it had referred itself to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). It is considering providing further support to the victims along with additional safeguards.

A Met Police spokesperson told the BBC a monthly update sent to victims on 11 August regarding Operation Cornpoppy had contained details of progress in the investigation.

Operation Cornpoppy is the Metropolitan Police investigation into people who may have facilitated or enabled sexual offending by Al Fayed.

The spokesperson said: "Due to human error, recipients' email addresses were visible to others on the distribution list. The issue was identified quickly and immediate action was taken.

"We understand the impact this may have on victims and sincerely apologise. Everyone affected was contacted directly on the day of the incident.

"The incident is being investigated as a matter of priority, and we are reviewing our processes to help prevent a similar breach from happening again."

The force said the breach affected victims who had opted in to receive updates from the investigation team, but recipients had been split into smaller groups, meaning email addresses were only visible within those groups rather than across the entire cohort.

The BBC understands around 140 people have signed up to the updates.

The force has previously said 154 victims have reported allegations connected to Al Fayed and that supporting survivors remains at the heart of the investigation.

It said the incident had been formally recorded within the investigation records and they would continue to monitor the circumstances and impact of the breach, including reviewing alternative methods of updating victims that would reduce the risk of human error.

The force added that victim-survivors remained its priority and said it was committed to providing updates to those involved in the investigation.

News.title: Thousands of Bonnie Tyler fans line the streets as coffin taken to Swansea home
News.content:
Legendary singer Bonnie Tyler has made a final journey to her Mumbles home, with thousands of emotional fans lining the streets to pay their respects.

The Total Eclipse of the Heart singer died "unexpectedly" on 8 July, aged 75, at a hospital in Portugal.

At the time, tributes poured in from a host of friends and stars including Catherine Zeta-Jones, Bryan Adams and Rod Stewart.

Despite Tyler's career taking her all over the world, she has been described by those living in the coastal suburb of Mumbles as a "Swansea girl through and through", and someone who "never forgot where she came from".

Huge crowds turned out as her coffin was driven through the place she called home.

News.title: Sellers puzzled by bulk orders suspect secondhand books being destroyed to train AI
News.content:
Something mysterious has been happening in the world of secondhand books.

Over the last few months independent booksellers have been observing a strange pattern of purchases which have seen scores of their novels being shipped to far-off warehouses.

In a typical week, Stuart Manley, from Barter Books, in Northumberland, would sell two or three thousand books. But one recent single bulk order from a Canadian company equalled what he would expect to move in seven days.

He says he has "never seen the like of this after 30 years in the second-hand book trade".

Mr Manley is not alone. Booksellers from around the world have been reporting similarly unusual mega orders.

They aren't sure what the final destination for their books is.

But the suspicion is that they are not being bought for avid overseas readers but instead something else with a voracious appetite for new information: AI.

News.title: When my dog died, my grief was overwhelming and complicated
News.content:
Gemma Champ, a writer from north London, rescued her cat Frankie as a kitten 17 years ago, when she lived in Abu Dhabi. Frankie died at home in January, and at first she felt "ridiculous for making such a fuss".

"I sent out a WhatsApp to all who'd known and loved him - and it turned out everyone had amazing memories of him. He wasn't just a cat. One friend said it was like 'a legendary beast from the great plains has left us.'

"We can see from social media that there's a whole community of people out there who have gone through the same experience and the same pain, so you don't feel like you're just being a drama queen - I think that's definitely how it would have been seen years ago."

After Greg James' dog died, the presenter said he wouldn't be on his show the next day. But getting employers to agree to this isn't always easy.

In 2019, Emma McNulty's 14-year-old terrier Millie died suddenly. Feeling sick with grief, McNulty, from Glasgow, said she was too upset to go into work. Unable to find someone to cover her shift, she said her part-time job in a sandwich shop was terminated. She then launched an online petition asking for employers to recognise pet bereavement.

No country mandates that employers offer paid time off after the death of a pet. Kara Stott, head of in-house legal and general counsel at law firm Peninsula, said more UK employers were starting to show flexibility with workers whose pets had died, even if a change to the law does not appear imminent.

But introducing formal pet bereavement policies has its challenges, Stott tells the BBC.

"Points to consider include how do you define a pet - does the policy just cover cats and dogs or would hamsters, rabbits, goldfish, horses, snakes, or other animals be included?"

Gemma, who is freelance, took a few days off work after Frankie's death, with the support of her "incredibly kind" client. "I doubt I could have done that if I'd been employed," she says, "and I think I'd have been weeping in the toilets at the office."

The reaction from friends and family to Frankie's passing confirmed that her sense of grief was real, she says, and she appreciated that people took it seriously.

"I do think, or hope, that people are learning not to dismiss this very profound and long-lasting relationship so easily."

News.title: Many Canadians are boycotting the US - here's where they're travelling instead
News.content:
Prior to US President Donald Trump's re-election, Kent Truscott and his family, from London, Ontario, had taken multiple trips south of the border, including to California and most recently New York in 2023.

But since late 2024, "my family and I have completely decided to boycott the United States", he told BBC.

That meant cancelling a trip last spring to Texas to watch the SpaceX Starship launch with his brother. The two had planned to fly down from Toronto, rent a car and stay a week to watch the launch, likely spending "thousands of dollars".

Truscott and his wife decided to spend that money in Canada instead â the Atlantic provinces of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, to be exact.

Their decision is a response to US tariffs and the president's comments about annexing their country. More than a year after Trump's return to the White House, many Canadians like Truscott are still holding firm on their boycott on travel to the US.

News.title: 'Fury' at Tarling death as cycling union calls for better helmets
News.content:
The cyclists' union has expressed "fury" over the death of British rider Fin Tarling during Friday's stage of the Volta a Portugal.

The 19-year-old NSN Cycling rider reportedly collided with a vehicle not involved in the race.

And the union's president Adam Hansen told BBC Sport there needs to be better helmet safety as cyclists hit record-breaking speeds during races.

"We are speechless and filled with anger," said the Cyclistes Professionnels Associes (CPA) on social media.

"It is not right that a young athlete's life should end this way, and we are furious that even today it is still not possible to prevent such serious accidents.

"We share in the grief of his family, friends, team, and everyone who knew Finlay. Rest in peace, young rider; we pray for you, and we will carry you in our hearts."

Tarling was the younger brother of Josh, a time trial specialist for British super team Netcompany Ineos, who has won a stage of the Giro d'Italia and a European Time Trial title.

Fin Tarling himself had finished strongly in the time trial a few days earlier in the race he would never finish.

He was part of a new generation of male and female British riders on the World Tour who grew up on the success of highly decorated road cyclists, such as Mark Cavendish, Chris Froome and Lizzie Deignan, during a golden decade for British participation in the sport from 2012.

Just like all young professionals, Fin spent hours every day trying to extract as much performance as possible. But he was known to love every element of cycling and was always in the saddle.

His parents, Michael and Dawn, frequently attended races and even set up their own team in their home in Ceredigion, west Wales.

BBC Sport understands organisers are considering a tribute to Tarling at the men's Tour of Britain, which starts on 2 September.

News.title: Military sent in to help emergency services fight wildfires across Wales
News.content:
The military has been deployed to help tackle wildfires across Wales.

Personnel and an Army helicopter are supporting firefighters in Cwmavon, Torfaen council has said.

People have been warned not to fly drones in the area because they will interfere with the military helicopter, and a fire service drone.

Meanwhile, police investigating a "deliberate fire" on the mountain near Pleasant Heights, Porth, said on Friday they had arrested four 14-year-old boys from Porth on suspicion of arson. They are on police bail.

The UK government issued an emergency alert to phones across England and Wales on Friday evening saying there was "a very high risk of wildfires nationally".

On Friday, Stephen Kinnock, Secretary of State for Wales, said military personnel had been deployed for logistical support and to help "ease the pressure on the ground".

Despite cooler temperatures on Saturday, crews across Wales are continuing to battle fires.

Mid & West Wales Fire and Rescue Service (MWWFRS) said crews had spent more than 90 hours on "operational incidents" in Llanwrtyd Wells, Merthyr Tydfil and Ebbw Vale.

"It has been tough, however, we have been overwhelmed by the support we have received during this time," the service said, thanking local businesses "that have kept us fuelled with food and drinks".

Residents had been evacuated from their homes after a fire near Llandovery, Carmarthenshire, with a councillor describing the situation as "scary", as the fire made its way towards the village.

News.title: Public urged to avoid 'surrounded' New Forest fire site
News.content:
The public has been urged to avoid an area where crews are working to dampen down a wildfire.

The blaze in the New Forest began when a van caught fire on the A31 last Sunday. The road will remain closed until at least Thursday, National Highways has said.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service (HIWFRS) said it has received reports of members of the public accessing the site where its crews are working.

It comes after an earlier update from the fire service on Saturday, saying the fire was now "fully surrounded" after firefighters worked through the night. HIWFRS added: "We will still be on scene for a number of days as we damp down and extinguish hotspots."

The service added: "Accessing an active fire ground puts people at risk, impacts our firefighting operations, risks damage to the critical equipment we have on site, and could therefore cause further delays to this lengthy incident."

News.title: Heathrow Airport roads reopen after mains burst
News.content:
All roads to Heathrow Airport have reopened after earlier disruption caused by flooding from a burst water main on a ring road.

The flooding along Inner Ring Road West prevented access to the central terminal area (CTA), which includes Terminals 2 and 3, a number of other buildings and the road network.

Heathrow Airport has confirmed the airport is now operating as normal and has apologised for the inconvenience after the road closures were made just before 06:00 BST.

Passengers are still being advised to use public transport where possible due to heavy congestion on the roads.

The travel disruption left some passengers struggling to get to their planes on time.

George Smyrniadis, 79, missed his flight to Frankfurt where he was headed for a school reunion on Saturday afternoon.

Smyrniadis, who got in touch via BBC's Your Voice, said: "I was upset. It's the first reunion I've missed since 1987.

"I was so downhearted I just wanted to get home.

"The whole airport seemed completely chaotic, but I got the impression the airlines just carried on as though nothing was wrong - and if you missed your flight you just missed it."

Smyrniadis said his trip from Portsmouth went well until he left the M4, at which point he was sat in traffic for 90 minutes travelling a distance which usually takes him about 10 minutes.

"By the time I got to security it was too late - it was already 09:30BST so they wouldn't let me go through any further."

News.title: Body found in search for UK student missing on Romania hike
News.content:
Tributes are being paid to an 18-year-old who went missing on a hiking trip to the Romanian mountains.

George Smyth, a University of Bristol student from Shropshire, had been missing since 23 November in the Bucegi mountains, despite daily searches, BraÈov Mountain Rescue said.

Avon and Somerset Police confirmed they had been notified by Romanian local authorities that a body had been found in the region. While formal identification has not yet taken place, the body is believed to be his.

"We are all devastated by George's death. He was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends," his family said.

They added: "We want to thank Salvamont Mountain Rescue, who have worked tirelessly since November searching for George; despite very difficult and often dangerous conditions. They are an amazing team, and have remained in constant communication, helping us greatly throughout this awful time.

"We would also like to thank Avon and Somerset Police and University of Bristol, who have gone above and beyond to try and find George, and to support us as a family.

"Although this latest news is incredibly painful, the torture of waiting is finally over, so we can now focus on bringing George home and saying goodbye. We would appreciate privacy while we continue to come to terms with this loss."

News.title: Bride dazzles in thrifty wedding with £2 charity shop dress
News.content:
A couple tied the knot in a thrifty-themed wedding with the bride dazzling in a Â£2 charity shop wedding dress.

Gina and Jacob Dodds, from Hoole in Chester, said "I do" in a ceremony held at the city's Storyhouse arts and cultural centre on Wednesday.

Both Gina's dress and engagement ring were bought from the Hope House Children's Hospice outlet while guests were also invited to wear outfits sourced from charity shops - raising money for a range of good causes.

"If we were going to have a wedding then we wanted it to be about more than just us - we wanted it to be about helping other people," she said.

News.title: Woman allegedly tasered, raped and beaten by ex-partner, court hears
News.content:
A woman was allegedly tasered, raped and beaten in her home by her ex-partner, a court has heard.

In a special court sitting at Lisburn Magistrates' Court, a man aged in his 40s was charged with two counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, threats to kill, non-fatal strangulation, entering as a trespasser to commit rape and assaults including causing actual bodily harm.

He cannot be identified to protect the identity of the woman.

The court heard the man had turned up at the woman's house on two previous occasions, once with a baseball bat, but it was "marked as a domestic".

Warning: This article contains details of sexual assault that some readers may find distressing.

A detective constable told the court on 14 August staff at the Ulster Hospital contacted police to report the woman had presented with significant injuries which she disclosed had been caused by her ex-partner who was also at the hospital.

Officers attended and the woman said she was asleep in bed when she woke to find the defendant was in the room having broken in and was holding a taser.

He physically assaulted the victim and attacked her with the taser.

She described him threatening to kill her and covering her mouth with his hand before raping her twice.

When he agreed to take her to hospital he stopped on a road and discarded the taser, which has also been recovered by police.

The woman sustained a broken nose and bruising to her face and neck.

The defendant was arrested at the hospital and provided a pre-prepared statement accepting that he let himself into the house but denying the offences insisting everything was consensual.

However, he could not account for the injuries.

News.title: Baby puffins make uninhabited island their new home
News.content:
Footage of a puffling - a baby puffin - bred on the Copeland Islands off the County Down coast has been captured for the first time.

The seabirds, synonymous with Rathlin Island off County Antrim, are not indigenous to the uninhabited Lighthouse Island, so no population existed there until an introduction scheme was launched around 2013.

There are now around 30 breeding pairs of puffins, which is being seen as a real success story.

They arrive to the island each April, and this year - in fact, just last month - trail cameras near their burrows in the ground filmed a young puffling out of its burrow, and an adult puffin bringing fish back to feed its young.

Attempts to attract puffins to Lighthouse Island included setting up fake "decoy" puffins, and a solar powered speaker system broadcasting its call.

A Kansas City great-grandfather died beside his wife of 50 years after a large rock crashed through the roof of their Jeep while visiting Glacier National Park.

Rex Schowengerdt, 73, and his wife, Chris, were beginning a months-long trip to several national parks in July, KCTV reports. The retired couple traveled around 1,300 miles from their Missouri home to Montana in their RV, with Glacier National Park as their first stop.

Rex Schowengerdt’s sister and brother-in-law joined them during their visit, which quickly took a tragic turn. On July 11, Schowengerdt’s brother-in-law was driving a hard-top Jeep along a narrow road near Logan Pass when a 45-pound rock broke loose from the steep cliffs and crashed through the vehicle’s roof.

Schowengerdt, a father of two, grandfather of five and great-grandfather of two, was sitting in the backseat with his wife when the rock crushed his skull and pushed bone into his brain stem,

“Because mom was sitting next to dad, dad slumped into my mom. But mom said when she looked over, dad had a smile on his face,” Amy Prince, Schowengerdt’s daughter, told KCTV Thursday, adding that her dad, who loved the outdoors, camping and running, was “so excited” to be at the national park.

open image in gallery Chris Schowengerdt (left) was sitting next to her husband of 50 years, Rex Schowengerdt, (right) last month when a rock crashed through the roof of a Jeep they were riding in while visiting Glacier National Park in Montana ( GoFundMe )

“It hurt initially to hear, but it kind of brings peace to me as well in a way because Dad was where he wanted to be and he was happy, and I know even before he left, he was happy,” Prince added.

Schowengerdt was taken by helicopter to a hospital but died five days later, on July 16, from a traumatic brain injury.

“Even after they flew my dad away, they still had to get down the mountain, which meant it took them two and a half hours in the same car that that happened in,” Prince said about the heartbreaking aftermath, adding that the family spent another hour traveling to the hospital to see him.

Prince said her father was in good enough health for doctors to determine that his lungs could be donated. The family hoped to have a traditional funeral and burial, but the high cost of transporting Rex’s body from Montana to Kansas City meant he was ultimately cremated.

open image in gallery Amy Prince, the couple’s daughter said her dad told her before he left on his fatal trip to never take the outdoors for granted ( GoFundMe )

The family is bracing for significant medical expenses, including a potentially costly air ambulance bill. They have set up a GoFundMe to help Chris Schowengerdt cover the costs.

Before leaving for the trip, Schowengerdt shared a message with his daughter that she now hopes to pass on to others.

“He said, ‘Amy, I want you just to remember that when you’re out in nature, don’t take it for granted. Look, really look and really see, and take a second look. And that’s something that he taught even my kids, who are adults now. I think it’s a legacy,’” Prince recalled.

Reform UK has set out plans to revolutionise the welfare state that would see almost three million people’s disability and sickness payments withdrawn or modified.

Under the plans, Reform would abolish personal independence payments (Pip) and the health element of Universal credit for working-age adults, The Telegraph reports. Reform’s Treasury spokesperson Robert Jenrick claimed that the proposals would cut £50 billion from the welfare bill.

He said that Reform would introduce a new, regularly-reviewed, health security allowance that would provide support only for the “gravely ill and severely challenged”.

Mr Jenrick said 6.9 million people were receiving disability benefits but “this is not an epidemic of broken backs and lost limbs” as since 2002 the share of working-age people claiming for mental health and behavioural conditions had tripled.

Under the planned reforms, due to be unveiled in detail on Monday, cash payments for low-level conditions would end and be replaced with disability support accounts, run by local councils and mayors, to cover costs such as equipment, adaptations, transport and personal assistance.

And employers could be obliged to pay a “return to work cover” insurance to fund the cost of the first two years after an employee is signed off sick.

Mr Jenrick said firms would then have a “strong economic incentive” to return the employee to work. People who had not returned to work within two years would go through a single, rigorous assessment conducted in person to “screen out vexatious and fraudulent claims”.

open image in gallery Robert Jenrick said ‘dumping our young people onto welfare isn’t compassion’ ( PA )

Writing in The Telegraph, Mr Jenrick said: “We will not pretend this is painless.

“Existing claimants will be reassessed over three to four years: we estimate that 2.16 million will keep their present cash entitlement in full, while 2.89 million will see theirs modified or withdrawn, concentrated where recent growth has been most explosive.”

He said the state must be there to support people who need it but “dumping our young people onto welfare isn’t compassion; it’s neglect”.

“We are not lifting people out of misfortune. We are abandoning them to it, and calling it kindness.”

Mr Jenrick said the Reform proposals would save “more than double” the £23 billion promised by Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives, with £22 billion of the savings coming from changes to disability benefits alone.

open image in gallery Helen Whately, Shadow Secretary of State for Work and Pensions ( Getty )

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said the plans were an attempt to distract attention from the investigation into a £5 million donation to Nigel Farage and his “pointless by-election” in Clacton.

She said: “Reform have been nowhere on the debate on welfare reform. They have flip-flopped on restoring the two child benefit cap and claimed they’ll only take benefits away from foreigners, which won’t do enough to bring down the overall bill.

“The Conservatives are on the side of working people and we’re clear about our plans. Restore the two-child benefit cap, end benefits for low level mental health conditions, remove benefits from foreign nationals and restore face-to-face assessments.”

A Labour spokeswoman said: “Reform’s £50 billion claim is fantasy economics, built on stripping support from disabled people and shifting costs onto employers.”

She added that the Labour Government’s reforms to welfare “deliver credible, independently-costed savings, not arbitrary numbers with no credible plan behind them”.

News.title: Five people shot at Virginia State University as police search for ‘multiple suspects’
News.content:

Five people were injured in a shooting at Virginia State University early Saturday as students got ready to start a new school year.

At least one student is among the wounded after the shooting near the university's Quad Annexes at around 1:30 a.m. local time. Police rushed to the campus and found five people suffering from gunshot wounds near student dormitories.

They were taken to hospitals, where one was in critical condition, county police said. The other victims suffered non-life-threatening injuries, according to police.

The university said in a statement that the shooting involved “multiple suspects” and urged people to avoid the immediate area.

“VSU Police and the Chesterfield County Police Department are actively investigating,” the university statement said. “The campus community should continue to avoid the area and follow all law enforcement instructions.”

There was a large law enforcement presence on campus in the hours that followed the shooting as the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Hanover County Sheriff's Office assist police.

Virginia State Police deferred questions to local police, who are leading the investigation. County police and campus officials said there would be more information later in the day.

‘Tragic’ start to the school year

Virginia State University is a historically Black university located in Ettrick, Virginia, about 24 miles south of the state capital of Richmond. The public university has about 5,700 students and was the first fully state-supported four-year college for Black Americans. Most of its students are undergraduates.

The shootings happened just before the start of the academic year at Virginia State.

Residence halls opened for students a week ago and classes are set to begin on Monday, according to the university's website. Many students had just completed the university's “New Trojans Experience” for incoming students.

The university has grown in recent years while attempting to improve safety and retain its historic charm, said Arthur Fridrich, the university's former director of distance education, who lives near the campus and visits regularly.

“To start a new year with this event is very tragic. It casts a shadow in the minds of all students, and for some it will be difficult to rid their minds of this term,” Fridrich said.

“For those that were shot, my heart bleeds. I hope that they all mend and somehow do not let this event define their lives.”

Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, said via social media that she and her husband were “praying for a quick recovery for those who were shot this morning at Virginia State University, and our thoughts are with the VSU community.” She also thanked first responders and law enforcement.

Sen. Mark Warner, also a Democrat, said it was “devastating to see another Virginia campus harmed by gun violence.”

There’s a corner of the Alexander Stadium in Birmingham that is seemingly forever Ireland.

At the top bend of the back straight, they arrived in their numbers, a sea of green creating a wall of noise as Kate O’Connor took European Athletics Championship heptathlon gold, just a few days after Mark English won the 1500m.

You can’t be a Northern Irish athlete without comparisons to Dame Mary Peters. At the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, O’Connor became the first to top a track and field podium in 40 years and the first woman to do so since Peters in 1974.

But the athletics icon never won this title, which really only leaves one thing for the world silver medallist: matching her Olympic success from 54 years ago in Munich, with Los Angeles now just under two years away and counting.

Her points tally of 6,751 is a new national record and ranks her second in the world this year, with Switzerland’s Annik Kalin, who arrived here ranked number one, finishing just outside the medals.

Winning is a habit and no wonder O’Connor, who is coached by her father Michael, is starting to think even bigger.

open image in gallery Kate O’Connor relished her gold medal ( Reuters )

“I’ve got a nice taste for gold medals now but I know the pressure and expectation increases with every competition, I’ll embrace that,” she said.

“That [the 800m finale] was the most nerve-racking two minutes of my life but when I heard cheers like that for me going around those two laps, there was no way I was going to let that gold medal slip through my fingers.

“I just wanted to cruise home and make sure I leave here injury-free and with a gold medal around my neck. I’ve dreamt of this moment since I started in this sport and it wasn’t long ago that it didn’t seem very likely.

“This year has been really tough for me personally. My Granny died during the year and I don’t think I give my Dad enough credit for how hard it hit him. But he still turned up to training day in, day out because this is my dream, but it’s his dream too.

“I have to dedicate this medal to her because she was our biggest fan. She would have been jumping for joy if she was here to see this.”

open image in gallery O’Connor could scarcely believe her win ( Getty )

O’Connor, at 25, is at the peak of her powers and, in fact, a year younger than Katarina Johnson-Thompson was when she won the first of her two world titles in Doha back in 2019.

Johnson-Thompson’s status as one of Britain’s great multi-eventers is secure but her future appears far from certain after she finished 21st, last of those who completed all seven events.

She always knew competing here was a stretch – let alone finding herself back on the podium.

The 33-year-old has been elusive this season, with just one fleeting appearance in the shot in Loughborough three months ago after struggling with a calf injury.

open image in gallery Katarina Johnson-Thompson endured a European Championships to forget ( AP )

She swerved the Commonwealth Games to focus on Birmingham but her hopes of upgrading her 2018 European silver were never realistic.

“I’m thinking of the future. I’ve always said that when I’m not competitive then I will start to ask questions,” she said. “Right now, I want to be in the moment, the hunger is still here. I can’t just want to be part of something, I want to compete.

“It’s far from my best and not the competition I wanted but it is what it is and I finished it.

“It’s not easy to come into a heptathlon out of shape. It’s not like other events when you can get knocked out in the heats and go home. You are out here with everyone watching for two whole days.

“It was important that I just finished because I fought so hard to be here. I’ve been coming to this stadium since English Schools, it’s a really important place for me.”

For Johnson-Thompson, the questions are now about how long; for O’Connor, they’re increasingly about how far.

open image in gallery O’Connor did enough in the 800m to seal victory ( Reuters )

Police in Michigan have released new details about a shooting spree that left six people dead, including the suspected shooter.

A teenage boy and four adults were killed Friday in shootings that sparked an urgent manhunt for the gunman, whose body was found in a wooded area alongside one of his victims. A teen girl survived the massacre and was in stable condition.

Officers responded Friday morning to reports of a shooting at a home about 170 miles (270 kilometers) northwest of Detroit, where they found the bodies of a 16-year-old boy, a 45-year-old man and 40-year-old woman, and a 13-year-old girl in critical condition, Michigan State Police said.

Authorities say the suspect, Chad Hickman, fled that scene, sparking a large-scale search. Police found the body of a 53-year-old man at a second home, and then a 29-year-old woman, dead alongside Hickman, in the woods.

Suspected gunman Chad Hickman was found dead after a manhunt in Michigan ( Michigan State Police )

All the victims died of gunshot wounds, police said. Their names haven’t yet been released, nor has a motive in the killings.

“This situation is heartbreaking for the community and challenging for the investigators involved,” Lt. Ashley Miller said in a Friday statement. Miller said Saturday the investigation is ongoing.

Hickman was convicted in 2024 of misdemeanor fourth-degree child abuse, according to court records. He was sentenced to one year in jail. In the same case, the court dismissed felony assault and criminal sexual conduct charges.

Gov. Gretchen Whitmer said Friday she was monitoring the situation. “My thoughts are with the victims, their families, and the Missaukee community,” she said.

News.title: US oil reserves are so low amid Trump’s Iran war the caverns holding them could be damaged
News.content:

America’s emergency oil stockpile has dropped to its lowest level in 40 years, with experts warning that ongoing withdrawals for the war with Iran could permanently damage the underground caverns holding the crude.

The warnings arrive as American drivers face unprecedented gas prices for late summer. Today’s AAA National Average for a gallon of regular gasoline sits at $4.07, marking the highest levels on record for mid-August.

Concerns over the physical limits of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve center on the unique geology of its storage network. The crude is held within 60 salt caverns thousands of feet below ground at four sites across Texas and Louisiana.

To extract crude, operators pump fresh water into the bottom of a cavern to force oil up to pipeline intakes. However, petroleum engineering professor Siddharth Misra of Texas A&M University told CNBC that repeated rapid drawdowns wash away salt walls.

This process “creates flatter, less stable roof and severely thins the critical salt pillars that separate adjacent caverns, greatly increasing the geological risk of a structural cave-in,” Misra said.

open image in gallery As the war with Iran drives America’s emergency oil stockpile to a 40-year low, energy experts warn that tapping the reserve so heavily threatens the structural integrity of its underground salt caverns ( Getty Images )

Misra noted that while 70 million barrels is the absolute threshold needed to keep intake pipes under oil rather than water, “the practical operational floor for the crude inventory is between 250 million and 300 million barrels.”

Below 300 million barrels, the risk of structural damage increases while the system loses its ability to pump oil at high speeds, as thinning oil layers allow rising sludge to reach upper intakes.

The reserve was designed to handle five full drawdowns over its lifespan. Instead, it has undergone dozens of cycles over 40 years.

Misra told CNBC that “because the system was not designed for this many cycles, the repeated injection of water and extraction of oil have caused severe cavern deformation, accelerated the rate of massive salt falls from the ceilings, and significantly weakened the overall structural integrity of the aging reserve.”

Department of Energy data released Monday showed SPR inventories dropping below 300 million barrels for the first time since the initial fill in the early 1980s. The current release of 172 million barrels will leave the reserve at roughly 243 million barrels upon completion.

Market analysts at Rapidan Energy estimated the reserve’s functional minimum sits around 170 million barrels, after which “cavern integrity and pumping infrastructure limitations argue against further draws.”

open image in gallery The Trump administration has dismissed concerns over structural damage, insisting the reserve’s salt caverns are being responsibly managed as a critical national security asset ( Reuters )

The Department of Energy rejected claims that the facilities were at risk.

Energy Department spokesman Ben Dietderich told CNBC in a statement that assertions regarding cavern collapse were false.

“The caverns are always full. All that changes is the ratio of oil and water that is filling them,” Dietderich said, asserting that the Trump administration was “responsibly managing the SPR as the critical national security asset it was designed to be.”

Worries about structural integrity have been voiced by both major political parties.

Republican lawmakers cited cavern health in 2022 when the Biden administration released 180 million barrels following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. That release dropped the SPR below 350 million barrels in 2023, before inventory was built back up to approximately 415 million barrels prior to the start of the Iran war.

Government oversight reports highlight long-standing physical strain on the facility. In a May report, the Government Accountability Office stated that “repeated partial drawdowns followed by refill can leach a single part of a cavern repeatedly, leading to undesirable shapes.”

While most caverns remained in “very good condition” after the 2022 release, the office noted that “every drawdown cycle expands cavern volume and reduces the spacing between caverns within the salt dome, which ultimately reduces their long-term viability.”

Energy Department officials previously told the accountability office they were “holding the SPR infrastructure together with ‘Band-Aids,’ and that it is uncertain how long they will hold.”

As of December 2025, more than a quarter of the reserve's capacity was unavailable due to ongoing cavern and construction outages.
