World.title: Republicans worry their chances of keeping Congress are slipping away. Inside the Trump campaign plan to change that
World.content:
President Donald Trump has finally given the green light to pour millions of dollars from his personal PAC toward boosting vulnerable Republicans in November, two people familiar with the plans told CNN, as some top campaign advisers privately acknowledge that Republicans’ chances of keeping control of both the House and Senate are dwindling.

Trump’s political team is still debating what the final dollar figure will be, though one person familiar with the discussions floated $30 million in the first tranche. Another official cautioned that the final amounts have not yet been decided. The long-awaited cash infusion is happening in the coming weeks, two people said, describing it as the first salvo in a stretch-run effort as November looms just three months away.

And it comes amid growing GOP concerns that severe headwinds over the Iran war and high gas prices could suppress voter turnout.

“There is a path where we keep the House and the Senate,” one source told CNN. “I’m not in a place today where I’m prepared to say we’re cautiously optimistic about that.”

Trump is also belatedly preparing to ratchet up his own campaigning schedule, with plans to travel at least once a week to hold a spate of rallies in battleground districts, one adviser said. His team first promised this move months ago, and Republicans have long argued it’s a crucial step to energizing MAGA voters critical to the party’s midterm chances.

“He loves to travel, but he hates to travel,” said one of his advisers, noting that domestic issues and the Iran war upended early plans to get him on the road more frequently. Trump has recently told his closest aides that he wants to be out more stumping for GOP candidates. But advisers acknowledge his enthusiasm could evaporate just as quickly.

President Donald Trump greets the audience before speaking at General Motors’ Milford Proving Grounds on July 27, 2026 in Milford, Michigan. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

“We’ll see how long that lasts,” the adviser said. “Once he’s traveling, he’s like: ‘Why am I doing this? I want to be doing other things.’”

Still, there’s widespread angst within the party that Trump has waited too long to get more directly involved. Lawmakers and operatives have privately agonized for months over the president’s reluctance to commit his vast sums to helping elect candidates across the country. The GOP is fighting to hold dozens of House districts and a handful of critical Senate seats amid voter backlash over rising prices and the deeply unpopular war in Iran — with no end in sight on either problem.

“President Trump is the unequivocal leader of the Republican party who is committed to maintaining Republicans’ majority in Congress. In just over one year, the President has made our country greater than ever before with the most secure border in American history, the largest middle-class tax cuts ever, and the lowest murder rate since 1900,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said in a statement to CNN.

“President Trump will continue to draw a sharp contrast with his commonsense agenda and the radical Democrats in Congress,” she added.

Leaning into the base

An adviser close to Trump acknowledged that, with the president’s approval ratings scraping new lows, there’s little expectation he can win over large numbers of independents and swing voters — which was part of his path to victory in critical swing states in 2024. Instead, Republicans believe their fate in November rests almost solely on turning out millions of the MAGA faithful who typically don’t vote in midterm elections.

“Without a doubt, we’ve got to make sure we get some of these voters who show up for Donald Trump in presidential elections to show up for these congressionals,” the adviser said.

But in recent months, Trump and Republicans haven’t offered much to energize their base. Congressional Republicans squandered the final weeks before the August recess fighting amongst themselves over legislation — specifically the president’s controversial elections bill that would cement federal voter ID laws and install more voting restrictions, which stands little chance of becoming law and never even made it to the Senate floor.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune watches as Trump speaks to the media as they arrive at the US Capitol to attend a closed-door luncheon with the Republican Senate Steering Committee to push his SAVE America Act on June 24 in Washington, DC. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

Congressional GOP leaders have long believed that their success in the midterms will largely hang on Trump’s ability to recreate his 2024 coalition. They need Trump to help turn out as much of his MAGA base as possible in crucial battleground turf — especially in states like Michigan, Ohio and North Carolina, which have critical House and Senate races that could determine control of Congress next January.

Republicans are defending critical blue-state seats too, like the pivotal Senate seat in Maine and several House seats in both New York and California. But the vast majority of this fall’s map is in places where Trump has already proven he can win, like in Iowa and Pennsylvania.

GOP campaign officials have also been urging their candidates from the start to lean in — not away — from Trump on the trail, according to House and Senate campaign operatives. That includes even the most centrist Republicans, like Rep. Mike Lawler, who represents a vulnerable seat in New York’s Hudson Valley and welcomed Trump this spring for a joint rally in one of the reddest parts of his district.

Lawmakers also need him to stay on message, driving out big crowds and turning on his election-year charm with talk of the GOP’s accomplishments on affordability. But Trump has made little headway in selling his domestic accomplishments — or ending a monthslong foreign war that he repeatedly vowed would only last four to six weeks.

A US Army carry team moves a transfer case containing the remains of 1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan of Ewa Beach, Hawaii, one of four US soldiers who were recently killed in the war with Iran, on Wednesday, July 22, at Dover Air Force Base, Delaware. Matt Rourke/AP

In private conversations with Trump, some advisers have sought to emphasize how significantly the war is dragging down Republicans’ chances, arguing that even voters who generally support his goals in Iran are unwilling to stomach a drawn-out conflict that’s raising prices at home.

The prospect of persistently high gas prices has particularly damaged Trump’s standing, people familiar with the internal discussions said, serving as a prominent visual reminder of an affordability crisis that many Americans feel has gotten worse under this administration.

“It’s higher prices; that’s what they’re upset about,” said one of the advisers.

Perhaps reacting to those pressures, both Vice President JD Vance and departing White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt this week started emphasizing that lowering gas prices was equally as or more important to Trump than keeping Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. That’s a shift from Trump’s frequent assertions that Tehran’s nuclear capabilities are all that matters.

“I think both goals are equally as important to the president: We want to keep gas prices low but also ensuring Iran can never get a nuclear weapon. Something he will see through no matter what,” Leavitt told reporters traveling on Air Force One Friday.

Vehicles wait to refuel at a Costco gas station in Wilmington, North Carolina, on Wednesday, July, 1. Allison Joyce/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Trump has nevertheless insisted publicly that he’s willing to prolong the war for as long as it takes to win it, downplaying the domestic impact even as he struggles to find a clear path toward achieving his aims in the Middle East.

Trump’s enthusiasm

Amid that worsening backdrop, Trump has repeatedly suggested recently that the midterms aren’t really his problem. And in addition to waving off Americans’ economic anxieties and declining to prioritize bringing an end to the Iran war, he’s also emphasized his own pet projects over the broader GOP agenda.

“I don’t have to be supporting all the people. You know, I have a busy schedule,” Trump said in an interview with Punchbowl News last week, adding: “I said to somebody, ‘I won. I’m not campaigning.’”

Those closest to the president insist he still cares deeply about ensuring Republicans win as many races in November as possible. But, one adviser cautioned, he won’t get involved in races he thinks aren’t winnable.

“He doesn’t want to carry dead carcasses across the finish line,” that person said, referencing Trump being incredibly protective of who he chooses to endorse. “He’s not going to endorse a loser and ruin his brand.”

But he does acutely understand that Democrats winning either the House or the Senate in November would have a highly negative impact on his final two years in office, they said.

“The next two years will be f*cking horrible if we lose both chambers. And Trump knows that,” that source said. Other officials have emphasized that Trump does not want to go through the same type of investigations and battles with Congress that he did during his first term, which included two impeachment trials.

Inside the midterms operation

The political operation surrounding the president consists of a tight group of loyal advisers who worked on Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign and other previous campaigns. It’s run by his former political guru, James Blair, who up until recently served as the White House deputy chief of staff for legislative, political and public affairs.

Other high-ranking members of the team include: Chris LaCivita, a co-campagin manager of Trump’s 2024 reelection campaign; Taylor Budowich, who previously ran MAGA Inc. and later led White House communications; Timothy Saylor, who previously helmed Trump’s 2024 data operations; and Tony Fabrizio, the president’s longtime pollster.

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who worked alongside LaCivita and the others throughout Trump general election campaign, continues to be heavily involved in all strategy ahead of November, the officials said.

There was a bit of a shakeup this week when Leavitt announced she’s departing her role as press secretary at the end of August, just two months before the midterms. Leavitt has long been viewed inside the West Wing as one of the president’s most effective messengers on the upcoming elections. As of Saturday morning, it was unclear when the role would be replaced.

Those on the team have described their strategy as being guided by the same principles they used to take them across the finish line in 2024. The most crucial aspect, they said, is their data operation. The president’s chief of staff will often remark to the group that everything must be driven by the extensive data they have amassed in recent years and used to energize members of Trump’s base.

White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles sits in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, in April. Nathan Howard/Reuters

“We know exactly who our voters are,” one of the president’s political operatives said. “Based on the data operation, we know how to reach them, and we know what it takes to get them off their ass.”

Trump’s advisers also cite a number of recent political wins they argue should help come November, including Republicans’ unprecedented effort to redraw congressional districts across several states, shifting a handful of seats toward the GOP and further limiting the number of races that are realistically up for grabs. That redistricting push — spurred directly by Trump — is a key reason that Republicans believe they still have a chance to keep the House.

Republicans claimed another victory after the Supreme Court struck down restrictions on the amount that official campaign committees can spend on individual candidates — a change that party operatives insist will help even up the financial arms race given the GOP has far more money than Democrats in PACs and outside groups.

“Our money’s going to go so much further,” one Republican campaign official said following the ruling. “We’re not going out there and saying we’re going to win a gazillion seats … but we feel like we’re probably in the best possible position we’ve been in.”

World.title: Egyptian, Cypriot FMs praise growing momentum in bilateral relations
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty received a phone call on Friday, August 14, 2026, from Cypriot Foreign Minister Constantinos Kombos.

The call focused on ways to advance Egyptian-Cypriot relations in light of the close partnership and continued coordination between the two countries.

The two ministers praised the growing momentum in relations between Egypt and Cyprus, as reflected in the channels of consultation between the two countries and their shared commitment to building on the progress achieved in recent years and taking bilateral cooperation to broader horizons, particularly in the economic, investment and energy sectors.

Abdelatty stressed the importance of continuing efforts to implement the agreements and memoranda of understanding signed between the two countries, translating the strength of their political relations into tangible joint projects and shared interests.

He also underscored the need to expedite the implementation of the memorandum of understanding on the employment of Egyptian workers in Cyprus.

Abdelatty further stressed the importance of continuing to develop the trilateral cooperation mechanism among Egypt, Cyprus and Greece, describing it as a successful model of regional coordination.

He called for expanding cooperation in the economic, trade, investment, energy and tourism sectors, while enhancing the role of the private sector in capitalizing on the promising opportunities offered by the partnership among the three countries.

Regarding regional developments, the two ministers exchanged views and assessments on the latest developments in the region and efforts to contain the escalation and prevent the conflict from spreading.

Abdelatty outlined Egypt’s intensive efforts and diplomatic contacts to support de-escalation efforts and promote political settlements to regional crises, stressing that the current stage requires intensified diplomatic action and concerted regional and international efforts to prevent the region from sliding into new cycles of instability.

Regarding developments related to Iran, the two ministers agreed on the importance of maintaining communication and coordination to support efforts aimed at resolving the existing disputes through diplomatic means.

They urged all parties to continue pursuing negotiations and mediation and to avoid military escalation, given the potentially serious repercussions for regional security and stability, as well as energy security, freedom of navigation, supply chains and international trade.

World.title: Egypt’s Omar Assar qualifies for WTT Europe Smash Sweden 2026
World.content:
Egyptian table tennis player Omar Assar qualified for the quarterfinal of the men’s singles at the WTT Europe Smash Sweden 2026 in Malmo, Sweden.

Assar, ranked 35th globally, advanced after defeating Denmark’s world no. 59 player 3-2 in the round of 16 on Friday.

He reached this stage after beating Hungary’s world no. 66 player 3-0 in the round of 32 on Thursday and a Chinese opponent 3-2 in the round of 64 on Monday.

Assar will face Slovenia’s world no. 15 player in the next round on Saturday.

The championship is held in Sweden from August 8 to 16.

World.title: Sisi, Zelenskyy discuss advancing bilateral ties over phone
World.content:
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi discussed with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy ways to strengthen bilateral ties across various fields, especially at the commercial and economic levels.

During a phone call initiated by Zelensky on Friday, August 14, 2026, President Sisi agreed to maintain joint cooperation for increasing joint trade exchange, while exploring existing cooperation opportunities in promising sectors to serve the interests of both countries, according to Presidential Spokesman Mohamed El-Shennawy.

The two sides also tackled the latest developments in the Middle East, where President Sisi highlighted Cairo’s ongoing efforts for de-escalating regional tensions.

In this regard, President Sisi emphasized the importance of resolving these tensions through peaceful means to maintain regional peace and stability.

President Sisi also called for concerted regional and international efforts to halt the current escalation in the region, taking into account its negative impacts on security, stability, and international trade.

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy hailed Egypt’s endeavors in this respect, saying he agrees with President Sisi’s view on the need to reduce the current escalation and tensions.

The Ukrainian president briefed President Sisi on the latest developments regarding the Russian-Ukrainian war, commending Egypt’s keenness to end the conflict.

Sisi reiterated Egypt’s position in support of a political settlement to the crisis, expressing Egypt’s readiness to support all efforts aimed at reaching a political settlement as soon as possible.

World.title: Petroleum Minister discusses speeding up phosphate fertilizer plant with Elsewedy Capital Holding
World.content:
Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources Karim Badawi discussed with Elsewedy Capital Holding Chairman Ahmed Elsewedy the latest developments and steps to accelerate the implementation of a phosphate fertilizer production plant in the Suez Canal Economic Zone.

According to a statement by the Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources on Friday, August 14, 2026, the project is being executed in partnership between the Mineral Resources and Mining Industries Authority, WadiCo and Elsewedy Capital Investment Group, as part of the State’s strategy to maximize the added value of Egypt’s mineral resources.

Badawi said the project represents an important step toward developing the exploitation of Egyptian phosphate and maximizing its economic returns by expanding local manufacturing and converting mineral resources into higher-value intermediate and final products, thereby supporting national industry and enhancing Egypt’s production and export capabilities.

The minister praised Elsewedy Capital’s participation in the industrial project, stressing that strengthening partnerships with the private sector is a key pillar in implementing manufacturing projects and maximizing the use of natural resources, while supporting the State’s efforts to localize industry and increase added value in the Egyptian economy.

During the meeting, Badawi directed that work continue to accelerate the completion of the project’s implementation procedures and address any challenges or obstacles that may arise during the implementation stages, while enhancing coordination and integration among all relevant entities to ensure adherence to the targeted timelines and accelerate progress.

He stressed that the Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources places maximizing the added value of mineral resources among its top priorities by expanding integrated industries based on Egyptian raw materials, thereby maximizing their economic returns and opening new avenues for investment, production and exports.

The project comes as part of the ministry’s efforts to shift the mining sector from the extraction and trading of raw materials toward establishing integrated downstream industries, thereby maximizing the returns from Egypt’s mineral resources and enhancing the competitiveness of Egyptian products in domestic and global markets.

World.title: Liberia: Herbalist Jailed for Frightening Woman Into Paying US7,200
World.content:
Sixty-year-old man accused of exploiting fear, traditional beliefs and threats in alleged death-scare scheme

Mobrovia-“I was hired to kill you,” was the alleged warning that turned fear into cash, that later landed 61-year-old Saah Fayiah Jr., alias Alahaji Bamba, in prison.

Liberian police say Fayiah allegedly posed as a traditional herbalist and convinced a woman, Pauline S. Zaza, a resident of Lower Margibi County, that her life was in immediate danger, before allegedly collecting US$7,200 from her through a series of demands for spiritual sacrifices.

According to a police charge sheet dated August 13, Fayiah allegedly told Madan Zaza that an unidentified man had paid him US$5,000 to kill her.

Police say Fayiah further claimed Zaza had only three days to live.

The alleged threat set in motion what investigators describe as a calculated scheme that allegedly exploited Zaza’s fear and belief in traditional spiritual intervention.

THREE-DAY DEATH WARNING

According to investigators, Zaza initially responded by sending Fayiah LD$5,000 after allegedly being told that her life was under threat.

Police say Fayiah later traveled to Fendell, where he allegedly performed what Zaza believed was a spiritual ritual.

Investigators allege that the encounter intensified the woman’s fears.

Fayiah allegedly told Zaza that spiritual forces were threatening her and that money was needed to perform sacrifices.

Among the alleged demands were funds to purchase a cow, goat and chicken.

What began with an alleged death threat would eventually result in thousands of United States dollars allegedly changing hands.

Police say Zaza ultimately paid Fayiah US$7,200 in several instalments.

But investigators allege the demands did not stop there.

ANOTHER US$3,000 DEMANDED

According to the police account, Fayiah subsequently demanded another US$3,000.

Zaza allegedly could not raise the entire amount.

Police say she managed to provide US$2,000.

Then came another demand.

Investigators alleged that on August 11, Fayiah requested an additional US$100 and instructed Zaza to meet him in Clara Town.

But this time, police say, investigators were waiting.

Fayiah was reportedly arrested during the planned meeting after Zaza had already complained to authorities.

THE WITNESS WHO FOLLOWED THE TRAIL

The investigation reportedly includes the account of Solomon Grant, a witness who told police he accompanied Zaza to meetings with Fayiah on six occasions.

Grant reportedly said Zaza believed Fayiah was a native doctor and sought his assistance because of the alleged threat against her life.

His account could become important if prosecutors seek to establish how the alleged scheme operated and how Fayiah allegedly maintained Zaza’s confidence in his claims.

FAYIAH DENIES THE ACCUSATION

Fayiah has reportedly denied the allegations.

According to police, he told investigators that his dealings with Zaza were connected to a land dispute and an effort to help her become wealthy.

He reportedly denied threatening Zaza or deceiving her into surrendering money.

But investigators say they found no evidence that Fayiah was a legitimate herbalist and no evidence supporting his alleged claim that someone had hired him to kill Zaza.

That finding raises a more troubling question at the heart of the case, how much money can fear extract from a vulnerable person when the person creating the fear presents himself as the one capable of providing salvation.

WHEN FEAR BECOMES A BUSINESS

The case highlights a sensitive issue in Liberia: the exploitation of traditional beliefs and fear for financial gain.

For many Liberians, traditional medicine and spiritual practices remain part of everyday life.

But police say the Fayiah case involves something fundamentally different, the alleged use of a fabricated threat of death to obtain money.

If proven in court, the allegations would suggest that the supposed danger was not merely a threat from an unknown attacker.

It was allegedly the foundation of the entire scheme.

The alleged message was simple, pay, or die. And each new demand allegedly came with another reason why payment was necessary.

CHARGED WITH THEFT OF PROPERTY

Fayiah has been charged with Theft of Property under Section 15.51 of Liberia’s Revised Penal Law and was forwarded to the Monrovia City Court on Friday, August 14.

The charge follows a police investigation triggered by Zaza’s complaint and culminating in Fayiah’s arrest.

He remains in custody as the legal process proceeds.

The prosecution will ultimately have to establish in court that the alleged payments were obtained through conduct that satisfies the elements of the criminal offense.

The police charge sheet represents allegations, not a judicial finding of guilt.

A CASE BEYOND US$7,200

At face value, the case is about US$7,200.

But the allegations raise a much larger concern.

If someone can allegedly convince another person that an assassin has been paid to kill her, and then allegedly position himself as the only person capable of preventing that death, where does spiritual counselling end and criminal exploitation begin?

And when fear becomes the currency, how many victims remain silent because they are embarrassed to admit they believed the threat.

For Zaza, police intervention allegedly ended the cycle on August 11.

For Fayiah, however, the next battle will be fought not through rituals or spiritual claims, but in a courtroom.

There, prosecutors will have to prove whether the frightening story that allegedly extracted thousands of dollars from a terrified woman was a genuine warning, or a carefully constructed deception designed to make money.

Fayiah has been remanded behind bars by Monrovia City Court Judge Ben Barco and he remains presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty by a court of competent jurisdiction.

World.title: Liberia National Tourism Authority and Wode Maya Conclude Two-Day Masterclass with Nearly 200 Creators
World.content:
A two-day masterclass led by Ghanaian content creator Wode Maya has concluded in Liberia, bringing together nearly 200 content creators for practical sessions on content creation, digital storytelling and the growing role of creators in promoting Liberia.

The masterclass, hosted by the Liberia National Tourism Authority (LNTA) at the Liberia Learning Center in Paynesville, was designed to equip members of Liberia’s creative community with knowledge and practical insights to strengthen their work and reach wider audiences through digital platforms.

The first day focused on content creators in general, with sessions exploring the fundamentals of creating engaging content, effective storytelling, audience building, personal branding and strategies for growing a presence across social media and other digital platforms.

The second day placed a particular focus on travel vloggers and creators, looking at how compelling digital stories can help showcase Liberia’s destinations, culture, heritage, people and tourism experiences to audiences both locally and internationally.

Speaking during the masterclass, Wode Maya stressed the importance of authenticity, consistency and purpose in content creation, encouraging participants to see their platforms as more than just spaces for entertainment.

“Content creators have the power to change the way people see a country. Liberia has so many stories, places and experiences that the world needs to discover, and creators have a responsibility to tell those stories in an authentic and engaging way,” Wode Maya said.

He encouraged creators to take advantage of the opportunities offered by digital platforms to build their personal brands while using their influence to contribute to the promotion of Liberia’s tourism potential.

Participants also explored the importance of authenticity and consistency in content creation, as well as the potential for creators to contribute to Liberia’s tourism promotion by presenting the country through fresh and engaging perspectives.

For participants, the masterclass provided an opportunity to gain new skills, exchange ideas and learn from an experienced content creator with a wide audience across Africa and beyond.

“This masterclass reminded us that the stories we tell can go beyond our individual platforms. We have an opportunity to use our creativity to showcase Liberia, highlight what makes our country unique and connect our stories with audiences beyond our borders,” said Maureen Jennifer Davies, a participant in the masterclass.

The programme also featured a panel discussion bringing together voices from Liberia’s creative space. Panelists shared their experiences, discussed opportunities and challenges within the industry, and examined how stronger collaboration between creators and the tourism sector could contribute to the promotion of Liberia.

The discussions highlighted the growing importance of digital storytelling in tourism promotion, particularly as social media and other digital platforms increasingly influence how people discover destinations, explore travel experiences and decide where to visit.

The masterclass comes at a time when digital platforms are playing an increasingly important role in how destinations are discovered, experienced and perceived, placing content creators at the centre of conversations about Liberia’s image and tourism potential.

With nearly 200 creators participating, the two-day programme not only provided a platform for learning and knowledge-sharing but also underscored the growing potential of Liberia’s creative community to help tell the country’s tourism story and take it to audiences around the world.

World.title: BCHT, Administration And Caucus Dedicate Baryatah Clinic and Bridge in District Two
World.content:
GBARGA, Bong County — At long last, Bong County Health Team, in collaboration with the County Administration and Legislative Caucus, has finally dedicated the newly completed Baryatah Clinic and Bridge in Jorquelleh District #2, with officials describing the projects as significant investments in healthcare delivery and road connectivity.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

The Bridge and Clinic projects were allocated under the 2018–2019 County Social Development Fund and national Budget Respectively through the efforts of former District Two Representative now Senator Prince Kermue Moye Sr. However, both projects faced significant delays over the years due to what many described as political interplays.

The dedication of the two facilities on Friday, August 14, 2026, is expected to improve access to essential healthcare services and ease transportation for residents of Baryatah and surrounding communities.

Speaking at the ceremony, Bong County Health Administrator Sam Siakor said the opening of the Baryatah Clinic followed sustained efforts by the County Health Team, local authorities and community members despite delays that affected the project.

Siakor attributed some of the delays to funding and administrative challenges but expressed appreciation to the contractor and other stakeholders for helping to bring the project to completion. He also commended Bong County Senator Prince Kermue Moye for securing funding through the national budget to support health infrastructure in the county.

Siakor disclosed that the County Health Team is also preparing to begin construction of the long-stalled Leleh Clinic project, with the procurement process completed and a contractor identified. He said Loitor Construction Company, managed by sons of the county, is expected to undertake the construction once the remaining administrative processes are completed.

In a special statement, Bong County Senator Prince Kermue Moye said the dedication of the Baryatah Clinic and Bridge demonstrates that development projects can be completed despite political and administrative challenges.

Moye said there had been doubts about whether the Bayatah Clinic would be opened and whether the bridge would be constructed, but noted that the completion of both projects has now demonstrated the commitment of the county’s leadership to development.

He said the Baryatah Clinic will help improve access to healthcare for residents of District #2, particularly women and children. The Senator, however, described the facility as an initial intervention and pledged to work with health authorities to provide additional infrastructure, including a maternal waiting facility and staff quarters.

Moye also disclosed that US$75,000 has been allocated in the current national budget for the completion and expansion of the Leleh Clinic. He said the funding will be accessed through the County Health Team to facilitate construction work on the project.

The Senator further pledged to pursue the construction of additional clinics in the district, describing the expansion of healthcare infrastructure as a priority for District #2.

On the Bayatah Bridge, Moye said its completion will improve movement and connectivity for residents and surrounding communities. He said the bridge is expected to facilitate easier access to markets, schools, healthcare facilities and other essential services, particularly for residents who previously faced transportation challenges.

Moye said the Baryatah Clinic and Bridge form part of his broader development agenda for District #2, which includes investments in healthcare, education, youth development and other public infrastructure.

Earlier, an official of the County Health Team, Gabriel S. Nyangwebah, announced the health personnel assigned to the newly dedicated Baryatah Clinic. Andrew T. Willie was named Officer-in-Charge, while Lorpu Paye and Gbasene Hill were assigned as Registered Midwives and Moses Tokpah as Registered Nurses.

Other staff include Silors Yarkpawolo and Joseph Emmanuel, Vaccinators; Tarwor Martin, Registrar; Aaron S. Dolo, Dispenser; Lorpu Yarkpawolo, Cleaner; and Seiweiyan Solomon, Security.

Speaking on behalf of Bong County Superintendent Loleyah Hawa Norris, County Human Resources Officer Marline Jarwoe thanked Senator Moye, the County Health Team and other stakeholders for their contributions to the projects.

Jarwoe called for continued cooperation among local leaders, health authorities and residents to sustain development initiatives across the county. She also urged health workers assigned to the Bayatah Clinic to demonstrate professionalism, compassion and commitment in providing services to patients.

Jarwoe cautioned health workers against distractions while attending to patients, emphasizing the importance of giving every patient adequate attention and care.

The dedication of the Bayatah Clinic and Bridge marks another addition to Bong County’s public infrastructure and is expected to strengthen healthcare delivery while improving transportation and connectivity for communities in District #2.

World.title: Saudi Rice Case: Kemayah, Co-Defendants Prepare to Face Trial Amid Strong Denials
World.content:
MONROVIA – Former Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah and 12 other former government officials are set to face trial Monday, August 17, in Criminal Court “C” over allegations surrounding the handling of Saudi-donated rice intended for disaster victims.

By: Willie N. Tokpah

But as the long-awaited trial approaches, the defendants have consistently rejected the central allegations against them, insisting that the indictment does not establish criminal responsibility and that the evidence should be tested in open court.

The case concerns 29,412 bags of 25-kilogram rice donated by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in April 2023 for vulnerable and disaster-affected Liberians.

Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Taskforce, AREPT, alleged that 25,054 bags, valued at approximately US$425,918, were unlawfully diverted, misapplied or distributed without proper authorization.

Kemayah, however, has maintained that he did not steal, receive or personally benefit from the humanitarian rice.

Following his arrest in June 2025, he described the government’s action as a “public witch-hunt” and questioned the strength of the evidence against him. He called for the case to be handled through a fair and transparent judicial process.

Kemayah’s Defense: No Control Over Saudi Funds

Kemayah’s position received additional attention after he noted that documents showed that the financial component of the Saudi humanitarian assistance was handled directly by the Saudi humanitarian authorities and the vendor, Fouta Corporation.

He noted that the documents indicated that the rice was supplied as humanitarian assistance rather than being purchased with funds placed under Kemayah’s personal or ministerial control,” noting, “Fouta Corporation correspondence also showed payments originating from the Saudi side.”

Further accounts indicated that Kemayah participated in the public handover and distribution process alongside government officials and Saudi representatives.

According to those accounts, he instructed officials that the rice should benefit vulnerable Liberians and should not be taken for personal use by public officials.

Those developments have become an important part of the defence narrative as the former minister prepares to answer allegations that he participated in the diversion of the rice.

The indictment nevertheless alleged that Kemayah and other officials held meetings concerning the rice and that Kemayah influenced the transfer of 13,895 bags from the National Disaster Management Agency to the General Services Agency. Prosecutors say that action improperly interfered with NDMA’s statutory responsibility for disaster assistance.

Those allegations remain accusations.

They have not been established as facts by a court.

Mary Broh Also Rejects Allegations

Similarly, Former GSA Director-General Mary T. Broh, another prominent defendant, has since also strongly rejected the government’s case.

Broh reportedly described the indictment as “sad and laughable” and said she had no history of corruption during her years in public service. She further maintained that documents being relied upon by investigators had already been provided to the government.

Broh also threatened legal action against the Government of Liberia over what she considered defamatory allegations contained in the government’s case.

Her position, like Kemayah’s, is that the allegations must be subjected to evidence and judicial scrutiny rather than treated as established wrongdoing.

Wayfa Ciapha Challenges Investigation

Another defendant, Wayfa F. Ciapha, has also mounted a detailed defense.

Ciapha, identified by prosecutors as the purported CEO of the Group of Seventy-Seven, publicly declared: “I did not steal or mismanage any rice.”

She reportedly submitted a 48-page defense explaining the movement of the rice and tracing the distribution process through government institutions, including the Vice President’s Office, NDMA and GSA.

Her position directly challenges AREPT’s assertion that the rice was distributed through an unauthorized conspiracy.

From Arrest and Prison to Courtroom

The case first generated attention in June 2025 when law enforcement arrested several of the defendants following the issuance of the indictment.

Kemayah, Broh and former NDMA Executive Director Henry O. Williams were among those arrested and taken before Criminal Court “C.” They were subsequently transferred to the Monrovia Central Prison, where they spent several hours before being released.

The defendants were released after their lawyers secured arrangements involving human sureties rather than conventional cash bonds.

A court arrangement allowed the accused to remain at liberty while the case proceeded through the judicial process.

The detention generated considerable political and public reaction.

Kemayah’s political party, the Movement for Economic Empowerment, condemned his arrest and characterized the action as politically motivated and undemocratic.

The former minister himself maintained that his detention did not establish guilt and insisted that the government should prove its allegations through evidence.

Trial Finally Set to Begin

After more than a year of legal proceedings and delays, Criminal Court “C” ruled on August 11, 2026, that the case should proceed to trial.

The proceedings are scheduled to begin at 9:00 a.m. on Monday, August 17.

The defendants face charges including theft of property, economic sabotage, misuse of public money, property or records, illegal disbursement and expenditure of public money, misapplication of entrusted property, abuse of office and criminal conspiracy.

The prosecution’s case will seek to establish that the defendants collectively participated in the unlawful diversion or misapplication of the donated rice.

For Kemayah and his co-defendants, however, the trial will provide their opportunity to challenge the allegations through evidence, cross-examination and legal argument.

AREPT has described the proceedings as an important stage in Liberia’s asset-recovery campaign, saying investigations and indictments must ultimately be subjected to judicial scrutiny before criminal responsibility and possible restitution can be determined.

The Taskforce has also said it remains committed to due process, defendants’ rights and judicial independence.

World.title: International Youth Day 2026 Unites Young African Leaders Around Common Aspirations
World.content:
Cllr. Charlyne M. Brumskine, Judge of the ECOWAS Court served as a special guest.

On August 12, 2026, over 100 young political and civic leaders from across Africa gathered for a two-hour hybrid celebration of International Youth Day under the theme, “Different Contexts, Common Aspirations.”

Hosted by Naymote Partners for Democratic Development and the Young Political Leadership School Africa (YPLS Africa), in collaboration with the African Democratic Alliance for Freedom and Progress (ADAFP), the event was broadcast live from the Democracy Innovation Hub in Monrovia, Liberia. More than 100 participants joined online, while 12 attended in person.

Opening the program, Eddie D. Jarwolo, Executive Director of Naymote and Secretary-General of ADAFP, emphasized the importance of creating opportunities for young Africans to connect, exchange experiences, and actively shape the continent’s future.

Hon. Nobuntu Hlazo-Webster, Deputy President of Build One South Africa and Member of the South African Parliament, offered practical insights on youth representation and leadership in democratic institutions. She challenged participants to recognize their power and responsibility:

“Nobody is coming to save you but you. You have so much power and resources at your disposal. I encourage you to leverage that power to change our continent.”

Alphia Faith Kemokai, Manager of YPLS Africa and Global Democracy Fellow, shared lessons from her work with emerging political and civic leaders across the continent, while YPLS Africa alumna Kadiatu Koroma spoke on “Values That Count Across Different Contexts: Leading Toward Our Common Aspirations.”

Special Guest Cllr. Charlyne M. Brumskine, Judge of the ECOWAS Court of Justice and former vice-presidential candidate of Liberia, encouraged participants to translate their aspirations into purposeful leadership, integrity, civic responsibility, and practical action. She declared:

“To every young person who boards a boat, gets on an airplane to another country, or crosses boundaries, there is a verdict on my leadership and on your leadership. Your charge is to make staying in Africa an act of opportunity, not an act of sacrifice.”

Moderated by Cameroonian media practitioner and YPLS Africa alumna Njix Sharon Nabeseh, the discussion examined the diverse political, social, and economic realities confronting young Africans. Participants identified the aspirations that unite them with dignity, opportunity, inclusion, economic security, accountable leadership, and meaningful participation in shaping their countries and continent.

The event also strengthened engagement with the emerging Continental Young Forum of Political Parties, a platform created to unit young members of political parties across Africa, an initiative of ADAFP and YPLS Africa that connects young political leaders across national, institutional, and partisan boundaries.

Through interactive discussions, participants exchanged experiences, raised questions, and explored opportunities for cross-border learning, networking, and collaboration.

The celebration reaffirmed a clear message: Africa’s young people may live in different contexts, but they share common aspirations and a collective responsibility to shape the continent’s future.

Different Contexts. Common Aspirations. One Generation. One Africa.

World.title: Liberia: Prophet Key Walks Free, Says Prison Experience Rehabilitated Him After Six-Month Contempt Sentence
World.content:
MONROVIA — Justin Oldpa Yeazehn, popularly known as “Prophet Key,” has regained his freedom after spending six months at the Monrovia Central Prison following a contempt conviction by the Supreme Court of Liberia.

By Webster Clayeh

Upon his release, Prophet Key said his time behind bars had changed him, describing the experience as a period of rehabilitation and personal transformation.

He also indicated that he had been relocated following his release, suggesting that his return to society would be accompanied by a deliberate effort to distance himself from some of the circumstances and conduct that preceded his imprisonment.

His release brings to an end one of the most closely followed contempt cases involving a Liberian social media personality in recent years. The case attracted widespread public attention after the Supreme Court took action against Yeazehn over statements made against Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay, members of the judiciary and the Chief Justice’s mother.

The Supreme Court sentenced Yeazehn on February 13, 2026, after he appeared before the Full Bench and admitted wrongdoing while appealing to the justices for mercy.

The Court found his conduct contemptuous and damaging to the dignity and authority of the judiciary. Its official record says the proceedings arose from a podcast in which Yeazehn accused the Chief Justice and Associate Justices of corruption and directed derogatory and vulgar remarks at the judiciary.

The sentence was not limited to imprisonment. The Court also ordered Prophet Key to publish an apology in three local newspapers for five consecutive days and to execute a bond committing himself to refrain from the kind of insulting and inflammatory language that had brought him before the Court.

Reports on the judgment said the apology was directed to the Chief Justice, Associate Justices, judges, magistrates and the judiciary generally, as well as Liberian women whom he had previously insulted.

In the months that followed, the controversial social media personality appeared to move from confrontation to contrition. A handwritten apology dated July 28 surfaced publicly in early August, in which he expressed regret for accusing members of the judiciary of corruption without proof. He also apologized to Liberian women for his offensive remarks and pledged not to repeat such conduct.

That apology became an important part of the public narrative surrounding his anticipated release. While supporters focused on the expiration of the six-month custodial sentence, questions emerged over whether every requirement attached to the Supreme Court’s judgment had been satisfied and whether the prison authorities had received the necessary legal authorization to release him.

Although August 13 had widely been identified as the date on which Prophet Key would complete his six-month sentence, he did not walk out of the Monrovia Central Prison that day.

The delay was linked to the fact that his imprisonment originated directly from an order of the Supreme Court. Current reports indicate that the prison authorities were awaiting a formal release order from the Court before they could discharge him. In other words, the expiration of the custodial period did not, by itself, result in an immediate physical release because the institution holding him required the appropriate judicial authorization.

That distinction became the center of public debate on August 13, with supporters gathering around the prison expecting his release while the necessary documentation had apparently not yet reached the correctional authorities. Reports later indicated that the Supreme Court issued the release order on August 14, clearing the way for his departure from custody.

World.title: Liberia: President Boakai Signs Port Decentralization Bill in Middle of Biggest Drug Crisis
World.content:
A year ago, the Liberian president said breaking up Liberia’s ports would risk the country’s maritime security. This week, with a mystery vessel case still unresolved and a cocaine scandal reaching his own drug chief, he signed the bill anyway — and left the question of who’s watching the new ports unanswered.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia – President Joseph Boakai has signed into law the legislation dismantling the National Port Authority’s decades-long monopoly, ending centralized control of Liberia’s ports and handing operational power to autonomous boards in Monrovia, Buchanan, Greenville and Harper under a newly created Independent Seaport and Inland Ports Regulatory Authority.

What is not yet clear is whether the final law includes the safeguards needed to keep four newly independent ports from becoming easier targets for drug traffickers than the single, centralized system it replaces.

The President had twice vetoed earlier versions of this legislation, citing legal conflicts, overlapping regulatory mandates, and risks to Liberia’s international maritime security obligations; the Senate responded by revising and repassing the bill, and the president has now signed the revised version. The timing is difficult to overstate: the signing comes as Liberia remains consumed by its largest drug scandal in years, one that has already produced a record $317 million cocaine seizure, criminal charges against an LDEA officer and a Paynesville bar owner, the recusal of the LDEA’s own acting chief over an unresolved vehicle allegation, and months of unanswered questions about a mystery vessel, the IB Atlantic IV, that first exposed how little visibility Liberia’s port and maritime system has over what moves through it.

A Reversal, Not Just a Signature

Somewhere in the Executive Mansion this week, a pen crossed a line the president himself drew twice before. That is what makes this signing newsworthy — not simply that a major piece of legislation became law, but that the man signing it is the same man who, on two separate occasions, told the Legislature in writing that it was not ready to pass. Boakai’s earlier vetoes of the port decentralization and autonomy bills were not procedural throat-clearing. He cited legal conflicts between the new port boards and existing regulatory bodies, overlapping mandates that risked institutional confusion, fragmentation of executive oversight, and — most pointedly, given everything that has happened since — risks to Liberia’s international maritime security obligations. Those were not small concerns when he raised them, and nothing about the summer that followed made them smaller. What changed, in the end, was not the risk. It was the political weather around it — enough pressure to pass some version of port reform that it eventually outweighed the president’s own stated reservations, at least enough to move his hand to the page.

An Eighteen-Month Runway

Two details emerged after the signing that reshape, without resolving, the questions surrounding it. The Minister of State, Samuel A. Stevequoah, confirmed to FrontPageAfrica that President Boakai signed the bill on the advice of the Minister of Justice — a detail that matters given the Justice Ministry’s own past warnings about the legislation’s legal conflicts, and one that suggests the administration’s internal legal objections were addressed, or at least set aside, before the president put pen to paper.

FrontPageAfrica has also confirmed that the legislation carries an 18-month transitional clause, meaning the new decentralized port structure will not actually take effect until 2028. That transition period cuts two ways, and which way it ultimately cuts is now the real story. Read generously, an 18-month runway is exactly the kind of window FrontPageAfrica previously argued was missing from the original, undelayed version of the bill — time to build a unified maritime security and counternarcotics framework before four independent ports go live, rather than discovering the gaps after the fact. Read skeptically, an 18-month delay is also a convenient way to defuse the immediate political pressure of signing security-sensitive legislation in the middle of a cocaine scandal, without requiring the administration to specify, today, what it plans to do with the time. Nothing announced alongside the signing indicates which of those two readings is closer to the truth. The next 18 months, not this week’s signature, will settle it.

What the Law Actually Does

The legislation ends the National Port Authority’s roughly 70-year monopoly over Liberia’s seaports, replacing centralized control with autonomous, county-based port boards responsible for the Freeport of Monrovia and the ports of Buchanan, Greenville and Harper. Overseeing the new structure is an Independent Seaport and Inland Ports Regulatory Authority, intended to regulate the newly decentralized system rather than run it directly. Supporters have framed the change as a long-overdue correction to decades of Monrovia-centered control that left Liberia’s secondary ports starved of investment and local say over infrastructure sitting in their own backyards — a legitimate grievance this newspaper has acknowledged even while warning against the timing of this fix.

The Missing Safety Net

Here is the question nobody in Monrovia seems eager to answer out loud, and it happens to be the one that matters most given the year Liberia has just had: does the final version of this law include anything resembling a unified maritime security and counter-narcotics framework spanning all four newly independent ports, or does security oversight now sit as fragmented as everything else the bill decentralizes? Neither the legislative history nor the president’s own remarks upon signing, as reported so far, make that clear one way or the other. A port system split four ways multiplies the number of doors traffickers can walk through, and multiplies the number of agencies each with a plausible-sounding answer for why detecting the next shipment wasn’t quite their job — precisely the dynamic this newspaper warned about when it urged caution on this bill last month, before the president had signed it and before the IB Atlantic IV had become a household name in Liberia’s drug scandal.

The mystery vessel case is not incidental background here; it is the clearest evidence available that Liberia’s current, centralized port and maritime security apparatus already struggles to answer basic questions about what is moving through its own waters. A ship sat off Liberia’s coast for the better part of a week before anyone acted, tied by a rejected letter to a now-dismissed RIA official, eventually chased by AFL boats that turned out to be too small to catch it once it ran for open water. If a single, centralized system produced that outcome, the burden was always on this bill’s supporters to explain, convincingly and in public, why four separate, newly formed authorities would do better rather than worse. Nobody has offered that explanation yet, at least not one this newspaper has been able to find.

Signed Amid the Worst Possible Timing

Whatever the merits of port decentralization as policy, the timing of this signature could hardly have landed at a more uncomfortable moment. Liberia is currently working through the fallout of a record $317 million cocaine seizure in Duazon, on top of a $19.2 million bust at Roberts International Airport in June. LDEA officer Moses Jallah and Paynesville bar owner George Harris are facing prosecution. The LDEA’s own Officer-in-Charge, Fitzgerald Biago, has recused himself from the investigation amid allegations he accepted vehicles from a bar owner tied to the case, with President Boakai personally giving the Minister of Justice 48 hours to report on the matter. Senator Amara Konneh has taken to calling the whole affair “Cocainegate.” Signing a bill that fragments port oversight into four pieces, in the middle of a scandal that has repeatedly exposed how poorly Liberia’s existing, unified institutions have policed themselves, is the kind of decision that will be read by critics as tone-deaf regardless of the bill’s underlying merits — and the administration has offered little public messaging so far to counter that reading.

What Critics Warned

Opposition to the bill was neither quiet nor limited to the presidency. Representative Musa Hassan Bility condemned the Legislature’s handling of the reform, calling the Port Autonomy Law “improper” and “dangerous.” The head of the Liberia Revenue Authority separately urged Boakai to reject the bill again, warning of revenue risks and unresolved legal conflicts between the new port authorities and existing agencies. Those warnings were about institutional and fiscal risk more than security specifically, but they reinforce the same underlying picture: a piece of legislation that even before its security implications are considered, drew sustained warnings from officials inside the government about how much this reform could go wrong in the execution.

The Question Nobody’s Answered

None of this means port decentralization was the wrong idea in principle, and FrontPageAfrica has said as much before. Buchanan, Greenville and Harper have real grievances about decades of Monrovia-centered control, and those grievances deserve a serious legislative answer eventually. But “eventually” and “in the middle of the country’s worst drug scandal in years, with the underlying security gaps still unaddressed” are not the same moment, and the president’s own vetoes once made exactly that argument. What Liberians deserve now, at minimum, is a clear public accounting from the administration of what changed between the version Boakai rejected and the version he signed — specifically, what safeguards, if any, will exist by 2028 to keep four independent ports from being four times as vulnerable as the single system that just spent a summer failing to catch a ship sitting in plain view off its own coast. The 18-month transition period is, in effect, the administration’s own self-imposed deadline for answering that question. Until it does, the safest assumption is the least reassuring one: that the law changed, and the vulnerability it was meant to address is being left for 2028 to sort out.

World.title: How a Liberia “Cartel” Took a 71-Year-old Canadian $100k
World.content:
A Canadian retiree’s search for African gold turned into a months-long con involving fake shipping companies, a phony “minister,” strongbox theater, and a scheme so elaborate he compares it to “an academy award performance.”

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia – Gerry Pettle wants one thing understood before anything else: he isn’t writing to embarrass himself.



“I am writing you on the advice of two friends of your country,” the 71-year-old Canadian says in a note to FrontPageAfrica explaining why he’s going public, “and not necessarily in agreement to make this complaint a public humiliation of myself.” He calls himself “a Canadian, born young fellow at the age of 71” — a wry touch from a man who, by his own account, was taken for more than $100,000 USD by a network of scammers in Liberia over the course of several months this year.

It started, as these things often do, with a friend of a friend.



A Favor from Sam



Pettle knew a man named Sam Berkel, who in turn knew a man named Paul — a Liberian expatriate originally from Toronto. Paul, Sam said, had a way to get gold out of Liberia. Pettle now calls it what it was: “a scheme.” At the time, he had no reason to doubt it.



Paul asked Pettle and Sam for $20,000 to secure a shipment of gold he’d bring back to Toronto himself. The two split the cost and wired the money in installments — a few thousand dollars a day, spread out to avoid suspicion. The gold never arrived. Paul never flew back. When Pettle finally reached him, the excuses began: a delay, then another delay, then the claim that Paul himself had been robbed — the gold and the money “switched” out from under him by unnamed thieves.



It should have ended there. It didn’t.



The Dubai Pitch



A week later, Paul had a new plan: he’d have a kilo of gold worked into jewelry and meet Pettle in Dubai, where Pettle could collect it, pay off the man Paul supposedly owed, and recoup his original $20,000 plus a profit. The cost of entry this time was smaller — $3,500 for airfare and jewelry-making — but the outcome was the same. The money vanished. So, for a while, did Paul.



When Paul resurfaced, he offered something even more improbable: a stranger claiming to have millions in marked American cash that needed “washing” for a fee. Pettle refused outright. “Paul, F off,” he recalls telling him. “You’re mental.”



Two days later, Paul was back on the phone with yet another connection — a man with a diplomatic passport, capable of moving gold across borders without permits. Paul said he didn’t trust the man directly but knew someone who did: a fixer who went by “Boylan,” whose real name, Pettle later learned, was Jensen Gonkarnue.



Boylan, Peter, and the Compound



Jensen — “Boylan” — called Pettle personally, addressing him warmly as “Doc.” He vouched for a Liberian gold trader named Peter John, describing a house near the residence of Liberia’s president as proof of legitimacy. On a call, Peter told Pettle he had hundreds of kilos of gold sourced from local miners and sent a photograph appearing to show roughly a thousand kilos stacked on a floor. All Pettle had to do, Peter said, was cover the shipping tax.



It was the first of many taxes.



Pettle sent $12,500 by USDT for the initial tax. Then came a $14,500 charge for air freight and insurance to a company calling itself Noble Shipping — complete with an invoice and a bank routing number, giving Pettle, for the first time, something resembling a paper trail. He and a new partner, Robert, paid it. The package, he was told, was on its way.



It was around this time a second trader, a man named Ben, contacted Pettle claiming to have five kilos of his own gold and to have heard of Pettle’s reputation through a woman named Bernice. A pattern was forming — taxes, shipping fees, insurance, one new stranger after another — but Pettle, already deep in, kept going.

Flying to Liberia



By the time Pettle boarded a flight to Liberia in June, he had lost thousands and gained nothing but promises. He was met at the airport by Boylan, carrying a single assayed kilo of gold as “collateral” against the money already spent.



The next day brought a scene Pettle still describes in almost cinematic terms: a drive down a rough, barely marked road to a barbed-wire compound, a honked horn, a gate that opened and closed behind the car, a second gate, and finally a run-down exterior giving way to a surprisingly polished interior — televisions, desks, a busy office floor.



There, in the office of a man identified only as “Mr. Hill,” security guards produced strongboxes belonging to Peter and Ben. Each man opened his own box with his own key, revealing, Pettle says, ten kilos in one and thirty in the other. Then two more men — introduced as Moses and Patrick — arrived unannounced with five kilos of their own.



Pettle agreed to take five kilos total, combined from all three sources, with Peter — who held a diplomatic passport — set to fly back to Canada with him and the gold. The running total by then was roughly $68,000.



Then came the final charges: $6,000 to expedite an “expired” export license, and additional tax for the extra kilos, bringing the total to nearly $29,000 more. Robert wired it. Everyone, Pettle recalls, seemed satisfied when the meeting ended.



The Passport Standoff



Afterward, Peter asked for the one kilo Pettle was still holding as collateral. Pettle refused — it was the only tangible thing he had for his money. He offered a trade instead: the gold for Peter’s passport, so that if he’d been cheated, he’d at least have a photograph to bring to authorities. Peter refused and left angrily.



Days later, a man named Elijah Teahjay — who Pettle says “looked the most legitimate” of everyone he’d met — invited him to a second compound, even more polished than the first, complete with flags and a formal reception area. There, armed guards wheeled in a case holding what Pettle estimates was 300 kilos of gold and told him to take his pick. The new deal: $24,000 up front, $110,000 per kilo on delivery in Canada, payable within 72 hours. The gold, Elijah assured him, would simply be handed to him after customs. “We do it all the time,” he said.



The Man in the Yellow Shirt



The unraveling began with a knock at Pettle’s hotel room door. A representative from Noble Shipping arrived unannounced with an official-looking export license and a new tax bill — $21,000, then, minutes later, a second bill for $27,500. When Pettle tried to photograph the documents, the man blocked his camera, insisting they weren’t his to keep, even though he’d paid for them.



Suspicious, Pettle called Elijah and sent him a photo of the receipt, threatening to involve police if it wasn’t legitimate. Within minutes, a large man in a yellow shirt appeared at the hotel, identifying himself as “Todd” — Liberia’s minister of minerals, he claimed, though he carried no badge, only a worn business card.



What followed, Pettle says, played out “like the end of a lousy movie”: Todd confronted the Noble Shipping representative in front of him, questioned him about the missing export license, and asked Pettle to get into a car. Pettle refused to get in fully, kept one foot on the pavement, and agreed only to meet again the next morning. Within minutes of that encounter ending, his phone lit up with calls from what felt like a dozen different people connected to the scheme, all anxious to know why he’d mentioned police.



Getting Out



By his final night in Liberia, Pettle believed he might be in real danger. As far as the network knew, he’d genuinely gone to authorities. A woman named Grace — another gold contact who’d surfaced days earlier — offered to come collect him from the hotel. He nearly accepted, then reconsidered: if Grace was part of the same web, leaving with her might not be safe either. Instead, a hotel worker moved him quietly to a different room for the night. He slept, and the next morning, he left the country.



An Unlikely Postscript



Pettle did file a report with local police — six officers, he says, took his statement and had him sign it. What strikes him most, looking back, is what they never asked for: the names of the men involved, which he had; the passport used, which he had; or a single phone number from the dozens who called him during the ordeal.



“This is the beginning of a dormant complaint,” Pettle writes. But his closing line is the one that lingers: despite everything, he says his real ambition is still “to come back and bring investment to your beautiful country” — if Liberia will have him.

World.title: Kitwe derby to headline transition season pool A ‎
World.content:
The Kitwe derby between record Super Division champions Nkana FC and defending champions Power Dynamos will headline Pool A of the 2026 MTN Super League Transition Season.

‎

‎The Zambian Premier League has announced that the Transition Season will be divided into two streams based on final positions from the 2025/26 season.

‎

‎ Teams that finished in odd-numbered positions form one stream, while even-numbered teams make up the other.

‎

‎The new campaign will kick off on the weekend of 2 and 4 October 2026.

‎

‎The start date was moved from the previously announced 12 September to accommodate continental commitments for Red Arrows and Power Dynamos.

‎

‎Record champions Nkana FC will begin their campaign away to newly promoted Trident FC at Sentinel Ground on 3 October 2026.

‎

‎Other teams in Pool A alongside Nkana and Power include: FC MUZA, Kansanshi Dynamos, Konkola Blades, Makeni All Stars, Trident FC, NAPSA Stars, Zanaco and Nchanga Rangers.

‎

‎Copperbelt giants Zesco United are in Pool B alongside Kabwe Warriors, Red Arrows, Roan United, Nkwazi, Mutondo Stars, Chirundu, Green Eagles and Green Buffaloes.

‎

‎The winners of Pool A and Pool B will eventually meet in a Championship Playoff Final.

‎

‎The winner of that final will be recognised and recorded as the 2026 Transition Season Super League Champion.

‎

‎Meanwhile, football analyst Bwezani Mbewe says the Transition Season will be a test of squad depth and recovery, with 18 matches squeezed into less than four months.

‎

‎“We finally have a clearer picture of what the 2026 MTN Super League Transition Season will look like, and one thing immediately jumps out: this is going to be short, sharp and demanding. There will be very little room for the traditional slow start.”

‎

‎The analyst pointed to December as particularly demanding, with matches scheduled around 5/6 December, 9/10 December, 19/20 December and 23/24 December before teams return on 2/3 January.

‎

‎“There is hardly a Christmas break in football terms. This format will not only test the best starting XI. It will test benches, recovery, travelling arrangements, medical departments and how coaches rotate their players.”

‎

‎He warned that a bad run of three matches could be very expensive because there is not enough time to recover points.

‎

‎Mbewe also noted that the ZPL has warned that fixtures remain subject to change due to broadcast schedules, international windows, CAF inter-club competitions, FAZ Cup fixtures and other unforeseen circumstances.

‎

‎“This Transitional League will reward teams that start quickly and, perhaps even more importantly, teams with enough depth to survive the schedule. The teams that manage their squads, travel and recovery properly may ultimately be the ones standing strongest at the end.”

World.title: UPND clinches Nakonde as NRPUP grabs Mwenzo constituency seat
World.content:
The United Party for National Development (UPND) has scooped the Nakonde Parliamentary seat while under the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) has won the newly created Mwenzo Constituency in Nakonde District, Muchinga Province.

Nakonde Constituency Returning Officer Mulekwa Matebele declared UPND’s Simon Simwanza duly elected after he polled 8,270 votes.

Announcing the results, Mr Matebele said Michael Kanyanya of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) came second with 7,128 votes, while Yizukanji Siwanzi of Citizens First (CF) obtained 391 votes.

Mr Mulekwa said 16,156 votes were cast, with 367 ballots rejected.

“I Matebele Mulekwa being the returning officer for Nakonde Constituency in Nakonde District do hereby declare that I have in accordance with the law counted the votes of the poll in the said constituency and that they have been given to: Siwanzi Yizukanji – Citizens First (CF) 391 Kanyanya Michael – National Reconciliation for Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) 7,128. Simwanza Simon United Party for National Development (UPND) 8270,” Mr Matebele announced.

“I further declare that a total of 367 ballot papers have been rejected as invalid and a total of 16156 were cast. Therefore, I declare that the said Simwanza Simon to be the duly elected Member of Parliament for Nakonde Constituency voted this day 15 August 2026,” he announced.

Speaking after being declared winner, MP-elect for Nakonde Constituency Simon Simwanza thanked God and President Hakainde Hichilema for the support given to him.

Mr Simwanza said the people of Nakonde have demonstrated maturity in choosing leaders, and pledged to address key challenges affecting the district.

He cited poor road infrastructure, inadequate clean water and sanitation as some of the major concerns.

He said areas along Kanyala Road recorded high voter turnout due to the poor state of the road, which links Nakonde to Malawi and is critical for trade.

“We will not disappoint the people of Nakonde. We will work beyond our limitations to ensure that the challenges raised are addressed,” he said.

Mr Simwanza served as Old Fife Ward Councillor from 2016 to 2021.

He previously contested the Nakonde Parliamentary seat in 2021 on the UPND ticket but lost to Luka Simumba of the then ruling Patriotic Front, who served as MP from 2021 to 2026.

Meanwhile, in Mwenzo Constituency, Mr Simumba made a comeback to Parliament after he was declared winner by Returning Officer Hastings Kaira.

Mr Kaira said Simumba polled 9,002 votes defeating UPND’s Nathan Siame who got 4,075 votes.

Mwenzo Constituency is a newly created constituency curved out of Nakonde Constituency following the delimitation exercise.

The verification and totaling of results at both centres was conducted in the presence of stakeholders, party agents and observers.

Voting in both Nakonde and Mwenzo constituencies closed at 18:00 hours on Thursday 13 August 2026 and counting of ballots commenced at polling stations before results were conveyed to the totaling centers.

The Nakonde Council Chamber served as the totaling centre for Nakonde Constituency, while Mwenzo Girls Secondary School was the totaling centre for Mwenzo Constituency.

World.title: Gary nkombo loses to UPND’s Vincent Lilanda
World.content:
Former long serving politician Garry Nkombo has lost the Mazabuka Central Parliamentary race to UPND candidate Vincent Lilanda.

Nkombo got 10,720 votes while Lilanda polled 20,420 of the 33,218 votes cast at 88 polling stations in Mazabuka Central Constituency.

Nkombo was seeking a fifth re-election as Mazabuka Central Member of Parliament, this time as an independent candidate after serving four consecutive terms under the UPND.

Mr Nkombo who also served government at Minister of Local Government and Rural Development during his tenure as Mazabuka Central MP experienced a fall out with the UPND and resigned from the party before contesting the 2026 elections as an independent candidate.

However, he has lost the parliamentary election which was contested alongside Alfred Hankede and Playson Hachintu who were also independent candidates, and Masumba Denwield of the Socialist Party.

World.title: CSALR Calls for Calm as announcement of results continue
World.content:
The Civil Society Alliance on Legal Reforms (CSALR) has called on political party leaders, their supporters and all Zambians to remain calm and respect the electoral process as the counting and announcement of results continue.

CSALR Chairperson Caroline Katotobwe said the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) remains the only body mandated to announce official election results and urged citizens to exercise patience and await the official announcements.

In a statement issued to the media today, Dr Katotobwe commended Zambians for conducting peaceful elections, saying the calm and order displayed at polling stations nationwide demonstrated the maturity of the country’s democracy.

She said CSALR remains confident in the voice of every Zambian who turned out to vote.

Dr Katotobwe, however, condemned reported acts of violence and what she described as manufactured actions aimed at undermining the credibility of the polls.

She said such actions undermine the will of the people and have no place in the democratic process.

Dr Katotobwe appealed to political party leaders to urge their supporters to remain calm, peaceful and respectful of authorities and electoral processes throughout the vote-counting period.

She said peace and stability should remain the country’s priority above all else

Dr Katotobwe also called on all stakeholders to respect the electoral process and the ECZ, while urging Zambians to wait for the official declaration of results
