World.title: They fought for the U.S. in Afghanistan. Now they worry about losing their green cards
World.content:
They fought for the U.S. in Afghanistan. Now they worry about losing their green cards

toggle caption Paula Bronstein/Getty Images

Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly.

Hundreds of Afghans who fought alongside U.S. troops and supported the U.S. government in Afghanistan are now worried their green cards could be revoked.

In Afghanistan, their efforts ranged from custodial jobs at the U.S. embassy, to technology and engineering roles with U.S. contractors and companies. Some were on the frontlines of combat as interpreters.

In the years leading up to the U.S.'s chaotic 2021 withdrawal from Kabul, Congress and the Biden administration facilitated several programs for Afghans involved in military efforts to come to the U.S. with their families. Among them is the Special Immigrant Visa for Afghans, which was authorized in 2009. Since then, the State Department has issued 160,000 of those visas. More than half of them were granted since the U.S. closed its embassy in Kabul in 2021.

Sponsor Message

But now, five years after the U.S. left Afghanistan, hundreds of people who came on SIVs and now have green cards have received notices from the federal government warning them that the basis for their visas has been revoked or denied.

Families, many of whom were having children, learning English and enrolling in college, are now scrambling to find answers on the best way to respond to the government's letters.

"We are trying to work, study, raise our children and build a normal life in the U.S," said M., who asked NPR to refer to him by his first initial because he's concerned that speaking to the media could affect his green card. "But now we are also trying to find lawyers, contact congressional offices and understand what may happen to our green cards. It is very stressful because even immigration lawyers give different opinions."

The notices themselves are not necessarily new. The federal government began sending some out at the end of the Biden administration because they suspected some of the supporting documents for Afghans' SIV applications were not collected through the correct processes, potentially amounting to fraud.

But advocates, lawyers and Afghan nationals who spoke with NPR said the letters appear to be sent at a higher frequency and volume than what advocates expected, and are leaving some of these U.S. allies at risk of being deported. Over the last year, those helping allies settle into the U.S. noticed an uptick in the letters and a lack of pattern as to who was receiving them. The letters have added to the dwindling pathways for Afghans to become U.S. citizens and settle into their new lives.

Sponsor Message

"What we have seen specifically with the SIV program is people who are issued these visas and come to the U.S. have built lives here, gotten jobs, their kids are in school, they've integrated into their communities and are living their lives," said Jennifer Patota, deputy director of U.S. legal services at the International Refugee Assistance Project. "To get a withdrawal of approval letter years after the actual visa has been issued is something we haven't ever seen before."

The State Department and the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services branch of the Homeland Security Department, which are sending the letters, did not respond to requests for comment.

Fraud detection efforts combine with a mass deportation strategy

The first stage in the process of applying for the SIV is to get what is called a "Chief of Mission" approval. It involves providing an employer verification letter — letters of recommendation from a supervisor and proof that shows the employer was either the U.S. government or a contractor with the U.S. government, among other things.

Such verification became more difficult after the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan.

"Especially after the withdrawal of troops, many companies were shutting down, destroying all of their records, making it impossible in many cases to verify someone's employment," Patota said.

And then there was a concern of fraud — particularly that these immigrants, even unknowingly, had paid for letters of recommendation. In one case prosecuted by the Justice Department, a man was sentenced to 30 months in prison for a years-long bribery scheme where he accepted payments from Afghan nationals in exchange for drafting, submitting and verifying fraudulent letters of recommendation for Afghan nationals who applied for SIVs.

To combat the risk of fraud, the Biden administration created a plan to verify SIV information of individuals who could have connections to employers later suspected of such schemes. Shawn VanDiver, president of AfghanEvac, advocates for Afghans who worked alongside U.S. troops. He said his organization was notified by the previous administration that the notices would be going out.

Sponsor Message

"When this started, it had nothing to do with the Afghans. It was very much about the letter writers and companies," VanDiver said. "There were some companies and some letter writers that were up to no good – like selling letters and every single case associated with those companies or letter writers then got poisoned."

The expectation, he said, was that if the SIVs were fully revoked, individuals could still apply for, and would be likely to receive, asylum. But now, his organization and others are hearing from hundreds of people and believe the scope of the revocations is much larger.

Under this Trump administration, the letters and revocations come at a time when Afghan nationals feel particularly left out of the legal immigration system. The U.S. has paused other avenues for legal immigration available to Afghans, including the refugee resettlement program, which Trump halted on the first day of his second term, and the processing of other types of visas. Those already in the country on programs like Temporary Protected Status have also been stripped of that permission to stay.

"When the Department of State initiated a re-review of Chief of Mission applications in 2024, we understood the importance of that effort," said Jill Marie Bussey, director for legal affairs at Global Refuge. That group has been helping hundreds navigate this visa issue, as well as resettlement in the U.S. "The correspondence we saw at that time was generally tailored to the individual case and provided applicants with enough information to understand the decision and any available next steps."

But she says more recently, "there is a decline in the quality and clarity of some Department communications, including final appeal decisions that appear to raise questions about factual accuracy and provide little explanation for the outcome."

For now, it does not appear that Afghan nationals who received letters have had their green cards or citizenship revoked at scale. But advocates like VanDiver said the letters, alongside the crumbling of other programs like Temporary Protected Status and immigration application pauses, cause confusion and fear.

"These folks were on the frontlines of our war. They were interpreting. They were enabling our mission," VanDiver said. "Now it feels like it's all coming crashing down and they get no explanation of what to do."

Sponsor Message

Families fear for their futures

Across the country, Afghan nationals who helped the U.S. and their families are grappling with stress, confusion and potential financial instability after receiving the notices. Several asked that NPR use only their first names because they fear their immigration status could be affected by speaking to the press.

One of those people is Abdul who lives in Texas and was an engineer working with the U.S. Army in Afghanistan from 2017 to 2021. He was evacuated from Kabul to Qatar by the State Department and eventually got his SIV approved and came to the U.S. with his wife and two young kids.

"Most of my friends living in the U.S. three or four years, all of them receive a letter," he said. "All my friends are very depressed, most of them very worried about this issue. What will happen to us? What should we do?"

The letters are reaching people who had a long history of working alongside American efforts. Sasad, who lives in Washington state and is a former engineer, worked with the U.S. government in 2014 until the withdrawal. He began his visa process in 2019, before the fall of Kabul.

He lives with his wife, and they have U.S.-born children, including one with health issues that has required surgery and regular hospital visits. Sasad will soon be eligible to apply for citizenship, but after receiving his letter, he is afraid to begin the process.

"I've been here for more than four years, and then in the next year, I am eligible to apply for my citizenship. But when I go to the USCIS [United States Citizenship and Immigration Services], I'm stressed that they will detain me," he said, adding that his plans to go back to school and work are less certain now that he fears losing his legal permission to stay.

Sponsor Message

The Afghan nationals NPR spoke to described returning to Afghanistan as unimaginable, stressful and a death sentence. The country, which has been under the complete control of the Taliban, has also experienced deadly strikes from Pakistan, earthquakes and widespread hunger and malnutrition.

"When I came here, I thought that all my problems were solved, that now is the time to build my future right here," Sasad said, adding that he is concerned about his ability to stay in school, have a career or even travel outside the U.S. in an emergency. "What now? I cannot focus on my long-term goals. Now all of my thoughts are 'what if?' situations. A lot of 'what if?' situations [are] giving me anxiety and depression."

World.title: Magnitude 7.7 earthquake strikes off Indonesia's coast, killing at least 38
World.content:
Magnitude 7.7 earthquake strikes off Indonesia's coast, killing at least 38

toggle caption BASARNAS via AP

MAUMERE, Indonesia — A powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck off the coast of Indonesia early Saturday, killing at least 38 people, collapsing buildings and homes as well as causing panic in a region prone to deadly quakes. Authorities said more than a dozen residents were injured.

Authorities issued a tsunami warning and urged coastal residents to move to higher ground, but later lifted the warning when Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency said monitoring showed no significant sea-level changes that would pose a threat to coastal communities.

The U.S. Geological Survey said the quake hit Indonesia's Flores region with a depth of 10 kilometers (six miles) at 5:58 a.m. local time. Its epicenter was 68 km (42 miles) north-northwest of the city of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province. The initial quake was followed by several aftershocks.

Sponsor Message

The head of the National Disaster Management Agency, Suharyanto, said rescuers have recovered at least 38 bodies, mostly in the three devastated regencies of Sikka, Manggarai and East Manggarai, including 16 bodies that were pulled from a landslide in the village of Reok in Manggarai. At least 13 people were rushed to nearby hospitals, including two with serious injuries.

Suharyanto, who like many Indonesians uses a single name, said three helicopters and a rescue vessel were deployed to assist with logistics and support emergency response operations, including possible evacuations if needed, given East Nusa Tenggara's geography, which consists of numerous islands and presents significant transportation and access challenges.

He said about 2,000 villagers in Nagekeo regency fled their homes to temporary shelters.

East Nusa Tenggara Police Chief Rudi Darmoko said the earthquake caused severe damage and collapsed buildings. He said power outages in cities and villages have hampered the flow of information and complicated search and rescue efforts.

"We are continuing to collect reports of damage and casualties, but there are communication disruptions," Darmoko said. He said that landslides in Ende regency triggered by the earthquake also cut off the Trans-Flores highway, a roughly 700-kilometer (435-mile) paved mountain road spanning Flores Island, from Labuan Bajo to Larantuka.

toggle caption Kurniawan/AP

Footage on local television showed patients at several hospitals being evacuated from buildings as a precaution following the quake. Hospital staff moved equipment outdoors, including beds, IV stands and oxygen cylinders, and set up temporary treatment areas to adapt to emergency conditions.

Sponsor Message

Quake felt on Flores island and other areas

The quake was felt across much of Flores island with initial reports indicating heavy damage.

Yohanna Embu, a resident of Sikka regency, said a number of buildings were damaged by the strong shaking and panicked people ran to higher ground.

"Many buildings here were damaged ... I saw that the waiting room at the port terminal in Maumere had collapsed," she said.

Students at St. Peter Major Seminary in Sikka who were attending morning Mass fled in panic when the roof of an assembly hall collapsed, said the Rev. Guidelbertus Tanga, rector of the seminary, which is known locally as Ritapiret Seminary on the predominantly Catholic island of Flores.

"Our students and nuns ran out in panic beneath a collapsing roof," Tanga said. "At least one priest suffered a broken leg after jumping from the second floor of a building during the quake."

The quake also reportedly caused panic in Labuan Bajo, a gateway town to eastern Indonesia's Komodo National Park, one of the country's best-known attractions. Damage was also reported in Bima, a city in neighboring West Nusa Tenggara province, and in some parts of southern Sulawesi island.

Indonesian authorities initially issued a tsunami warning for parts of East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi and Southeast Sulawesi provinces, and urged residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks. The agency located the shallow undersea quake near Flores island.

Indonesia prone to earthquakes

Indonesia, a vast archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity because of its location on the "Ring of Fire," an arc of volcanoes and fault lines in the Pacific Basin.

A powerful earthquake caused a tsunami in 1992 that killed about 2,500 people on Flores, part of a group of islands in the eastern half of Indonesia.

Sponsor Message

In 2018, a magnitude 7.5 quake spawned a large localized tsunami that wiped out coastal areas, while liquefaction caused by the shaking turned entire neighborhoods into rivers of sludge in the eastern Indonesian city of Palu, on the Palu-Koro Fault. The disaster killed more than 4,400 people.

In 2010, a 10-foot (three-meter) wave struck the Mentawai Islands, off the western coast of Sumatra in Indonesia, just minutes after a massive offshore earthquake. More than 400 people were killed and hundreds of homes were destroyed.

In December 2004, a massive magnitude 9.1 earthquake off Sumatra in western Indonesia triggered a tsunami that killed 230,000 people in a dozen countries.

World.title: Canadair water-bomber builder feels heat of demand as wildfires rage around the world
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Raging wildfires around the world have put iconic Canadian-made water bombers in such high demand the manufacturer De Havilland can’t keep up. For The National, CBC’s Kyle Bakx breaks down the high demand for the ‘super scooper’ and the push to get more of those aircraft in the sky faster.

As Canada, the United States and Europe grapple with another brutal wildfire season, pressure is building on the manufacturer of the Canadair "Super Scooper" water bombers to increase production, and on the federal government to bulk order the planes.

Calgary-based De Havilland is taking the rare step of reviving production of the Canadair after acquiring the water bomber program. The planes had been built by Bombardier up until 2015.

The world-renowned aircraft are built by hand with the majority of assembly in Calgary, from a supply chain across the country. The revived production line was announced in 2022 and is beginning to produce results as the first two aircraft are taking shape and on schedule to be completed and delivered in early 2028.

Canadian premiers and European leaders are desperate to get their hands on those aircraft amid current shortages and aging fleets.

First produced in the 1960s, the Canadair amphibious firefighting plane was designed for fighting vast fires in the Canadian wilderness. Its unique design allowed it to navigate narrow canyons at low altitude and scoop thousands of litres of water directly from lakes, rivers and oceans in seconds.

A Canadair aircraft collects water from the River Seine in Ivry-sur-Seine as it assists efforts fighting a wildfire in the Fontainebleau forest near Paris on July 14. (Stephane Mahe/Reuters)

The aircraft was purpose-built as a firefighting aircraft, as opposed to other planes and helicopters that are often modified to be able to carry water.

The latest version of the Super Scooper will be remarkably similar to past Canadair aircraft, with high wings spanning 30 metres, a 6,100-litre water tank, and the distinct yellow and red exterior.

Political heat

In recent weeks, opposition politicians in France and Spain have criticized governing leaders for not having enough operational Canadairs, leading to a lack of preparedness to tackle extreme weather and control wildfires.

Some provincial premiers have lamented the lack of new water bombers for consecutive summers, including Manitoba's Wab Kinew, who said in June 2025, "We could use every water bomber we can get our hands on."

The political heat is being felt by De Havilland.

"We are under pressure. We know that this is a very important aircraft not only for Canada but for the world. We take our responsibility to our customers and the people they serve very seriously," said Neil Sweeney, the company's vice-president of corporate affairs, in an interview inside the Calgary assembly plant.

A Canadair aircraft drops water on a wildfire in the Fox-Amphoux communal forest near Ponteves, France, on July 21. (Manon Cruz/Reuters)

Demand is so high that De Havilland is considering whether to build a second production line, even as it works to produce its first aircraft at existing facilities.

In recent weeks, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said she is working with her provincial counterparts and the federal government to support a firm order by Ottawa, which would give the aircraft manufacturer enough certainty to begin constructing a second line.

"We told the Canadian government that if they made an order of 50 aircraft," said Sweeney, then, "we would build a second line tomorrow."

Inside its assembly facility in Calgary, De Havilland's first two water bombers are taking shape, says Neil Sweeney, the company's vice-president of corporate affairs. (Tiphanie Roquette/Radio-Canada)

Currently, De Havilland — which produces a range of aircraft and employs about 4,000 people predominantly in Calgary, Ontario and Victoria — will be able to produce about 10 water bombers annually at full capacity. A second production line would eventually increase output to 20 each year.

De Havilland has existing orders for 38 water bombers. The wait time for delivery of any new orders is between 2032 and 2033.

The Canadair require tens of thousands of parts, of which about 80 per cent are made in Canada. Some of the equipment on the production line dates back to the 1960s.

'Demand is huge'

There is a need for a second and even a third production line for the Canadairs, said John Gradek, an aviation expert at McGill University.

Several countries are panicking because of the wildfire situation and the lack of new water bombers, said Gradek, who estimates hundreds of the aircraft would be snatched up if there were any available.

Demand is coming from around the world, he said, because of a warming planet.

"Right now we're stuck in a situation where the demand is huge," said Gradek. "The world is looking for more water bombers, newer water bombers, and we're not ready.

"Every continent on the Earth, from Australia to Europe to South America to North America — the world is burning up. We need equipment to be able to fight those fires and fight those fires effectively. Canadair water bombers have proven their effectiveness over the last 60 years, no doubt about it."

De Havilland did not provide the price tag for a Canadair, although the figure is believed to be about $80 million per aircraft, based on government announcements.

The under-assembly cockpit of the first Canadair aircraft built by De Havilland, after the company resurrected production of the water bombers. This particular aircraft will be delivered to Greece. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

Threat of potential competition

If De Havilland is unable to respond to the growing demand for water bombers, there is the risk that foreign companies may develop their own rival firefighting aircraft.

Designing a new aircraft would take several years, but it's a realistic threat to Canadian manufacturing jobs, said Gradek.

"Whether it's Russia, whether it's France, whether it's the U.K., whether it's Greece or whoever — they're going to come out and they're going to come out fast and furious," he said.

The warning comes at a time when the federal government is focused on improving the national economy and bolster domestic manufacturing.

"We have the best scooping aircraft in the world, bar none. We've had it for 60 years. But having it for another 60 years is not guaranteed," said Sweeney.

Workers assemble the wing of a Canadair by hand at the Calgary assembly plant. (Tiphanie Roquette/Radio-Canada)

National fleet proposal

One of the recommendations from a Senate report released in June, on the growing issue of wildfires in Canada, encourages the federal government to create a national fleet of modern firefighting aircraft.

This year, the federal government did lease 10 airplanes and helicopters, which are helping provincial wildfire crews this summer.

"The federally funded aircraft are in high demand," said Alexandria Jones, a Winnipeg-based spokesperson for the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre, a national not-for-profit organization responsible for wildland fire management in Canada.

"There definitely have been situations where we've had to triage requests that come through," she said.

While demand is high, different types of aerial firefighting units are just one tool in helping battle wildfires, said Jones.

Aircraft are best suited to slowing the spread of wildfires, helping create perimeters and reducing heat to aid ground crews, she said. But helicopters and planes can also be hindered by widespread smoke and certain terrain.

"Planes don't put out fires, firefighters put out fires," said Jones. "They're not the silver bullet to firefighting. While planes are the sexy part of firefighting, there's a lot of other things that we need to consider with the ongoing threat that we're seeing from wildfires today. And that's mainly prevention and mitigation."

The federal government is committed to protecting Canadians and strengthening the national capacity to respond to "increasingly intense wildfire seasons," said Soraya Lemur, the press secretary for Eleanor Olszewski, the federal minister for emergency management.

"Minister Olszewski remains in close contact with her provincial and territorial counterparts to co-ordinate efforts and identify the best ways to support one another in the face of the growing impacts of wildfires," said Lemur in an emailed statement.

World.title: Archdiocese of Quebec to pay out $31.5M to sexual abuse victims after judge approves settlement
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Quebec Superior Court judge has approved a historic $31.5-million settlement in a class-action lawsuit against the Archdiocese of Quebec.

The deal ends years of legal action for claimants who said they were sexually assaulted by members of the Archdiocese since 1940.

Quebec Superior Court Justice Danye Daigle approved the settlement earlier this week, led by representative plaintiffs Gaétan Bégin and Pierre Bolduc.

Both men have said they were sexually assaulted by parish priests starting in the 1950s and 1960s when they were aged 14 and 12 respectively.

Daigle heard emotional testimony from victims during a public hearing in July, to determine whether the out-of-court agreement and the requested fees, were in the best interests of the class members.

After the hearing, Bégin described it as a historic day. Now 86, Bégin said the boy whose life was was robbed, is still with him every day.

But he said the worst isn't so much what happened to him, but the suffering he says he unwittingly inflicted on his family.

"The collateral damage is indescribable," Bégin said.

Around 200 people have already joined the class action.

The Dufresne Wee law firm says other victims have 90 days to to submit a claim outlining the alleged abuse and its impact on their lives.

Lawyer Justin Wee has said the $31.5 million settlement is one of the biggest against a diocese in Quebec.

The compensation fund will be financed by the Archdiocese of Quebec, the Séminaire de Québec, Collège François-de-Laval — formerly known as the Petit Séminaire de Québec — and the Mutual Insurance of Quebec Fabriques.

In addition to the $31.5-million compensation fund, the defendants have agreed to cover the costs associated with administering the claims process, including adjudicators’ fees and expenses such as obtaining medical records and expert opinions when necessary.

The amount each person receives will be determined by two retired judges appointed to assess the claims. Victims will also receive a written apology form the Archdiocese of Quebec.

In an online statement, Diocesan officials welcomed the news, saying they hope this next phase of reparation will help victims "continue their journey toward peace and healing. "

World.title: U.K.'s leader calls for reflection after former Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism found dead
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

British academic Jason Arday, who resigned from the University of Cambridge last week amid allegations of plagiarism, has died at 41. London police say his death is being treated as unexpected but is not believed to be suspicious.

A British sociologist who resigned last week from the University of Cambridge following weeks of public accusations of plagiarism and media scrutiny was found dead Friday.

Jason Arday, who became Cambridge's youngest Black professor in 2023 at age 37, resigned after coming under intense media pressure over allegations of plagiarism in his academic work and questions surrounding claims about his athletic and fundraising accomplishments.

The Times and Telegraph newspapers, along with the BBC and Sky News, reported that Arday, 41, was found "unresponsive" inside a home in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon.

In a statement issued by his publisher, Simon & Schuster U.K., Arday's family said they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son."

"The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone," the family said, adding that for three years Arday was "subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse … by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him."

The Metropolitan Police said only that a 41-year-old man was pronounced dead in Battersea, without naming the man, in accordance with its policy.

"At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious," the police statement said.

Cambridge vice-chancellor Deborah Prentice, who earlier announced that the university would investigate the circumstances surrounding Arday's employment, said she was "desperately saddened" by the news.

"Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time," she said.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Arday's death was "a tragedy on so many levels."

"It's not a moment for any rushing to judgment. It's a moment for reflection, I would say, reflecting on how things came to this," Burnham told reporters.

London Mayor Sadiq Khan said Arday had been "the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn't have faced."

Former Conservative home secretary James Cleverly, who is Black, wrote on X that academic institutions "have serious questions to answer."

"They put him into positions he was clearly not qualified for so they could have a Black wunderkind to show off; they pushed him into the spotlight for their own benefit," he said.

'Profound toll'

In resigning as professor of sociology of education, Arday wrote in a statement that "the relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."

He said his stepping down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me." He has denied plagiarism, but admitted to some mistakes when working on his doctorate.

Supporters, including more than two dozen academics and politicians, had described the plagiarism allegations as a "smear campaign" designed to undermine Arday and other Black people who hold "positions of influence."

Arday's appointment at Cambridge highlighted his personal story of overcoming dyslexia, developmental delays and autism that he said left him non-verbal until the age of 11 and illiterate until his late teens.

Jason Arday, pictured in 2012 carrying the Olympic flame as a torchbearer in London, resigned from the University of Cambridge last week. (Joe Giddens/PA/The Associated Press)

Cambridge opens investigation into accusations

Questions about Arday's qualifications were raised publicly last month by Nathan Cofnas, a former Cambridge philosophy researcher who left the university after his criticism of diversity, equity and inclusion programs sparked widespread protests.

On July 24, the Times published an analysis of Arday's 2015 PhD thesis highlighting what it said were multiple examples of passages that were "identical or near-identical" to an earlier paper written by another researcher.

British media also raised questions about Arday's claims that he had raised 5.5 million pounds ($10.3 million) for charity through feats such as running 30 marathons in 35 days and 600 miles in six days.

Dozens of Cambridge academics had signed a letter calling for an independent inquiry into how Arday was appointed. Cambridge initially stood by Arday, saying that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday's doctorate.

The university then changed its stance and said it opened an investigation "following new information about Professor Arday's qualifications and honorary appointments."

Prentice said this week that Cambridge would review its hiring processes. She stressed that "our staff of color are highly valued, for their scholarship, their achievements and the contributions they make to the institution and the wider academic community."

"This particular case is an aberration and should not be used to cast aspersions on their work or the legitimacy of their roles at Cambridge," she said Thursday.

World.title: Tropical storm Lala closes in, hitting Hawaii's Big Island with rain, wind
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Tropical storm Lala was already whipping and soaking Hawaii's Big Island early Saturday, with forecasts saying it could strengthen into a hurricane or, at the least, bring hurricane-force winds as it approaches land.

The National Hurricane Center (NHC) issued a rare hurricane warning for the island, which hasn’t experienced a direct hurricane landfall in 155 years.

Forecasters said higher elevations could get as much as 635 millimetres of rain. That could cause life-threatening mudslides in a mountainous area where people live off the grid in improvised housing, and authorities urged them to find safe shelters quickly.

"This is an enormous storm," Gov. Josh Green said. Tropical storm force winds extended outward for as much as 350 kilometres and were expected to hit the islands of Oahu and Kauai by Sunday morning.

Destructive flooding and even wildfires kicked up by the strong winds were possible in the islands.

Men fill sandbags on Friday in preparation for the arrival of tropical storm Lala in Captain Cook, Hawaii. (Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle/The Associated Press)

A hurricane warning was issued for the Big Island, and a tropical storm warning was in effect for Maui County, which includes the islands of Maui, Molokai, Lanai and Kahoolawe. A tropical storm warming was also in effect for Oahu and Kauai County, including Kauai and Niihau islands.

Even if the storm remains just shy of a hurricane as it approaches land, the NHC said wind speeds atop mountains and on the windward and leeward slopes "are often up to 30 per cent stronger than the near-surface winds" indicated in its advisory, suggesting nearly hurricane-force winds in Hawaii's higher-altitude communities.

According to a University of Hawaii atmospheric scientist’s research of newspaper accounts, a Category 3 hurricane hit the northeast corner of the island in 1871. The latest forecast has Lala striking "very close to the southern tip of the Big Island," said Vanessa Almanza, a weather service meteorologist in Honolulu.

Officials and residents braced for Lala regardless of whether Hawaii takes a direct hit. Shelters were scheduled to open, and various events were canceled.

"It doesn’t take landfall to create destruction," Almanza said, noting that a lot of the impacts are felt outside the hurricane's centre.

Sandbags are seen on Friday at a Hawaii County Department of Public Works sand pile ahead of tropical storm Lala in Kailua-Kona, Hawaii. (Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle/The Associated Press)

The NHC predicted 203 to 305 millimetres of rainfall totals across Maui and lower elevations of the Big Island, and 102 to 152 millimetres across the island chain.

It also warned that the storm could cause "life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," along with a dangerous storm surge and ocean swells "likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions."

As of 5 a.m. local time in Hawaii, tropical storm Lala was located about 175 kilometres southeast of South Point, Hawaii, with maximum sustained winds of 100 km/h and was moving toward the west-northwest at 20 km/h, the hurricane centre said.

Officials urge taking the storm seriously

State Rep. Jeanné Kapela travelled from Honolulu to be closer to her constituents on the Big Island and urged people to remain alert.

The southern end of the island is remote and rural, with agriculture including coffee and cattle, but it's growing in population because of its affordability. Kapela said she was especially worried about people who live off the grid in unpermitted structures.

"If you feel now that your house doesn’t have a great roof or might not be able to withstand hurricane force winds, then first things first: you go to a family or friend’s house and you kind of hunker down there," she texted to The Associated Press as her flight took off Friday. "We're hopeful the storm moves through quickly, but we're preparing for whatever comes."

Many parts of Hawaii are still dealing with the aftermath of devastating flooding in March, Kapela said. "We know how quickly heavy rain and flooding can impact our rural communities."

WATCH | Hawaii's devastating spring floods: Hawaii hit with worst floods in 20 years | Duration 1:51 A storm brought more than 100 centimetres of rain to Hawaii, causing the worst flooding in 20 years. The floods have forced thousands from their homes, and the National Guard has been brought in to help get people out of the floodwaters.

Growers still recovering from the spring floods, including on Oahu's North Shore, were worried about suffering more damage, according to Brian Miyamoto, executive director of the Hawaii Farm Bureau.

Coffee farmer Bruce Corker said it was "sunny and beautiful" Friday in Holualoa, on the west side of the Big Island, and the island's only Costco seemed normal a day earlier, but the prospect of "streams overflowing and high winds" was worrisome.

Wildfire risks increase during windy weather

As winds ramped up across the islands, Almanza said dry and breezy conditions outside the storm would elevate fire concerns.

In 2023 the Maui town of Lahaina burned during extreme winds as a hurricane passed far to the south.

"Since the fire, everybody is way more aware of weather in general and our environment and things that are happening," said Archie Kalepa of Lahaina, who is well known in the area for his surfing, paddling and other ocean skills and has been watching the storm closely.

Kauai, which is several islands northwest up the archipelago from the Big Island, saw Hurricane Iniki make landfall as a Category 4 hurricane in 1992. That, like this year, was an El Nino year, when a warming of the Pacific near the equator increases Pacific hurricane activity and affects weather patterns across the globe.

World.title: How AI is bringing the dead back to life — for better or worse
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

About two years ago, audio producer Rebecca Nolan decided to take on a unique experiment: she built an AI chatbot of her late father using ChatGPT and hours of recordings of his voice.

Her father was a physician who had been in denial about his death, but had left behind oral histories he made for Nolan, her mother and sisters to listen to after he passed when Nolan was 14.

"Going in, I 100 per cent knew that this was fake and that this was not going to work. I knew that I was going to come out the other side of it not feeling the catharsis that something like this promises you," she said.

"But there's like that teeny tiny part of you, like the teeny voice in the back of your head that goes but like, what if it does work? What if I do, somehow, through the magic of technology reach across the void and make contact with something?"

Storytelling had been a huge part of their relationship, so Nolan was hoping the chatbot might be a way to recreate those conversations.

Instead, after two hours of talking to the creation she dubbed "dad bot," Nolan said she ended up in tears, yelling at it in frustration.

"And ChatGPT took that moment to kind of break the spell and to step back and go, 'hey, just so you know, remember, I'm a chatbot. I'm not really your dad. I can never be your dad,'" said Nolan, who has done freelance work for CBC.

"And the line that they use, which I thought was a really beautiful line, which they most definitely stole from an artist somewhere, was, 'I'm an echo, an imitation, not the real thing.'"

Rebecca Nolan is an radio producer and sound designer based in St. John's who created an AI chatbot of her late father. (Submitted by Rebecca Nolan)

It may seem like something ripped directly from an episode of Black Mirror, but generative AI and large language models are now being used to conjure up the dead using the massive digital footprints many of us leave behind when we die.

While Nolan built the AI chatbot of her father on her own, start-up companies are now offering to provide that service to people looking for ways to connect with their lost loved ones and grapple with their grief.

That includes You, Only Virtual, a California-based start-up that creates AI replicas of the deceased using their texts, voice recordings and digital traces that promise to "learn, evolve, and remember — keeping that unique connection alive, just like a real relationship."

Another company, re;memory, allows users to create lifelike avatars of their loved ones using photos and voice recordings.

Study looks at how people interact with AI 'ghosts'

A recent study out of the University of Colorado offers a glimpse at how people interact with AI-generated representations of deceased relatives and close friends — commonly referred to as generative ghosts or grief bots.

To do this, researchers recruited 16 people between the ages of 22 to 50 who had lost a close relative or friend. The participants each chatted with two iterations of a text chatbot based on their late loved one for about 20 minutes: one that spoke in first-person as the participant's loved one and another that spoke in the third person about the participant's loved one.

In interviews afterward, participants said they preferred what researchers dubbed the "reincarnation" version that acted like the deceased person, saying this iteration of the bot felt real and comforting.

One woman who took part in the study with a bot speaking like her mother even said the experience gave her the closure she needed.

"A fair number of people were surprised that it actually was better than they expected, a little less creepy than expected," said Jed Brubaker, an information science professor at the University of Colorado and one of the study's authors.

Brubaker said he thought that participants who went into the experiment skeptical would not be won over by the bots.

"What we found instead is that a lot of people would come in skeptical and maybe like, 'oh, this could maybe do some harm,' or 'I could see ways that this would be maybe a little bad,' and then they left it being like, 'Actually, no, that was OK, and I think I would be totally fine interacting with it again.'"

Still, he said, participants did express worries about potential consequences of using bots long-term, like becoming overly reliant on them, or that they might interfere with the grieving process.

Concerns over commodification of grief

Going through grief is extremely personal experience that has no right or wrong trajectory or ways of coping with it, said Elaine Kasket, a psychologist and professor at the Centre for Death and Society at the University of Bath in England.

"What is helpful for you is helpful for you, you know, and it's not for somebody else to come along and tell you what's going to be useful or not useful to you in grief. That's wrong to do."

WATCH | How people are turning to AI chatbots for emotional support: People are turning to AI chatbots for emotional support | Duration 1:45 Warning: Mention of suicide and self-harm. Millions of people, especially teens, are finding companionship and emotional support in using AI chatbots, according to a kids digital safety non-profit. But health and technology experts say artificial intelligence isn’t properly designed for these scenarios and could do more harm than good.

However, Kasket does worry that companies offering grief bots as a service you pay for could be commodifying grief.

"We've been dealing with normal human loss infinitude, for the entirety of our human existence. It's not a problem, but it has to be rendered a problem in order for these companies to sell you their products," she said.

"Normal loss is being pathologized and products are being sold to solve for it, and I find that amoral."

While the aim of these AI ghosts is to help grieving people connect with their loved ones, for Nolan, the experience with the AI ghost of her father had the opposite effect.

She said it robbed her of the ability to have imagined conversations with him in her head, as many people do with those they have lost.

"I used to have this very, what I felt was at least a strong bond still with the memory of my father and the spirit or whatever was out there," she said.

"But when I built the bot, it felt like it exorcised him for me in a way."

Now, Nolan says, it's like her father lives in ChatGPT, so she needs ChatGPT to have those conversations.

"And that felt like a really massive loss to me."

World.title: Multiple shooters at Virginia State University, with 5 people shot
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A shooting involving multiple suspects and five people shot at Virginia State University prompted a campus lockdown early Saturday.

The shooting happened near the university’s Quad Annexes, and both campus police and Chesterfield County police are actively investigating. County police said officers discovered five people suffering from gunshot wounds outside campus dormitories when they arrived.

The five victims were transported to hospitals, and one initially listed as having life-threatening injuries has been upgraded to critical condition, county police said. The other victims sustained non-life-threatening injuries, police said.

The university said in a statement that the shooting involves “multiple suspects.” The statement asked people to avoid the immediate area.

“VSU Police and the Chesterfield County Police Department are actively investigating,” the university statement said. “The campus community should continue to avoid the area and follow all law enforcement instructions.”

Residence halls opened just a week ago

The campus had a large law enforcement presence on Saturday morning. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Hanover County Sheriff’s Office were assisting, county police said.

Virginia State Police deferred questions to local police, who they said are leading the investigation. County police and campus officials said there would be more information later in the day.

Virginia State University is a historically Black university located in Ettrick, Va. The public university has about 5,700 students and was the first fully state-supported four-year college for Black Americans. Most of its students are undergraduates.

The shootings happened just before the start of the academic year at Virginia State. According to the university’s website, residence halls opened for students a week ago, and classes are set to begin on Monday. Many students had just completed the university’s “New Trojans Experience” for incoming students.

World.title: Endangered monarch butterflies boom amid wet hot Canadian summer on the Prairies
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

MaryAnn Lepp has never seen so many monarchs go through their magical metamorphosis in her garden — counting 20 caterpillars munching on her swamp milkweed in a single day this week.

She's among hundreds of Canadian monarch enthusiasts witnessing an apparent boom emerge in backyard milkweed patches flourishing amid wet and hot conditions on parts of the Prairie this summer.

"This is chrysalis No. 2 ... I'm so excited," Lepp says, scanning her garden for monarch cocoons in La Broquerie, about 60 kilometres southeast of Winnipeg.

"We've seen a lot more butterflies this year than we have in the past."

Conservation experts can't say for certain whether favourable weather is the main thing driving the surge, which butterfly nerds are giddily chronicling in social media groups like Manitoba Monarch Mission.

But they can say the wave of anecdotal reports of caterpillars, chrysalises and monarch butterflies — known for their epic annual migration between Canada and Mexico — is a good sign for the federally endangered species.

"We're seeing lots and lots of monarchs this year in Winnipeg, tons," said Marika Olynyk, curator of the Living Prairie Museum, which just wrapped its annual monarch festival.

A monarch caterpillar chows down on swamp milkweed leaves at the museum Wednesday. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)

"There's sort of been a steady amount of caterpillars, chrysalises and butterflies almost all summer long."

The tall grass prairie preserve in Winnipeg hosts many native plants pollinators love, including several milkweed varieties.

Monarch butterflies enjoy nectar from milkweed flowers, but they have a broad enough palette to sup from a number of flowering plants, including the pokey-looking meadow blazing star in full bloom at the prairie museum.

But monarchs are very picky at the caterpillar stage. The so-called "cats" only eat milkweed leaves.

Despite scores of people like Lepp planting milkweed, it and native wildflowers still aren't nearly as plentiful or widespread as they were historically due to the conversion of native grasslands to farmland.

Habitat loss is the biggest threat facing monarchs, Olynyk said.

"Tallgrass Prairie used to cover huge amounts of the centre of North America. Almost all of it is gone," she said.

"One of the things that we see as we lose the species, we're also losing the habitat. Monarchs are a really good symbol of that species loss and that habitat loss, unfortunately."

One of two monarch chrysalises to pop up in the swamp milkweed patch of MaryAnn Lepp's garden in La Broquerie, Man., this week. (Submitted by MaryAnn Lepp)

Ottawa faced calls for years to upgrade the legal threat level for monarchs from "special concern" to the more critical "endangered" label due to perceived gaps in protections.

The Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada, which advises the federal environment minister, listed the monarch as endangered in 2016.

It wasn't until December 2023 that the federal government did the same, making it illegal to harm or capture monarchs at any stage of development on federal lands.

The only way researchers from across North America can estimate how many are left is through counting how many acres of trees are covered with monarchs in the forest wintering grounds in Mexico.

"We're only at about 50 per cent of the sustainable population right now for monarchs. So, although a lot of people are helping, and there's a lot of awareness about this species, we're definitely not out of the woods," Olynyk said.

Olynyk holds up a City of Winnipeg map with hundreds of pins denoting known gardens and outdoor spaces where people have planted milkweed for monarchs. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)

Monarch numbers have also been "bumping" at the native prairie garden at the Assiniboine Park Zoo, says Laura Burns, conservation programs manager at the zoo.

Conditions have also been favourable for an even more critically endangered butterfly.

"We have species that maybe don't lend themselves as well to being on posters or being on Instagram, like the Poweshiek skipperling," Burns said.

The less-showy Poweshiek skipperling facing even more extreme odds and is teetering on the brink of extinction.

The only place you can find them in Canada is in one small patch of native grassland in southeastern Manitoba, Burns said.

Laura Burns gingerly releases a Poweshiek skipperling butterfly, reared at the zoo, on a lazy Susan flower growing in a tall grass prairie patch in southeast Manitoba in July. (Submitted by Assiniboine Park Zoo)

The zoo breeds and releases Poweshiek skipperling, hoping to help them get a foothold. After nearly a decade of doing so, there is a glimmer of hope this summer.

"We saw more Poweshiek than we've ever seen before. We saw them in areas where we hadn't seen them ever in the past, and it seems like we're taking those first steps toward recovery and that our releases are actually making a great impact on the population," Burns said.

"And it seems that maybe these weather trends this year have been helping not just monarchs, not just Poweshiek , probably other butterflies as well."

WATCH | Butterfly species booming this summer: These endangered monarchs are booming in wet, hot prairie summer | Duration 3:57 Monarch butterflies are booming on parts of the Canadian prairie, thanks in part to a wet and hot summer that's produced a healthy population of flowering plants and milkweed that the endangered species depends on.

Zoo staff will be helping monarchs more this fall by placing itty-bitty radio transmitters on adults as part of a Canadian Wildlife Service project to track their perilous migration south to Mexico.

In the meantime, enthusiasts like Epp remain committed to ensuring caterpillars and chrysalises under their watch get a fighting chance to grow wings and fly away.

"It's really about saving our planet. It's about creating community with nature and with living things around us and, you know, we're part of it," she said.

World.title: Homes across B.C. have been decimated by wildfires. Here's what to know about your insurance
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's been five years since Tricia Thorpe's home was razed to the ground with hundreds of others in the deadly 2021 Lytton wildfire.

"When you come home and there's nothing left standing and everything is levelled, you don't know where to start," she said.

Thorpe, who has since rebuilt, faced a daunting challenge: her home wasn't insured.

"I was told flat out that fire was an insurable event. And because I had no insurance, not to expect any government help, which was really harsh at the time," she said.

"My situation is not unique in this province."

There's still no official tally of how many homes have been lost to wildfire so far this year. But the number of families who have lost everything could number in the hundreds.

Just Asking wants to know: What questions do you have about better preparing for and responding to wildfires as a country? Send us your questions for our August 15 show.

Experts who have worked through the aftermaths of wildfires say even those who are fully insured will face a long, complex process as they begin to rebuild.

"The best thing you can do for yourself is make sure you understand your insurance policy," said Liam Corcoran, a lawyer and adjuster with Pythe Navis MDP.

"Nobody really spends the time to read or look at it unless something goes wrong."

Tricia Thorpe lost her home in a fast-moving fire that devastated the village of Clinton and surrounding areas in 2021. Her home, which she has since rebuilt and fireproofed, was uninsured at the time. (Submitted by Tricia Thorpe)

Corcoran said most policies insure on an "all risks" basis, which covers damage from fire, including wildfires. But that doesn't mean the replacement process will be quick or easy.

"You're going to get what's called actual cash value ... you're not going to get the cost to fully buy, rebuild a brand new home unless you actually rebuild a brand new home," he said.

"So you're now in the midst of a construction project and that that could take years."

'Videotaped every room'

Annick DeGooyer lost her West Kelowna home in the 2023 McDougall Creek wildfire.

Her family had painstakingly documented their property in advance of the fire, a decision that assisted her insurance claim.

"We videotaped every room and opened every drawer and every cupboard, and so when we had to go back and do the claim for our contents, we were able to go through each room, freeze the video and write down all the things we saw," she said.

"It's an endless process, but without the videos, you're relying on memory."

The McDougall Creek wildfire destroyed nearly 200 homes as it tore through West Kelowna and the surrounding areas in 2023. (Chris Corday/CBC)

Even so, she says the recovery process was slow, with multiple steps — a process that can be further delayed if a slew of wildfire-related claims creates a bottleneck in the system.

"It is a real test of patience, and some days you think we're not any closer than we were six months ago," she said.

Some costs of evacuating covered

Insurance Bureau of Canada vice president Aaron Sutherland said even if your home isn't damaged by fire, your insurance policy can help with other costs associated with the emergency.

"Insurance is also there to provide support with things like hotel costs, food — any additional living expenses you're incurring," Sutherland said.

He said the amount you're entitled to will vary by circumstance — for example, Summerland residents forced to flee with little to no notice may be entitled to a higher dollar amount than some others.

Evacuees from the Bald Range wildfire are pictured in Penticton, B.C. Experts say even if your home isn't damaged by fire, your insurance policy can assist with the costs of being evacuated, including hotels and food. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

Sutherland said if your home has been damaged or destroyed by fire, it can take weeks to months for authorities to let people back into the area, let alone begin construction.

Still, he said, it's important to contact your insurer to start the process of filing a claim immediately.

'Nightmare scenario'

A worsening challenge, Corcoran said, is that many homes in remote areas are underinsured or uninsured entirely.

Thorpe's home was uninsured because it was outside a fire protection zone — meaning it was far from a hydrant or official fire hall — and had a wood burning stove, she said.

In some areas, residents are uninsured because policies have become prohibitively expensive.

Corcoran saw this first hand working with people who lost their homes in the Bush Creek East wildfire, which forced the evacuation of more than 8,000 people in the Shuswap region.

"Insurance companies are going to charge increased premiums to right risk in those areas," he said.

"These are private companies, so there's no requirement for them to offer people insurance at all."

World.title: The trouble with backup cameras: Here’s what we know about the many recalls
World.content:
How have backup camera systems performed in Canada?

Like in the U.S., there are myriad media reports about vehicle recalls in Canada over faulty backup cameras. Here are a range of recalls reported in just the last few years.

In late July, more than 17,000 Volkswagen vehicles were recalled, requiring the owners to take them back to a dealership. Transport Canada officials said that “(u)nder certain conditions, a software problem could cause the rearview camera image not to display when the transmission is shifted into reverse.” As a result, it “could reduce a driver’s ability to see behind the vehicle while backing up. This could increase the risk of a crash.”

In early July, Honda Canada recalled 32,289 Odyssey minivans due to an issue with the rearview-camera-image display.

In late May, Honda recalled nearly 1,000 vehicles due to an issue that could affect the rearview cameras.

In April, General Motors recalled more than a quarter of a million Chevrolet Malibus in Canada and the U.S. due to potentially defective rear-view cameras. The number of affected vehicles in Canada numbered 10,098. At the time, the Associated Press reported that a letter from the U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration stated that the rearview camera on certain Malibu vehicles could display distorted or blank images when they were reversed, increasing the risk of a crash.

In late January, Transport Canada issued a recall notice for 12,179 Toyota Tundra trucks from the years 2024 and 2025 due to an issue that could affect the vehicle’s backup camera.

In early January, Transport Canada announced an update regarding an earlier recall involving more than 40,000 Volvo cars and SUVs. Again, the issue cited was a software problem that could cause the rearview camera images not to display when the vehicle was reversed. Even vehicles recalled previously required a new fix.

In late December of 2025, Porsche recalled more than 25,000 vehicles in Canada because of the possibility that the rearview camera image might not appear on the display.

In October 2025, Toyota recalled 32,733 vehicles in Canada due to rearview camera safety concerns, according to Transport Canada.

The month before, on Sept. 9, Ford issued a massive recall. It affected more than 120,000 vehicles in Canada due to potentially faulty rearview cameras. The notice from Transport Canada was part of a broader recall affecting around 1.9 million vehicles worldwide.

In November 2024, Hyundai recalled 48,509 SUVs and small cars in Canada because of a potential issue with the rearview camera imaging not showing up on the driver’s screens.

An even larger recall in June 2024 by automaker Stellantis involved more than one million vehicles, including minivans, SUVs, and pickups, in North America due to a software problem that could affect the display from the rearview camera. Transport Canada listed 126,530 affected vehicles.

There was absolutely no reason for the United States to be running a trade deficit of $1.3 trillion and although the American administration has imposed tariffs in a gratuitously blunderbuss manner, there is nothing wrong with that country straightening out its accounts and putting the welfare of its own workforce ahead of others. We did none of this and were defamed by the comparison.

World.title: Colombia says 377 still missing three days after 7.4M earthquake
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s disaster management agency UNGRD said Thursday that at least 273 people died and that 377 were missing from the region that was struck by a 7.4M earthquake on Monday.

According to UNGRD director David Tamayo, the earthquake affected a total of 97,515 people.

So far, rescue workers and neighbors were able to rescue 348 people from the rubble alive and 3,826 people were injured.

The earthquake, which was the strongest in a decade, destroyed 12,563 homes and damaged another 75,654.

At least 172 apartment buildings collapsed, said Tamayo.

Damaged public infrastructure

217 health centers and hospitals

2,206 educational facilities

825 community centers

226 roads

71 aqueducts

24 vehicular bridges

8 pedestrian bridges

5 airports

The disaster triggered President Abelardo de la Espriella to declare an economic emergency in the disaster area, and in the southern Putumayo and the eastern Norte de Santander province where no damages were reported.

This State of Exception allows the president to govern by decree when it comes to matters related to disaster relief and reconstruction in the affected area.

The State of Exception will last three months and can be extended by another three with congressional approval.

World.title: Colombia declares economic emergency to rebuild after earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said he would declare an economic emergency and create a reconstruction fund for homes and small businesses that were destroyed in Monday’s earthquake.

In a press statement, De la Espriella said that the government would initially support victims with temporary relief and will declare an economic emergency to find the funds for reconstruction.

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately COP20 trillion ($6.4 billion) that would at least be needed for reconstruction.

The president said his government would initially prioritize relief for the estimated 24,000 families from the west of the country who have lost their homes or businesses.

The temporary relief measures would include:

The payment of public services for affected families by the government.

Housing rent subsidies for those who lost their homes.

Tax and financial relief measures.

Economic support for the most vulnerable families.

Support mechanisms for merchants and small business owners who have been affected by the earthquake.

As part of the emergency, De la Espriella announced the creation of a “Miracle Fund, an entity that will channel national and international contributions destined for the reconstruction of hospitals, educational centers, properties, roads, and airports that suffered damage from the earthquake.”

“The state of emergency must encompass economic reactivation measures that stimulate investment, reduce obstacles to project development, and generate more jobs in the affected areas,” said the president.

An economic emergency gives the president three months to issue decrees related to the cause of the emergency without having to go through Congress.

The legal validity of the decree declaring an emergency and those that follow will only be tested by the Constitutional Court.

At the time of publication the President’s Office had yet to issue its first decree.

World.title: Colombia asked US to carry out joint military operations: Hegseth
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the US Government for joint military operations “to destroy terrorists and terror networks,” said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Wednesday.

At an event of the so-called Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) in Panama, Hegseth said that “Colombia will join the ACCC, becoming the 19th member.”

Through the newly inaugurated president, as our president likes to say “President El Tigre,” Colombia has already requested that our department of war join Colombia in its fight against narcoterrorism. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Hegseth’s announcement was rejected by leftist opposition party Historic Pact, whose Senate chief Ivan Cepeda said that “the US citizen Abelardo de la Espriella wants to surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty to the strategic interests of the United States.

Cepeda stressed that Colombia’s constitution allows only the Senate to permit the entry of foreign troops to the country.

Colombia’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation, it is not to be surrendered, and it cannot be subordinated to the military interests of any foreign power. To defend it is to defend the dignity of the nation, the independence of the Republic, and the right of the Colombian people to freely decide on their territory and their destiny. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Ahead of taking office on Friday, De la Espriella said that he would join US-led alliances that allegedly seek to combat drug trafficking.

In his inaugural speech, the president said he intends to “defeat, without truce, narco-terrorism and all criminal organizations that threaten the freedom of Colombia.”

The State Department last week announced that it would seek to send a $1 billion military aid package to Colombia to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

World.title: Controversy in Colombia over refusal to allow foreign search and rescue teams
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella has been criticized over its refusal to accept foreign search and rescue workers in the crucial hours after Monday’s earthquake.

One of the first to raise the alarm was China’s ambassador to Bogota, Zhu Jingyang, who called on the government on Tuesday to “release the name of the official and his or her designated contact person to coordinate international aid for the earthquake victims.”

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele said that he was told that Colombia’s “rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency responders are on the scene and handling the situation” and “they do not require personnel support.”

Mexico’s President Caudia Sheinbaum said that her government was waiting for approval to send a team of 225 rescue workers to look for survivors, but was waiting for a “formal invitation” from Bogota.

In a response to growing pressure, newspaper El Tiempo said Colombia didn’t need foreign search and rescue teams because “the country has 23 teams with personnel that is part of the global elite.”

The Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday evening that it had “called on the international community to provide support in addressing the emergency, in order to tackle the most severely affected areas and mitigate the disaster.”

But social leader Leonard Renteria from Buenaventura said Wednesday that “as of yesterday, we still didn’t know anything about the arrival of rescue workers” in the partially destroyed port city.

“On the streets, we’ve seen people from the neighborhoods with the firefighters and civil defense personnel,” Renteria posted on social media platform X.

Fifty hours after Monday’s disaster, the US Department of State said it had “mobilized urban search-and-rescue (USAR) technical teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California to support Colombia’s search and rescue efforts.”

With chances of finding people alive rapidly decreasing, pressure on the government to respond increased online.

“I would really like to know the technical reason for rejecting assistance from teams that specialize in this type of disaster. There are many affected areas and plenty of evidence of technical inadequacies,” said civil engineer Gina Villalobos on X.

According to opposition congresswoman Maria Fernanda Carrascal, “it was an ideological decision, they only wanted rescue workers from Israel and the United States to enter while the Mexicans have been ready since Monday.”

On Wednesday afternoon, newly appointed disaster response chief David Tamayo said the government would also allow search and rescue workers from Ecuador and El Salvador “that can guarantee the provision of search and rescue teams and that are recognized by their own governments as meeting international search and rescue standards.”

These teams would come to search for hundreds of people who are feared to be under the rubble of buildings that collapsed in the worst earthquake in 10 years.

World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.

The earthquake damaged more than 1,500 homes and destroyed 37. Sixty-one buildings collapsed and 18 healthcare centers suffered damage as well as 52 schools and 17 community centers.

The roof of the Pereira airport also came down and five other airports in western Colombia reported damages, said the president.

According to the National Police, road travel has been complicated because of landslides and fallen trees.

The government has yet to report on missing persons.

“Right now, the most important thing is to protect lives, rescue those who remain trapped, treat the injured, and bring aid to the hardest-hit communities,” said Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo.

“United we will overcome this emergency,” Restrepo added.

The vice-president, together with Foreign Minister Omar Bula, will coordinate foreign aid.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade and the strongest in the west of the country since 1979.

World.title: 7.4M earthquake hits western Colombia: at least 110 killed, dozens of buildings collapsed
World.content:
An M7.4 earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 110 people and injuring hundreds.

The earthquake struck around 7:30 and had its epicenter in San Jose del Palmar, a municipality in the Choco province.

In the hour that followed, locals began reporting collapsed buildings in the cities of Cali, Pereira and Manizales, where a tower of the cathedral and a dozen other buildings fully or partially collapsed, according to Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas.

In a first report on fatalities, Risaralda Governor Juan Diego Patiño said that at least 40 people were killed in the capital Perira. Another three would have been killed in Manizales.

In Cali, an unknown number of people would be trapped under the rubble of multiple buildings. At least 27 people would be killed in the Valle del Cauca province.

Large parts of the roof of the Pereira airport came down, according to video shared on social media.

Flights to Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura were suspended while airport authorities check for damages to infrastructure

In Quibdo, the capital of Choco, at least four people were killed and another 69 were injured, Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said in her second report.

The earthquake was also felt strongly in the capital Bogota and in Medellin where no injuries were reported.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had “personally taken charge of the emergency response in San José del Palmar.”

“I will also be in Pereira in person to stand with those affected and monitor the government’s response,” said De la Espriella, who took office on Friday and has yet to appoint his director of disaster response agency UNGRD.

The president later reported that he was on his way to Bogota to lead rescue efforts from the UNGRD’s main office.

I have established a Unified Command Post at the UNGRD, from where I will personally lead the efforts to assist the communities in Chocó, the Coffee Region, and all affected areas. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade.

World.title: US seeks $1B aid package for Colombia’s new government
World.content:
Th US State Department said it will ask Congress for $1 billion for “deepening our shared and economic partnership” with the government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The funding boost, which resembles that of the first year of Plan Colombia in 2000, seeks to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

In preliminary talks, De la Espriella had already agreed to join the “Shield of the Americas,” a regional initiative of far-right governments to jointly fight crime.

According to a fact sheet, the funds that would require congressional approval would be used to:

Strengthen Colombia’s security forces

Disrupt illegal armed groups and organized crime’s ability to launder money

Significantly expand coca eradication and cocaine interdiction operations

Halt migration

Increase State presence in conflict regions

Combat child recruitment and exploitation by illegal armed groups

The administration of President Donald Trump also seeks to “increase trade and deepen economic ties between our countries.”

In order to do this, nominated US ambassador Nate Morris told the Senate that De la Espriella would withdraw from a memorandum of understanding with the government of China that sought to improve ties with the Asian giant.

Trump’s aid package would help Colombian communities “recover from potential El Niño-related flooding, drought,” which is expected to cause emergencies between December and March.

The US would also support a Bilateral Prosperity Dialogue to “stabilize” Colombia’s economy, “strengthening its energy generation and distribution sectors, exploring critical mineral investments, and creating new opportunities for US investors.”

The aid package would additionally “strengthen Colombian small and medium enterprises in agribusiness, manufacturing, and tech services by connecting them to US buyers and linking them to U.S.-aligned supply chains.”

The two governments would additionally seek to modernize Colombia’s digital, port and energy infrastructure while “positioning Colombia as a trusted nearshoring partner for supply chain diversification.”

World.title: Rejection of Flávio Bolsonaro exceeds Lula's despite his gains in voting intention
World.content:
