World.title: Georgian Constitutional Court judge issues dissenting opinion on cases involving protests on pavements
World.content:
Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

A dissenting opinion by Constitutional Court judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze has been published on the punishment of people for holding protests on pavements.

Kverenchkhiladze believes that imposing administrative detention on people for peaceful protests and assemblies could cause harm that may later prove impossible to remedy.

The Tbilisi City Court began hearing the so-called “pavement cases” in December 2025. Since January 2026, dozens of demonstrators have faced administrative detention for holding protests on the pavement outside parliament.

Several people petitioned the Constitutional Court to challenge the ban on protests on pavements. They also asked the court to suspend the disputed provisions until it issued a final ruling. The Constitutional Court began hearing the cases but refused to suspend the provisions. Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze believes the court should have suspended them.

However, according to lawyer Giorgi Burdjanadze, Kverenchkhiladze was in the minority among the judges of the Constitutional Court’s First Chamber when they considered the issue.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion

“If the threat of administrative detention or imprisonment forces a person to repeatedly refrain from taking part in an assembly or publicly expressing their position, that opportunity can no longer be restored,” the judge wrote.

He said this was why such a restriction could cause “irreparable harm”.

Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze’s dissenting opinion also includes arguments that lawyers raised before the Tbilisi City Court when it considered cases related to protests on pavements. However, the judges did not take those arguments into account.

One such argument concerns the temporary disruption of people’s normal movement in their daily lives.

Judge Giorgi Kverenchkhiladze

Kverenchkhiladze notes that pedestrian movement on pavements can be disrupted for various reasons, including parking violations, commercial or construction activities, and other circumstances. However, the state has never considered imprisonment a necessary measure to protect freedom of movement in such cases.

“Temporary restrictions on pedestrians’ freedom of movement do not represent an interest for which a democratic state would normally resort to imprisonment as a means of protection,” the judge wrote.

Kverenchkhiladze also drew attention to the severity of the sanction. He said harsh punishment not only demonstrates the state’s attitude towards a particular action, but can also discourage people from taking part in protests altogether.

“The severity of the sanction provided for by the disputed provisions indicates not only the degree to which the act is considered reprehensible, but also the strength of the ‘deterrent effect’ it may have on the exercise of freedom of expression and freedom of assembly,” Kverenchkhiladze stressed.

Context

Georgia has seen continuous protests since 28 November 2024. Thousands of people took to the streets after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze of the Georgian Dream party announced that the government would not put EU accession talks on the agenda for the next four years.

Since then, Georgian Dream has repeatedly restricted freedom of expression through new laws. These measures have included bans on wearing masks and using pyrotechnics at rallies, as well as criminal liability for repeatedly blocking roads during protests.

The most far-reaching of these repressive legislative initiatives came with amendments banning assemblies on pavements. Under the new rules, organisers of any assembly or demonstration on a pavement must notify the Interior Ministry five days before the event. The ministry can also propose an alternative time and location for the protest.

The new rules also introduce administrative detention as the initial penalty for violations, except in certain special cases.

Judge on protests on pavements in Georgia

World.title: One of Australia's 'most violent' killers makes bid for freedom
World.content:
An underworld killer who murdered four people, including three members of the same family, is fighting to be released from prison after almost four decades behind bars.

Alistair Farquhar MacRae, who once told a court he should never be released from prison, was initially granted parole, but that decision is now under review.

MacRae shot and killed Dominic Marafiote in July 1985, before he buried the 42-year-old father of four under a chicken shed in a pre-dug grave at his rural property at Merbein, near Mildura.

MacRae then drove to Adelaide and killed the Mildura green grocer's parents, Rosa and Carmelo Marafiote, at their Woodville North home.

Rosa and Carmelo Marafiote were killed by Alistair MacRae. (Supplied)

The career criminal, who worked in Melbourne's underworld for years, also committed a fourth murder.

Albert O'Hara was killed by MacRae in Victoria, six months before the Marafiote murders.

Mr O'Hara, like Dominic Marafiote, was lured to MacRae's property as part of marijuana deals, before he was shot dead and buried on the property.

MacRae, who was handed four life sentences with a non-parole period of 36 years, has been in jail in Victoria, then South Australia, since his arrest in December 1987.

Dominic Marafiote was shot dead and buried by Alistair MacRae in 1985. (ABC News)

MacRae would be one of Australia's most dangerous offenders, according to Central Queensland University criminologist Xanthe Weston.

"These are what I would describe as execution style murders, so they're obviously premeditated, they're very carefully planned and they show no emotion at all," Associate Professor Weston said.

"He would rate as one of the most violent offenders I think Australia has currently seen."

Parole review underway

The 77-year-old, who is currently in the Yatala pre-release centre, was granted parole in June but that decision is now under review with the new Parole Administrative Review Commissioner David Lovell.

A preliminary hearing would be held on Tuesday next week.

While secrecy surrounds details of parole reviews, Commissioner Lovell has granted the ABC permission to report that a review is underway.

While it was unclear who asked for the review, only the Attorney-General Kyam Maher, the Police Commissioner Grant Stevens and the Commissioner for Victims' Rights Sarah Quick have the right to request a review under the Correctional Services Act.

But they are restricted from making any comment on the process.

Convicted murderer Alistair Farquar MacRae is fighting to be released from prison. (ABC News)

Associate Professor Weston said a parole review for MacRae had always been a strong possibility.

"I'm not at all surprised that there are cause for a review of this individual being released into the community given the seriousness of these crimes," she said.

"Four murders is quite extreme and I think that the community is rightly concerned that this individual may be released and could go on to harm others given the right circumstances."

The MacRae review has come as a controversial review process is underway for the youngest of the Snowtown killers, James Vlassakis, who also killed four people.

MacRae had been eligible to apply for parole since December 2023.

Michael O'Connell says the possibility of MacRae's release has been playing on the minds of the victims' family members. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Former Commissioner for Victims' Rights Michael O'Connell said MacRae had told the South Australian Supreme Court he should remain behind bars for life.

"It surprises me that he's applied for parole given some of the comments he made at the time of his conviction," Mr O'Connell said.

On the day he was sentenced over Rosa and Carmelo's murders, MacRae had told the court that he did not "function in normal society".

"I have been charged and found guilty of four murders and still there is talk of my possible release," MacRae said at the time.

"To allow me to be released would place a bigger value on my life and my freedom and a lesser value on the lives of my victims.

"The only way of showing my true remorse is by you showing the same leniency that I gave my victims and that is absolutely none.

"I ask I be allowed to give to the families of the victims the only thing I have or may have left in my life and that is I be allowed to forfeit any possible chance of release, that is all I can do to show my true remorse."

Alistair MacRae killed Rosa and Carmelo Marafiote at their Woodville North home. (ABC News)

If the review allowed the parole board's initial decision to stand, MacRae could be free within months.

"The question now is, is he a suitable person to be released back into the community? … and I'm yet to be convinced that he is and I'm sure many family members are yet to be convinced that he is," Mr O'Connell said.

"The fact that there's a possibility he was going to be released would have played on their minds for decades, but now the reality has hit.

" From a victim's perspective, knowing that the person's out and about, living their life, getting on with things, that can hurt and it hurts extremely. "

Mr O'Connell said there's also been speculation that MacRae may have murdered other people during his long period in Melbourne's criminal underworld.

"The fact that he's suspected of being involved in other murders, one would hope that other police departments around Australia have been alerted and possibly some of those cases have come to the fore," he said.

When asked about MacRae, Victoria Police said in a statement they were "not in a position to confirm if nominated individuals are under active or previous investigation for matters".

World.title: Memory lapses, fake invoices and a reprimand: Key moments from ICAC
World.content:
Fake invoices, a "stupid joke" and a reprimand in the hearing room — it has been another revealing week at NSW's corruption watchdog.

The NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) is examining allegations involving illegal political donations and whether people linked to fugitive property developer Jean Nassif sought to influence political and government outcomes.



Operation Rosny has almost hit the halfway mark.

Here is a look back at the key moments from the week and what is coming next.

'Don't give me that look'

Lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood spent three days in the ICAC witness box, and it is not the last the commission will see from him.

Mr Greenwood often made the job of counsel assisting a struggle, with repeated answers of "I don't know" and "I don't recall" when asked about key events or conversations.

At one stage, he said he could not remember details from a phone call he had that morning.

Mr Greenwood often responded to questions with "I don't know", and "I don't recall". (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

There were several tense exchanges and, at one point, Mr Greenwood snapped, saying to someone in the room: "Don't give me that look."

It is not clear who the 37-year-old was referring to, but the outburst earned him a scolding from Commissioner Fabian Gleeson SC, who reminded him to listen to questions and maintain respectful conduct and "decorum".

He was also pressed about a text exchange that emerged earlier in the inquiry, when he told lobbyist Jean-Claude Perrottet he had given him "filthy schools money" and had put up with his "f***ing whinging".

When asked about it, Mr Greenwood chalked it up to a "stupid joke" between friends, saying he was trying to rile Mr Perrottet.

But Counsel Assisting Peggy Dwyer SC put it to him that the "filthy schools money" referred to Catholic Schools NSW (CSNSW) funds allegedly being funnelled into Liberal Party recruitment.

There were tense exchanges between Mr Greenwood and Dr Dwyer this week. (Supplied: ICAC)

Mr Greenwood also said he could not recall what work his lobbying firm, Beckington, was doing for its client, Dallas McInerney, despite being paid $6,000 a month by the then-CSNSW CEO.

The commission has heard Mr Greenwood and his former business partner Christian Ellis allegedly used Beckington to issue "sham" invoices disguising prohibited political donations.

Monthly donations questioned

Mr McInerney, spent two days in the ICAC witness box this week, as one of the key figures in the inquiry.

He stood aside from the role after he was named in the ICAC's investigation.

As anticipated, he faced a barrage of questions over his dealings with federal Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, who was named earlier in the probe.

In the first week of hearings, the commission was shown a message Mr McInerney sent to NSW Reformers co-founder Robert Assaf about Mr Taylor, in which he declared: "I want to shake down Angus for 10k."

Mr McInerney gave evidence over two days and is due to return next week. (ABC News)

Another message, from former Liberal staffer Dylan Whitelaw, claimed Mr McInerney secured a $15,000 payment from Mr Taylor, and ongoing monthly donations of $3,000 for the Reformers' work.

Mr McInerney acknowledged seeking financial support from Mr Taylor but insisted it had nothing to do with the right-wing Liberal faction group, the NSW Reformers, a group at the centre of the inquiry.

He said it was instead intended to support NSW Liberal internal elections and conservative candidates in key seats.

Mr Taylor denied making any payment and is not accused of wrongdoing.

Who's up next at inquiry?

Mr McInerney is expected to appear again on Wednesday before former Liberal minister David Elliott takes the stand.

The ICAC is also examining whether donations linked to Mr Nassif were exchanged for political favours, including attempts to damage Mr Elliott's career.

It previously heard NSW Liberal Party operatives allegedly compiled a "David Elliott shit sheet" — a dossier of political and personal allegations aimed at damaging his career.

Mr Elliott is due to give evidence mid next week. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

Mr Whitelaw also told the commission Mr Greenwood and Mr Ellis claimed to have photographs of Mr Elliott involved in an alleged extramarital affair, although he was never shown them and accepted it may never have occurred.

Mr Greenwood said he commissioned the document to defend his business interests, rather than target Mr Elliott politically.

He also said he did not believe the allegation of an affair was true and said he received a photograph of Mr Elliott arriving home that he intended to use to suggest misconduct.

He alleged the photo was supplied by former Labor councillor and lawyer for fugitive developer Mr Nassif, Sharangan Maheswaran.

Mr Elliott rejected the allegations, previously telling Nine Newspapers he looked forward to the possibility of providing his "own observations".

In an intercepted phone call, Mr Nassif said of Ms Petinos: "She's 'gonna be my girl." (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

On Friday, Shadow Jobs and Industry Minister Eleni Petinos will become the second Liberal frontbencher to give evidence.

Ms Petinos is not accused of any wrongdoing.

An intercepted phone call played earlier in the inquiry suggested Mr Nassif believed she would replace then-fair trading minister Kevin Anderson in a cabinet reshuffle.

"I'm gonna step on his neck and strip him from his job," Mr Nassif said.

"Just give me two months, because the consumer affairs minister, she's 'gonna be my girl, and the fair-trading minister, she's 'gonna be one of my girls too."

Two months later, Ms Petinos replaced Mr Anderson in the reshuffle.

Former NSW building commissioner David Chandler resigned in 2022 following an investigation commissioned by Ms Petinos's office, but that was later reversed and he remained in the role until 2024.

World.title: NRLW's Roosters fly against Broncos amid controversy
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters have strengthened their grip on a second consecutive NRLW minor premiership by enacting a modicum of grand final revenge in a 34-20 victory against Brisbane.

In a stirring rematch of last year's decider, in which the Broncos triumphed, it was the Roosters' sparkling attack that proved the difference at Lang Park on Saturday.

However, the game was overshadowed by a controversial bunker decision to award Roosters winger Brydie Parker a try despite her teammate Jess Sergis pushing Broncos centre Deleni Paitai in the back in the lead-up to the 35th-minute score.

The Tricolours added another three unanswered four-pointers to their tally while prop Brianna Clark was sent to the sin bin for a dangerous tackle.

Although Ali Brigginshaw's stand-in Georgia Bartlett closed the deficit in the 56th minute, Parker brought up her hat-trick, and Sergis crossed again to keep the Roosters (7-0) undefeated.

After suffering its worst loss in club history to Canberra last round, Brisbane started hot by finding two of the first three tries through a speedy Tamika Upton and interchange Chelsea Lenarduzzi.

But on the stroke of half-time, a potential Broncos penalty try wasn't awarded despite winger Kerri Johnson getting tackled in the air centimetres from the line.

The Roosters, however, surged home to keep their one-win advantage on top of the ladder with four games to play.

Eels earn first win as Bulldogs suffer pair of sin-bins

At Western Sydney Stadium, a pair of damaging sin-binnings helped Parramatta end its winless start to the season as it weathered a willing Canterbury comeback to win 30-18.

Having lost their opening six games of the campaign, the Eels started fast as hooker Taneka Todhunter and halfback Rachael Pearson crashed over after Canterbury interchange Latisha Smythe was binned.

Even after the 22-year-old returned, both second-rower Mahalia Murphy and five-eighth Cassey Tohi-Hiku crossed to help Parramatta to a 22-0 half-time lead.

The Bulldogs thrust themselves into the contest when centre Monica Tagoai charged onto a pinpoint kick from Tayla Preston before substitute Evelyn Roberts and prop Alexis Tauaneai snared four-pointers.

But a second sin-bin to back-rower Tamika Jones for a hip-drop tackle proved costly as fullback Abbi Church went on a 95-metre tear to complete the victory.

Titans continue hot streak with sixth win in a row

Gold Coast claimed a sixth-consecutive win for the first time in the club's history and moved into second place, as they staved off St George Illawarra 26-10 at Robina Stadium.

Celebrating their 50th NRLW match, the Titans charged out of the gates, scoring three unanswered tries, but winger Maria Paseka stormed over to reduce the home team's lead to 14-4 at the break.

Prop Ruby-Jean Kennard-Ellis gave the Dragons hope of a major boilover, although Gold Coast flicked a switch, and a classy kick-and-chase by sevens convert Teagan Levi before a try to second-rower Evania Isa'ako sealed the victory.

AAP

World.title: Commissioner leading defence force reform wants to 'hold people to account'
World.content:
The woman tasked with helping to steer systemic change in Australia's defence force says she is not looking to simply tick a box.

For the first time since her appointment as the inaugural commissioner of the Defence and Veterans' Service Commission (DVSC) in May, Penny McKay has given her first interview.

"Change might not happen overnight. But we will be here for the long haul," she told the ABC.

The need for her role was born out of the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide, which concluded self-harm among veterans and serving members constituted a national crisis, driven by systemic and cultural failures.

And now, tucked away in a brick building, a stone's throw from Parliament House, she leads the organisation tasked with ensuring the response to the outcomes of that mammoth probe are more than just promises.

A task Ms McKay said her and her team are "not naive to".

Penny McKay, Defence and Veterans' Service Commissioner (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"We want to be transparent about what we're doing: our job is shine a light on what's happening in defence and in DVA and other agencies that are connected to wellbeing," she said.

" I want to hold people to account where required. "

In her first meeting with her hand-selected advisory group, she indicated the team's sights are trained on the government.

Is change possible?

The Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide asked for an independent, statutory authority with enhanced powers, to improve suicide prevention and wellbeing outcomes for serving and ex-serving members.

The Commissioner's role was created as a recommendation of the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide. (Supplied: ADF)

It essentially wanted and created a watchdog — someone to continue to promote change and accountability long after it tabled its final report.

Within the umbrella of wellbeing and suicide prevention falls an entire cache of issues: military sexual violence, bullying, culture, backlogs with compensation and service claims, mental health and more.

Before the Royal Commission even began, there were more than 50 inquiries and 750 recommendations made to Defence that had "little to no impact that they can see on the ground", according to Commissioner McKay.

She said she understands there's skepticism in the community about whether cultural change is possible.

"I'm keenly aware that the issues that we're dealing with are not new largely. In fact they're long-standing issues," she said.

Defence support services: The Defence all-hours Support Line is a confidential telephone and online service for ADF members and their families 1800 628 036

Open Arms provides 24-hour free and confidential counselling and support for current and former ADF members and their families 1800 011 046

Soldier On is a national support services provider for Defence personnel, contemporary veterans, and their families. Contact during office hours 1300 620 380

"Ideally I would like to promise that we can change the world, but I dare say that's a little bit naive.

"What I want to say is that we will try our damnedest to do it.

"The commission is looking for meaningful implementation of reform."

The organisation is set to lead an independent military sexual violence inquiry later this year; one of the first issues it is set to tackle.

Commissioner McKay wants the inquiry to be "future focused", which will come through hearing from those with firsthand knowledge.

"I think we're going to hear some really traumatic disturbing experiences from people with lived experience of military sexual violence," Commissioner McKay said.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government formally responded to the Royal Commission in 2024. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"What I would say to anybody who has experienced military sexual violence is that it's unacceptable and we want to make recommendations that will make real change, so we want to hear from you."

A date for the first hearings for the inquiry is yet to be said, and the government has not announced a deputy commissioner to lead it.

Recommendation implementation survey

The first meetings of the Commissioner's inaugural advisory group were held this month.

A total of 16 people from various military and non-military backgrounds were selected to provide advice to the Commission; including a reverend, a psychiatrist, a lawyer and several serving members.

The ABC was invited to film part of the first round table, where the question was asked just how many of the Royal Commission's 122 recommendations had been implemented.

Commissioner McKay met with the advisory group for the first time this month. (ABC News)

Veterans Affairs Minister, Matt Keogh, has previously said 32 recommendations had been implemented, with two-thirds expected to be implemented by the end of this year.

"The Defence and Veterans' Service Commission (DVSC) Inquiry into the progress made by Australian Government Agencies to implement the recommendations of the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide remains ongoing," a spokesperson for his office said in a statement.

Commissioner McKay is leading an inquiry into the implementations of the recommendations, which is to be reported to the government in early February next year.

She said she has not surveyed the implementation of all the recommendations yet, but "a number of the recommendations that have been reported as fully implemented, possibly won't be reported as fully implemented by the Commission".

The Defence and Veterans' Service Commission aims to drive systemic reform and cultural change in Defence. (Department of Defence: Andrew Sleeman)

Commissioner unfazed by lack of military experience

Commissioner McKay comes to the role with a wealth of experience in the legal field as a state, territory and commonwealth prosecutor, but she has never served or worked in defence.

It's a point she said she is frequently asked about, but believes it's not a disadvantage.

"My career from woe to go has had common threads of accountability, transparency and integrity," she said.

"I'm really interested and I'm really drawn to roles that require people to be held accountable for their actions and if they promise to do something, they do it."

She said she was married to a serviceman for 20 years served, her four children are defence kids and comes from a family with a proud military history.

ADF member feels like he has been 'treated like a problem' after DV attack A year on from the landmark Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide, ADF members say cultural issues have not been addressed.

"I think it's also important that the person in this role comes with fresh eyes, comes with independent eyes, doesn't have conflicts of interest that might mar what we say," she said.

It is enshrined in law that the Commissioner who leads the DVSC cannot have served within the past five years.

When asked how she's going to grade her performance during and at the end of her five-year tenure, Commissioner McKay said it'll be on three things: trust, structural and systemic change and change on the ground.

"If I can gain a level of trust in the veteran and defence community … if I can influence the departments and the governments to make those," she said.

"I also then think it's then about whether people on the ground — the veterans, the defence members, and their families — are really seeing positive change."

Commissioner McKay is unfazed by not having previously worked in defence. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Commissioner McKay said she's aware there's a lot of scepticism about whether the Commission will be able to deliver change, and a lot of hope placed in her to do so.

"I hope that that hope is not displaced. I will do everything that I can to make sure that it's not," she said.

"We will be here for the long haul, the commission is not here a one and done.

"We're going to be looking at issues over years and maintaining that focus on what has and what hasn't been done."

World.title: Victorian farmers welcome rain ahead of expected dry summer
World.content:
As some sunshine and clear skies begin to emerge across Victoria, many farmers across the state are both rejoicing and ruing recent heavy rainfall.

Some growers in western Victoria have lost up to 15 per cent of their crops, while others have turned to drones to spray crops in inaccessible paddocks after up to 150 millimetres of rain fell across the state and caused flooding last week.

But despite the wet conditions, spirits remain high, with the critical spring months ahead and the forecast El Niño weather pattern in spring and summer predicted to be one of the strongest on record.

Broadacre cropping farmer Russell Hocking has lost about 15 per cent of his crop to flooding.

He predicted he could lose a further 10 per cent of his crop, which is visibly waterlogged, if the paddocks do not dry up soon.

Operating across two properties at Prairie, north of Bendigo, and Werrimull, west of Mildura, Mr Hocking said he had experienced the good and the bad of the recent rain.

"The whole Mallee looks excellent, but our farm at Prairie is extremely wet," he said.

"The barley's pretty sick, lentils are very sick, the wheat and oats look okay.

" We're just sneaking by at the minute, but we're hopeful of a sunny, dry couple of weeks ahead. "

Both properties have already exceeded their average annual rainfall, with the Prairie farm getting 410mm so far this year, and Werrimull receiving 348mm.

An aerial photo taken on July 9 shows extensive flooding around Russell Hocking's Prairie property. (Supplied: Russell Hocking)

Both properties headed into sowing with more than 200mm of rain for the year.

By July, the conditions at Prairie had taken a turn for the worse.

A four-day deluge dumped 80mm on the property at the end of June and start of July and resulted in widespread flooding of low-lying crops.

In the past week, Prairie has received close to 40mm, while the farm at Werrimull had 25-30mm in the same rain event.

About 15 per cent of crops on Russell Hocking's Prairie farm have been lost. (Supplied: Russell Hocking)

However, Mr Hocking said he was "still quite positive" about the season, with a full profile of moisture heading into spring.

"The farm at Werrimull, I'd say barring a frost, it's hard to see things not being average, above or even well above average," Mr Hocking said.

Wet paddocks force aerial spraying

Agronomise farm consultant Simon Craig said the wet conditions had increased disease pressure, and a heightened demand for fungicide was resulting in supply shortages.

"Certainly, the rain has increased demand, and growers are probably going to have to be a little bit more open to looking at different chemical products," Mr Craig said.

He said the lack of availability was forcing growers to "think outside the box" to stay on top of disease.

He said growers needed to act now.

"A lot of the fungicide products we require in those crop types are protectants, so they've got to be applied before the disease appears in the crop," he said.

Simon Craig says growers have had to think outside the box to manage disease risk. (Supplied: Simon Craig)

Mr Craig said growers had to find a way to spray their paddocks or risk serious yield losses.

"There's a few other options now than what there was many years ago, like drone and helicopter spraying," he said.

Price-wise, Mr Craig said aerial spraying was more than double the cost of tractor spraying.

"You're looking at probably $8-$10 a hectare doing a contractor boom spray," he said.

"However, with a plane, you're probably looking anywhere between $24-$26 a hectare."

On the waiting list

South-west Victorian dairy farmer Craig Dwyer said he was on the waiting list for aerial spraying on his property at Bullaharre.

"We've had to get ourselves in the queue for the chopper, which I think is arriving midweek to put out our next batch of fertiliser," Mr Dwyer said.

" It's just too wet to traffic paddocks at the moment. "

Mr Dwyer said the property had almost reached its threshold for water, but after two years of drought, all rain was welcome.

"I don't think you'll ever hear me say the words, 'It's far too wet,'" he said.

'The dams are full'

In north-east Victoria, Lima East cattle farmer Damien Gerrans received just under 100mm last weekend.

"The dams are full and the creeks have burst their banks," Mr Gerrans said.

"It's the biggest rain event we've had in a while but the season has been great so far.

"We're still watching the long-range forecast for an early and dry summer, but this sets us up well.

The rain has flooded Mr Gerrans's low-lying country, and he has had to move his herd to higher ground.

"If they were still down on the flats they would be knee deep [in water]."

World.title: Fans line streets of Welsh village to farewell pop legend Bonnie Tyler
World.content:
Hundreds of fans have lined the streets of a seaside Welsh village to bid farewell to late singer Bonnie Tyler as her coffin was brought home.

The Grammy-nominated Welsh pop star, beloved worldwide for her 1983 chart-topping power ballad Total Eclipse of the Heart, died last month in a hospital in Portugal. She was 75.

Fans crowd the hearse carrying Bonnie Tyler as it makes its way to her Welsh hometown. (Alistair Grant)

Tyler was hospitalised in May in Faro, where she had a home, for emergency intestinal surgery.

Locals and fans from around the United Kingdom and beyond took to the streets of Mumbles, near the city of Swansea, to see the hearse, which carried her coffin, draped in a Welsh flag, on Saturday, August 15.

Dozens waited outside the singer's former home or left floral tributes there.

"She was always coming home and making sure that she came back to her fans in Wales," said Carys Edwards, 18.

" Her songs really did touch a lot of people here in Wales. We loved her a lot. "

Tyler was born Gaynor Hopkins, a coal miner's daughter in public housing with an outside toilet in Skewen, Wales, about 11 kilometres outside Swansea. She grew up with three sisters and two brothers.

The singer earned three Grammy nods, and in 2013 represented Britain at the Eurovision Song Contest, where she came 19th.

She was honoured as a Member of the Order of the British Empire in 2022 for her services to music by Queen Elizabeth II, thanks mainly to Total Eclipse of the Heart.

Beloved Welsh pop star Bonnie Welsh died in Portugal last month at age 75. (Alistair Grant)

The ballad shot to the top of the charts in Britain and the United States and has had more than 1 billion streams, boosted by real eclipses in 2017, 2024 — and most recently during this week's solar eclipse.

She was also known for other hits including It's a Heartache and Holding Out For a Hero, from the soundtrack of the film Footloose.

A celebration of Tyler's life for family and friends will take place at a church in Swansea on Monday, before the singer's coffin makes a final journey through her hometown of Skewen.

AP

World.title: Maguire fumes as Broncos season plunges further with 15th loss
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos coach Michael Maguire has said his side will be well beaten next week if they produce a similar performance to Saturday night's 40-6 defeat to the New Zealand Warriors.

The reigning premiers have had an awful season, with Saturday night's defeat their 15th of the campaign.

Brisbane was blown out of the water early at Lang Park, with the Warriors scoring three quick tries as the Auckland-based side kept the pressure on the Sydney Roosters and Penrith Panthers in the race for the minor premiership.

Metcalf, Walsh injured as Warriors thrash Broncos Warriors half Luke Metcalf has suffered yet another injury in a defeat of Brisbane.

Maguire has defended his players throughout the 2026 campaign, but after Saturday's 34-point defeat, where the Broncos never looked in the contest, he let his players know in the post-match press conference that the effort was not up to standard.

“Not good enough, just plain and simple. We won’t want to do that next weekend because we’ll cop the same," he said.

"It was really disappointing, that one. We’re not playing the style that we know we’ve practised."

Brisbane faces last year's minor premier Canberra next week, with the Raiders also having a poor season and out of finals contention.

But on the same day Brisbane struggled to fire, the Raiders produced an upset win over top-four aspirants Cronulla.

Brisbane's stand-in captain Pat Carrigan was asked by a reporter on Saturday night if it was hard to remain motivated for the remaining matches with finals out of the picture.

But Maguire stepped in and answered.

“I reckon that’s garbage. We’re playing the team next week [Canberra] that’s in the same boat. We’re playing for the Broncos,” Maguire said.

“It’s easy to motivate people when you’re playing for the Broncos. They’re playing for a very good club.

“The boys are playing for the Broncos jersey that they wear. That is not good enough. I normally keep calm at these things. We need to have a good hard look at ourselves.”

Brisbane is still a chance of finishing last this season, if the St George Illawarra Dragons defeat Wests Tigers on Sunday.

World.title: Housing project to help domestic violence survivors secure rental
World.content:
Kathleen Hope has been working with domestic violence victim-survivors for 15years and is acutely aware of how hard it can be for them to start again.

"The barriers are limitless, but right now we have a housing affordability and availability crisis, plus the costs here on the Sunshine Coast are extraordinary," the SunnyKids CEO said.

"When you have to start from scratch, when everything you have built up in your life is gone, you're dealing with your trauma and your children are dealing with trauma … finding a rental under those conditions is absolutely impossible."

But now there is a much-needed lifeline in the Queensland charity's transitional housing project.

The kitchens are fully equipped for families to use. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Six townhouses have been built and will be available for women and their children to lease at a significantly reduced rate, with no rental history required.

"We're putting safety nets around these families who leave our emergency high-security refuge. We're looking at anywhere from six months to two years [lease]," Ms Hope said.

"The house is fully furnished, right down to the bed linen and face washers. We really want this to be a fresh start for those who have been through way too much.

"Ninety per cent of the time, they're leaving with nothing.

" The cost of storing items, removalists, all things like that, is not a priority for families who are fleeing in the middle of the night because of violence they've experienced. "

The townhouses include three bedrooms, with fully-furnished children's rooms. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

From the ground up

Funding the $6 million project has been a community effort.

More than 70 Sunshine Coast businesses, tradespeople and suppliers donated their time, materials and services towards the construction of another home on the Sunshine Coast, which was then auctioned off to raise money for the build.

"We've had community support, fundraising, plus private wealth and philanthropy — it's just been amazing," Ms Hope said.

Dozens of businesses donated their services and materials to build a home that was then auctioned off for the charity. (Supplied: SunnyKids)

The land and funding for three of the townhouses were donated by Peter and Ann Smales from Firefly Education.

The Sunshine Coast couple introduced SunnyKids to builder James McCartney, who was more than happy to lend a hand.

"Domestic violence is a massive problem Australia-wide. We hear about it on the news. Every week another woman gets killed," Mr McCartney said.

The builder said it was heartbreaking to see women and children struggle in the region's tight rental market, where the vacancy rate was less than 1 per cent, according to Real Estate Institute of Queensland figures.

"I've seen women and kids sleeping just up the road, sleeping in cars. They must have an absolutely shocking life. It doesn't make you feel good," Mr McCartney said.

" To move into something like this must be just unbelievable. They'd feel like they've won the lotto. "

The homes include donated cubby houses. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Huge demand for rentals

Real estate agency principal Jodi Price will manage the townhouses on behalf of SunnyKids.

"This is a really good way that we can help get clients into the long-term rental market," Ms Price said.

"They're having a proper rental history, routine inspections, we'll be able to provide more support and training around how to be good tenants and what expectations are in the long run."

Kathleen Hope with Jodi Price, whose real estate agency will manage the property. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

She said "affordable" rentals on the Sunshine Coast averaged $700 to $800 a week and typically attracted 30 to 50 applicants.

"To be at the top of the pile of that pool is really important because owners have so much choice that you need to be able to tick every box," Ms Price said.

After three years working on the project, Ms Hope said it was an "emotional day" to receive the keys for the properties, which she believed would save lives.

"A lot of people will choose to stay in an unsafe environment because they don't have any other choice," she said.

"We've got big plans … but this is absolutely a model that can be replicated.

"This is the community really putting their money where their mouth is and jumping on board."

World.title: Are the parents all right? Why raising children feels harder than ever
World.content:
Genevieve Muir, with her two younger sons, says parents have far more knowledge about child development available to them now, which can add to a sense of pressure about how they do the job.

In the first part of a new series on modern parenting, we look at why mums and dads are in such a state of distress, and how being “good enough” actually really is enough.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

She is the daughter of a family therapist and has a social work degree but, still, parenting in 2026 is so complex that Genevieve Muir likens it to “learning an entirely new language” to the one known to previous generations. Thirty years on from when a Californian sociology professor coined “intensive parenting” for the engagement-heavy style that became the benchmark for western child-rearing, parent educator Muir sees people struggling – sometimes “sinking”. The mother of four is frank about her early battle not to lose it herself. Muir has worked with 40,000 parents and thought hard on the question, “is parenting more personally demanding now (in well-off countries) than in the past, or does it just feel that way?” “It’s my favourite subject,” says Muir, whose sons are aged 9, 12, 15 and 17. Western parents – often influenced by “child-centred, expert-guided, emotionally absorbing, labour and financially expensive” intensive parenting – certainly think it is tougher. This is reflected in Pew Research Centre data showing 70 per cent believe it is harder than two or three decades ago. Genevieve Muir, who has helped more than 40,000 parents, says raising children is now like “learning an entirely new language”. Wolter Peeters Fears for their kids’ mental health topped the list of parents’ worries in that 2023 study, but by the middle of this year, both the American chief medical officer and the Australian Parenting Research Centre (PRC) had issued warnings about parents’ own perilous psychological state.



In May, Australia’s largest study of parents and carers, the PRC’s Parenting Today, found almost 60 per cent of the 10,000 surveyed were in moderate or high level psychological distress, struggling with loneliness, self-doubt and lack of self-compassion. The Victorian government and Minderoo Foundation-funded research found 57 per cent of parents feel lonely as carers, 43 per cent feel guilty, and 47 per cent think they are not doing as well as they should be. A staggering 53 per cent “could not forgive themselves for their parenting mistakes”. Related Article Motherhood ‘Thanks, Mum, but I don’t want your life’ – is the load that buckled their mothers putting off Gen Z? Parental wellbeing declined steadily over the past decade, 66 per cent feel sleep-deprived, and nearly half have persistent self-doubt. Dr Vivek Murthy, the US Surgeon General, warned two years ago that chronic parental stress had become “a critical public health issue”, blaming “new stressors that previous generations didn’t have to consider”. Muir sees societal changes and the shift towards engagement-heavy parenting in which the stakes feel high as two drivers of the quiet desperation. Work-life has changed, a sense of village has declined, and economic pressure has ramped up so much that two incomes are often vital. “We have new knowledge about what kids need, so on top of work we’re intensively parenting,” says Muir. “Now, most people only have one or two kids, and we really put a lot of hope into how they will turn out; there is more fear and more comparison.”



Feeling they need to “optimise” all aspects of childhood, rather than just rearing children like parents of the past, has seriously upped the psychological stress. Information overload – seeing endless content about concepts once confined to clinicians or academics, such as attachment theory, neurological or behavioral science, and child psychology – adds to confusion and self-doubt. This is supported by Daniela McCann, director at the Australian Psychological Association who says the fast-moving stream of expert advice, information, social comparison and messaging about optimising child development can be overwhelming. “While that greater knowledge can be really beneficial, the downside is it creates pressure and anxiety; thinking that the standards of good parenting are exceptionally high and mistakes have long-term consequences.” Technology’s intrusion into the way day-to-day life runs for both parents and kids puts pressure on parents psychologically because it promotes negative feelings about their performance, says child health specialist and parenting expert Dr Kaylene Henderson. Dr Kaylene Henderson (with her children, who prefer their names not being published), says parents are carrying a heavier load now than in the past.



“For the first time, a generation of parents is expected to be connected to workplaces even when they’re at home, and that means mental presence for children isn’t always possible,” she says. “That very much contributes to parental guilt.” A well-intentioned vicious cycle The “guilt and shame” that Murthy says is pervasive among parents he has met across America got a big mention in his health advisory. Henderson says parents feel they need to be so vigilant in part because of the loss of a sense of safety and community they grew up with. They sense their kids need far more supervision than they had, and this at a time when more couple families have both parents working full-time even from early on. “Parents are definitely more stressed, and more anxious,” Henderson says, and children “definitely seem less resilient, and less capable than they once might have been – we are stuck in a very well-intentioned vicious cycle”. “Everyone is trying to do their best, but the load feels much heavier,” says the mother of two girls and a boy aged 18, 16 and 14 respectively.



McCann, a pyschologist, agrees, saying parenting has “broadened” for this generation and, while her own parents would have considered something like being bullied at school to be primarily the child’s problem to navigate, now “parents are expected to be caregivers, educators, digital safety monitors, emotion coaches and advocates for all things.” As well as being more hands-off, past parents had little access to anxiety-inducing information about the minutiae of children’s day-to-day lives. “That expansion to the parenting role has really made it not just feel more complex and emotionally demanding, it actually is [more so] than it was for families of a generation or two ago,” McCann says. Related Article Childcare Four weeks of leave, 12 of school holidays: The parenting equation that doesn’t add up Because schools are aware that more children are anxious, they are adding more communication to the already vastly increased amount sent home in the past. Henderson describes it as “schools calling out louder to parents through their inbox”, even though the attention of many parents is maxed out. Her reassuring mantra is that simply focusing on the foundational relationship parents have with their children supports both to thrive, and that relationship guides the majority of long-term outcomes parents all hope for. “We’re the first generation of parents who’ve had access to research that can guide the way we interact with our children, which is positive, but that’s not what’s getting out there – it’s [content by] people with a marketing budget,” says Henderson. She entered the parent education scene because she felt some information being pitched at parents was setting them up to fail, and “that felt unfair and cruel”.

World.title: There’s no more Mother and Son, but Denise Scott has found a new path to travel
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV There’s no more Mother and Son, but Denise Scott has found a new path to travel Bridget McManus August 16, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Denise Scott was a reluctant genealogical traveller the first time around, declaring a complete lack of interest in her lineage on the 2020 season of Who Do You Think You Are? But when Shaun Micallef came knocking for his looser version of the format, Scott thought it was time to have another crack, and maybe mend a fence with her former Vega FM co-host. Not that the pair were the Kyle and Jackie O of mid-noughties Melbourne radio. But, failing to gel on air, they’d avoided each other ever since. Travelling to the medieval town of Goslar in Germany, to research Scott’s missing maternal line, they reconnected over wurst, silver mining and yodelling. Denise Scott and Shaun Micallef in Germany for season two of Origin Odyssey. “Shaun and I are awkward with one another, at the best of times,” says Scott. “On the radio, we were on different planes. I’d be talking about my partner John’s farts and Shaun would be talking about aliens arriving in ant form … So walking into Goslar together, and there’s the mountains and there’s the cathedral with the bells ringing and the cobblestones … And having nonsensical banter in the most beautiful place in the world, I loved it.” This second season of Shaun Micallef’s Origin Odyssey also features Pia Miranda, Tony Armstrong, Kate Langbroek, and Matt Okine, Scott’s co-star in the ABC reboot of the Ruth Cracknell-Garry McDonald sitcom Mother and Son, which has ended after two seasons.



“I’m relieved I won’t have neighbours in the street going, ‘Oh, I like you, Denise, but you’re no Ruth Cracknell’,” she says, laughing. “I do think the show was great. But there was that shadow … Even my oncologist was absolutely horrified. Not about my cancer, about the fact that I was doing a remake of Mother and Son.” Editor's pick Exit Interview

Australian TV ‘I felt a little bit of impostor syndrome’: How a sandwich guy claimed the MasterChef title She filmed Origin Odyssey a year after her treatment for breast cancer. “I was uncertain as to whether I could do it, physically, because it’s a really tight turnaround,” she says. “You fly to Frankfurt, start filming as soon as you get off the plane, and then you’re up early for five days, and then you’re back on the plane to Melbourne. “It was kind of easy in that I really respect Shaun. I think what he does is brilliant, and I suspect that he might have some respect for me. And we talked non-stop. He was very into talking caringly about my cancer. Actually, it would get funny at times, but he was interested and very empathetic.”



Shaun Micallef with Denise Scott’s Mother and Son co-star Matt Okine in Ghana for Origin Odyssey. In Goslar, Scott learnt about her maternal great-great-great-grandfather, Carl Boch, a miner who migrated to Australia. This branch of her family tree had remained unclimbed, out of respect for her late mother Margaret, the source of much of Scott’s stand-up material. (Scott’s now back on the road with a limited tour of her Melbourne International Comedy Festival show, Tickety Boo.) Related Article Australian TV ‘It’s not easy. It’s not glamorous’: How Matt Preston found a renewed sense of purpose on TV Scott isn’t sure what Margaret would have made of her discoveries in Germany. But the past few years have prompted her to rethink her assessment of her mother’s life as “tiny”. “When I was diagnosed with cancer, I was sitting in the hospital and I looked out the window in Heidelberg – in Melbourne, not Germany – and I could see the school I went to, the train line that I travelled on till I was 18,” she recalls. “I saw the church where my parents were married. I saw the small hospital where my dad died, and the road that you travel on to get to my house that I’ve lived in for the last 45 years.



“And that’s when I thought, ‘F---, my life is small! Why did I ever think it was big?’ In my own head, I thought it was quite an amazing, edgy, big kind of life. And I realised it’s tiny. And then [I thought about] my mum, who I did criticise for having a tiny life, and I realised, ‘No, she just had a life she liked, and she had a garden, and she had her friends and, gosh, it was very, very similar.’” Shaun Micallef’s Origin Odyssey returns at 7.30pm on Tuesday, August 18, on SBS and SBS On Demand.
