World.title: LNG document should not have been hidden, ombudsman says
World.content:
Officials should not have withheld a key document behind the government's decision to proceed with a "divisive" LNG terminal, the chief ombudsman has ruled.

The document - released in full following the ruling - concluded access to liquefied natural gas (LNG) was unlikely to affect average electricity prices and there were other ways to improve New Zealand's energy security.

The climate advocacy group that laid the complaint said the lack of transparency over such an expensive and contentious project was concerning.

The document summarises the findings of Concept Consulting, which the Ministry for Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) commissioned to model the effect of building the LNG facility.

The ministry has downplayed the consultants' conclusions, saying the set of slides was a "draft of an informal working document" and therefore officials did not correct anything they disagreed with.

However, Chief Ombudsman John Allen found the document provided "important context and limitations" for the advice and modelling.

He found the reasons for withholding it were not valid, and even if they were, there was "very high" public interest in releasing it, especially in an election year.

The government confirmed its plans for a Taranaki LNG facility in June. RNZ / Louis Dunham

"The government's plans for an LNG import facility in Taranaki has proven divisive," he wrote.

"There is also accountably in the expenditure of public funds, and I note that the plan is estimated to cost upwards of $1 billion."

Rather than a rough draft, the document was "fairly advanced", Allen said in his decision.

"MBIE had already engaged in back and forth with Concept and had the chance to improve on and refine its earlier drafts."

LNG will not help with electricity prices most years - document

The government confirmed in June it was proceeding with plans for a facility in Taranaki, saying importing liquefied natural gas was the best option to see off a "dry year" risk, when hydro lake levels are low, while more renewable energy was developed.

A group of 11 climate and consumer advocacy organisations wrote to the Auditor-General earlier this week, urging his office to open an inquiry into the procurement process.

RNZ has previously reported on a partially-unredacted version of the consultants' document, which revealed there was "low need" for LNG imports.

The latest version includes a summary slide, labelled 'Key insights', which concluded that access to LNG "shouldn't materially affect average electricity prices".

Proposed LNG import terminal unlikely to cause disruption Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

LNG access "should" reduce prices in the most extreme dry years, the document said.

However, that was only if renewables did not keep up with demand growth, there was further decline in domestic gas supplies - beyond what was projected - or there was a "black swan" event where all of the coal-burning units at Huntly Power Station were out of action.

"Other resources can provide a similar system security service to LNG", the document concluded.

The alternatives it had modelled included coal at Huntly, extra underground gas storage - such as one proposed at Tariki gas field - and building even more geothermal, wind and solar generation capacity.

The government has said that having an LNG facility would save households $265 million a year, because the security it will provide would help to cut forward prices on the energy market.

It has since pointed to a fall in those future prices, attributing that to the LNG announcement.

The Electricity Authority - among others - has attributed the fall in prices to a glut of renewables coming online, with more planned for the near future.

Multiple groups have said falling prices to renewables coming online. RNZ

Lawyers for Climate Action spokesperson Laura MacKay, whose organisation complained to the ombudsman, said a promised reduction in electricity prices had been "a key justification" for LNG.

The new information undermined that argument, she said.

"The absolute key point for me is why have these particular conclusions been withheld?

"It's confusing, and I do honestly find the lack of transparency really concerning."

Her organisation had first asked for a full version of the document in February,

"If LNG is such a good idea, why has it been so difficult to access this kind of relevant and important information?"

MBIE withheld gas supply data

Both MBIE and the government have criticised Concept Consulting's modelling since the first set of redactions were lifted in June, saying it relied on "optimistic" assumptions about domestic gas supply.

The latest version of the document shows the consultants considered their assumptions, which used MBIE's own low-end projections, were "conservative".

Emails previously released to RNZ show ministry officials worked closely with Concept Consulting to develop the scenarios the model tested.

However, a letter from MBIE accompanying the newly-released document reveals the ministry did not share the latest gas supply data it had with the agency.

"That data showed that gas reserves had dropped by 23 percent relative to the previous year's estimates," energy markets policy director Rebecca Heerdegen wrote.

"At the time, rather than revealing commercially sensitive information, we did not correct or engage with Concept's opinion that the gas assumptions are conservative."

Because the work the ministry had commissioned was the modelling outputs themselves, "we did not seek to correct Concept on opinions they expressed in the slide pack where we disagreed or held additional information that Concept was not privy to," she wrote.

Concept has since independently completed further modelling, with the results drawing similar conclusions to its original report.

In an additional report it created for the four electricity gentailers last month, it repeated its earlier findings that many of the factors that led to high energy prices in 2024 no longer existed.

"The dry-year problem is not getting worse - indeed the overbuild of renewables is reducing the need for flexibility resources from thermals or demand response."

RNZ asked Energy Minister Simeon Brown whether the government is still planning to sign contracts for the LNG facility prior to the election.

Brown said the procurement process was well advanced and was commercially sensitive as discussions continued with two parties.

"The Government expects to make a decision before the election. As I announced in June, the Government is negotiating with the gentailers on a fair funding model as part of the sector taking responsibility for the dry year problem.

"New Zealand's energy scene is changing. The expected closure of the Māui gas field and Methanex likely ceasing operations in New Zealand means that next time we have a dry year, we won't have the only safety net that prevented a full energy crisis in winter 2024."

Brown said the government was committed to ensuring New Zealanders had access to "affordable and reliable power".

"New Zealand needs back up generation when faced with a dry year, with MBIE having assessed 11 options for managing the dry year risk. That analysis found LNG was the lead option to terms of providing that back up generation, can be delivered quickly, and will provide spillover benefits to other parts of the economy."

World.title: Water back in Porirua after burst pipe caused outages
World.content:
Water is back in Porirua after a burst pipe left parts of the city with widespread outages.

Tiaki Wai said crews worked late into the night to repair the pipe that led to outages for the city centre, Rānui, and Elsdon.

At around 2:20pm on Saturday a 300mm main burst on Mepham Place causing asphalt on the road to crack.

Pātaka Art + Museum, Café Kaizen, Porirua Library, and Te Rauparaha Arena and Aquatic Centre had all closed due to the burst pipe.

World.title: Taranaki Kōkako recovery to get $1 million boost
World.content:
A funding boost will enable a Taranaki conservation group to extend work protecting the region's recovering Kōkako population.

The East Taranaki Environment Collective (ETEC) has received $603,760 from the Department of Conservation Fund.

It will be used for predator control, habitat restoration, and monitoring across more than 46,000 hectares of native forest and ecosystems in north-eastern Taranaki.

Kōkako population soars in Hunua Ranges Nine To Noon Download MP3 8m

Meanwhile, Te Kāhui o Taranaki will receive $432,840 to map, monitor and restore critically endangered coastal turf ecosystems within the Taranaki Iwi rohe.

The Iwi-led project would carry out restoration planting and involve local communities in the long-term protection of this rare habitat.

ETEC welcomed the investment in its North-East Taranaki Kōkako Landscape Project, which was also expected to leverage more than $1 million in additional cash and in-kind support from partners, landowners, organisations and volunteers.

Project partners included Te Runanga o Ngāti Tama, Tiaki Te Mauri o Parininihi Trust, Ngāti Maru, Te Runanga o Ngāti Mutunga, East Taranaki Environment Collective and NZTA Te Ara o te Ata Pest Management Area.

Tiaki Te Mauri o Parininihi Trust chair, Davis McClutchie, said the funding was significant for kōkako recovery in Taranaki.

"The successful recovery of kōkako requires much more than moving birds. It relies on long-term investment in predator control, habitat restoration, monitoring, and strong partnerships between iwi, landowners, community groups, and agencies.

"This funding enables us to continue that work at scale while creating valuable opportunities for our uri and community partners to build skills and knowledge through kōkako surveys, monitoring programmes, field training, and hands-on conservation experience."

McClutchie said building local capability was critical to the long-term success of the kaupapa.

Conservationists determined to bring back North Island Kokako Afternoons Download MP3 12m

"By involving whānau and communities in monitoring and management, we are growing the next generation of kaitiaki while strengthening the collective effort needed to restore biodiversity across the north and eastern Taranaki landscape.

"Kōkako are becoming a powerful symbol of what can be achieved when people come together with a shared vision for the future of our environment and the wellbeing of generations to come."

The investment came at an exciting time for kōkako recovery in Taranaki, he said.

Monitoring showed encouraging signs that populations were breeding, expanding and potentially reconnecting across the wider landscape, reflecting years of sustained predator control and habitat protection.

ETEC Chair Rob Maetzig said the funding was more than an investment in a single organisation.

"This project focuses on joined-up action to protect kōkako populations in North East Taranaki. It is also a major win for the wider collaboration underway and a step towards the vision of an Eastern Taranaki biodiversity corridor, stretching from Parininihi to Whanganui National Park."

Maetzig said no single organisation could achieve landscape-scale conservation alone.

"The success of this work depends on strong relationships between iwi, community groups, landowners, funders, councils, businesses and government agencies. This funding helps strengthen those relationships and accelerate the work already happening on the ground."

The project demonstrated how government investment can amplify community effort and attract co-investment, he said.

"Together we are creating healthier forests, stronger wildlife populations and a more resilient landscape for future generations."

Conservation Minister Tama Potaka said the Taranaki organisations were valuable allies in the battle to restore habitats.

"This is what good conservation investment looks like. Government backing local ambition, with Iwi, landowners, community groups and volunteers bringing funding, time, expertise, and practical support to the table."

Potaka said that through collaboration, taxpayer funding could achieve greater outcomes.

"From the coast to the ngahere, this is mahi tahi in action. Our government, Iwi, landowners, community groups, and volunteers combining their strengths to deliver lasting gains for Taranaki's environment."

World.title: Hamilton knife attack puts four people in hospital
World.content:
A knife attack in Kirikiriroa Hamilton has put four people in hospital, one with critical injuries and another serious.

The police said a 23-year-old man was in custody and they want to reassure people they didn't believe there was an ongoing threat, after what they said would have been a disruptive and frightening time for people in the suburb of Maeroa.

Emergency services were called to Churchill Avenue around 9pm on Saturday.

The police said as the attack unfolded, one victim fled on foot to seek help at a nearby property and was followed there by the offender.

It is alleged that an occupant there fired a gun, but caused no injury.

The police said the arrested man would face charges, and was asking for anyone with relevant information to contact them.

World.title: NZ Warriors overwhelm Broncos at Suncorp Stadium, but lose Luke Metcalf to injury
World.content:
NZ Warriors have overcome another injury to star halfback Luke Metcalf to dominate reigning NRL champions the Brisbane Broncos 40-6 and consolidate their top-four spot on the competition table.

Enjoying strong support at their second 'home', Suncorp Stadium, the Warriors quickly found their stride, with second-rower Jacob Laban and five-eighth Chanel Harris-Tavita crossing for early tries.

They lost fullback Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad to the sin bin for a hipdrop tackle that sent counterpart Reece Walsh out of the game with an ankle injury, but wing Alofiana Khan-Pereira intercepted a pass on his own goal-line and sprinted the length of the field to extend the margin.

Metcalf slotted the conversion, but immediately grabbed his right hamstring and left the field, leaving his team in disarray as they reorganised their backline.

Two penalties to Harris-Tavita saw the Warriors earn a 20-0 halftime advantage, before Nicoll-Klokstad scored early in the second half to continue the avalanche of points.

Wing Dallin Watene-Zelezniak scored with a trademark dive at the corner flag and centre Ali Leiataua taunted the defence with a palmed dummy pass, before powering over himself.

As the scoreboard ticked over, the Warriors drew within eight points of the second-placed Penrith Panthers on points differential, but conceded a soft try to Kiwis front-rower Xavier Willison that set them back.

Centre Leka Halasima began to cramp up late, but shrugged that off to save a try and then score one himself at the other end, as the Warriors had the final say.

They remain in third place on the ladder, two points behind leaders Sydney Roosters and level with the Panthers, trailling by 10 on differential.

World.title: Canterbury hold out Bay of Plenty to retain Ranfurly Shield
World.content:
Canterbury have held on to the Ranfurly Shield with a thrilling 33-28 win over Bay of Plenty at Te Kaha Stadium in Christchurch.

It was their first defence - after they beat Otago last weekend - but it was looking decidedly shaky with 14 minutes to go when the scores were locked at 28-all.

It had been 21-7 to Canterbury at halftime, with the holders notching three tries after having a decided edge in possession and territory.

Bay of Plenty scored just before halftime from a tap penalty, but their challenge looked to be going backwards when Ngane Punivai scored for Canterbury early in the second half.

But the momentum shifted big-time with the Steamers roaring back into the game, scoring three tries to level up the scores.

Canterbury hit back with a try to Toby Bell with 10 minutes to go and then had some nervous moments after a try by Andrew Knewstubb was ruled out. Bay of Plenty mounted a sustained attack taking the game into added time before a knock-on sealed their fate.

Canterbury will defend the shield again on Thursday when they host Northland.

In other matches on Saturday, Otago scored three tries in the last 10 minutes to pip Manawatū 29-27 in Palmerston North, while Hawke's Bay came from behind to beat Auckland 44-31.

World.title: Water main bursts in Porirua, causing hours of disruption
World.content:
A burst water main in Porirua was being repaired on Saturday night, with water outages expected to end around 10.30pm.

A 300mm main burst on Mepham Place around 2:20pm on Saturday, causing asphalt on the road to crack.

That led to outages for the city centre, Rānui, and Elsdon.

"It is anticipated that service will be interrupted for at least eight hours," mayor Anita Baker said on Saturday afternoon.

Pātaka Art + Museum, Café Kaizen, Porirua Library, and Te Rauparaha Arena and Aquatic Centre all closed as a result of the burst water main.

A water tank was ordered for affected residents.

In the following hours, Tiaki Wai confirmed the outages had been contained to numbers 1-16 on Champion Street and all of Mepham Place.

World.title: Auckland Airport enters next phase of international terminal redevelopment
World.content:
Auckland Airport is moving into the next phase of its international terminal redevelopment, with retail and duty-free areas being refurbished for departing and arriving travellers.

The airport said the retail upgrade is its most significant airside refurbishment in a decade.

Work is underway on duty-free areas at international departures and arrivals, including two stores near departure gates.

The airport said the refurbished areas will have new layouts and a wider range of products, with beauty and fragrance at the centre of the changes.

Auckland Airport Chief Commercial Officer Mark Thomson said the changes are aimed at giving travellers a more engaging experience and greater choice.

"This is a deliberate move to strengthen our retail mix, provide an enhanced customer proposition, and modernise the space."

The redevelopment will also include new standalone retail stores, while the airport said further improvements to food and beverage areas are planned later this year.

Two standalone stores due to open later this year are skincare and bodycare brand Aesop and French fragrance brand Le Labo.

Some of the refurbished duty-free areas have already reopened, with the remaining retail refurbishment expected to be completed by December.

The airport said the overall footprint of its duty-free area will not increase as part of the redevelopment.

The international terminal transformation has been underway since January, with the work being carried out in stages while the terminal remains operational.

World.title: Warming climate forcing marathon changes to keep runners cool
World.content:
Paul Grinvalds has completed 114 marathons in all 50 US states, but he still wilts when he races in temperatures beyond 16 degrees Celsius.

It's the same for most runners, as the body can't cool down during exertion, and heat makes that even harder.

"One thing about marathoners is typically we're kind of stubborn," Grinvalds, 68, said.

"So if we have a goal and it's hot, a lot of times we're still going to try to do that goal, which is just stupid because you're almost guaranteed to have a very painful experience."

Such an experience can also be dangerous, a reality that marathon organisers are having to confront as climate change, caused mostly by the burning of fuels like coal and gasoline, pushes temperatures up.

Hotter temperatures are forcing marathon organisers to rethink when they hold events. (AP: Charlie Neibergall)

To improve the chances of having the 42-kilometre race in cooler weather, organisers are shifting race dates, starting earlier and even giving options for participants to cut their runs short.

Organisers of the Sioux Falls, South Dakota, marathon last year similarly moved their annual race from August to September after cancelling the 2024 race due to hot conditions.

Other races across the United States, including the Air Force Marathon in Dayton, Ohio, the Little Rock Marathon in Arkansas, and the Long Beach Marathon in Southern California have also moved start times to earlier in the morning in search of cooler temperatures.

In Los Angeles in March, warm conditions prompted race organisers to give runners the option of stopping after 18 miles and still receiving a finisher's medal.

Less than 5 per cent of participants opted for the shorter finish and only 14 of roughly 27,000 runners were treated at a hospital, with all released the same day. Still, the move led to some online derision.

"We welcome the feedback and it's certainly something that caused a lot of discussion, but when we're grading ourselves on it, it has to do with how safe our runners were on the day of the event and we're very happy with the outcome," Meg Treat, a spokesperson for the marathon said.

At the Twin Cities Marathon, race director Ed Whetham called the decision to cancel the 2023 marathon "devastating" for runners and the organisation.

Whetham said it prompted an extensive analysis of weather patterns that resulted in the decision to permanently delay the race by a couple of weeks.

That analysis showed that by holding the race later in October, runners would have a far greater chance of optimal conditions.

Given that snow sometimes falls in the Twin Cities in late October, there is a greater chance of chilly conditions, but Whetham said, "We'll take a 39-degree (4C) start over a 70-degree (21C) start."

Temperatures are expected to keep rising

The contiguous US just had its warmest July ever recorded this year, and the Earth had its hottest year on record in 2024.

The World Meteorological Organization forecasts that between 2025 and 2030 the Earth's average global temperature will likely rise by more than 1.5C compared to the 1800s.

Why the world's top aerial skiers went Queensland The world's top skiers are heading to Brisbane for the final leg of the International Ski and Snowboard Federation Grand Prix this weekend. It might be the first of many for more reasons than one.

The warming is already making conditions worse for most marathons, according to a study of 221 races by the climate research group Climate Central.

By 2045, optimal conditions for recreational runners — 6-7C — would be less likely at 46 of the 51 US marathons analysed.

"The ability to go outside, to exercise, to take advantage of your human body and being healthy, that's something that's getting challenged by climate change," Andy Pershing, who led the Climate Central research, said.

Jessica Murfree leads a University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill lab studying climate change's effect on sports.

She said organisers of marathons, bicycle races and other competitions — from tennis to college American football — increasingly must consider changing event dates and times and adopting other safety measures, as climate change makes the weather hotter and more volatile.

Murfree said the concern extends beyond organised sports to whether people can even get outside on increasingly warm days, pushing people to exercise indoors or opt for activities like swimming.

"If we can't walk, if we can't exercise or go for runs, it's too hot, can we still stay physically active while remaining cool?" she asked.

Marathons are especially hard in warm weather

Any kind of exercising in the heat can be challenging, but running a marathon in warm, humid conditions is especially difficult because it's hard to prevent overheating when a person keeps pushing themselves for hours.

And the faster a person goes, the more heat their body produces.

Chris Minson, a University of Oregon professor who researches how people can adapt to extreme heat and other environmental conditions, said the optimum temperature to run a marathon is about 10C.

As the temperature creeps in the mid to high teens, the body has a tougher time supplying blood to muscles while also keeping the body cool.

"As you get to warmer temperatures you end up having a bigger competition between blood supplying your muscles to keep running, to keep nutrition going, and blood flow to your skin for thermal regulation," Minson said.

Minson said it takes a tremendous amount of energy to run quickly. But of that energy, only about 25 per cent is used to move the body forward. The rest goes to deal with the heat that is created by rapid movement.

Even worse than high temperatures is high humidity, which prevents sweat from evaporating and cooling the body.

Minson added that by regularly exercising in warm weather, people can acclimate to high temperatures and perform better in the heat, though likely not as well as they would in cooler conditions.

Athletes who acclimate to high heat also can perform better in lower temperatures than if they had not exercised in warm weather, he said.

Douglas Casa, a kinesiology professor who leads the Korey Stringer Institute, which studies sudden deaths in sports, said the Twin Cities Marathon's change was prudent, especially considering the way in which many runners approach races.

"If someone was smart enough to say, 'OK, it's a little hotter today than usual, I'm going to run a 7-minute mile instead of a 6:30 mile,' then they won't get any hotter than normal," Casa said.

"It's just that runners are sometimes very locked into what they normally do and what their goals are."

World.title: NRL updates: Metcalf, Walsh injured as Warriors thrash Broncos
World.content:
Luckless Warriors half Luke Metcalf has suffered yet another injury in a 40-6 defeat of Brisbane, who lost their own superstar Reece Walsh to a possibly season-ending ankle issue.

The third-placed Warriors drew level on competition points with Penrith in second place, but are now poised to lose another playmaker on the run to the NRL finals.

Metcalf clutched at his right hamstring after landing the conversion for the Warriors' third try, and cut a devastated figure leaving the field in Brisbane on Saturday night.

Overlooked for most of the season, Metcalf had been playing only his second game since April after starring in last week's defeat of the Panthers.

But the St George Illawarra recruit's dream of leaving the Warriors as a premiership winner is now in doubt, just when he appeared back in favour at the Kiwi club.

It is the latest injury blow for Metcalf, who returned from his second anterior cruciate ligament rupture earlier this season, only to suffer a hamstring injury two weeks later.

Minutes before Metcalf's new injury, Walsh was crunched in a hip-drop tackle that landed Warriors fullback Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad in the sin bin.

Walsh initially attempted to play on, but in his next involvement he threw an intercept that allowed winger Alofiana Khan-Pereira to streak away and score.

He left the field as Khan-Pereira's try put the Warriors up three scores and on the way to a fifth victory in six games.

Brisbane's finals hopes are well and truly over, but Walsh's injury may also impact his hopes of playing for Australia at the World Cup from October.

Earlier, the Warriors made a fast start and scored first as Jacob Laban grabbed Wayde Egan's pass and snuck outside Ezra Mam to the tryline.

Warriors halfback Metcalf is learning to carry a nation The halfback of the New Zealand Warriors plays with an entire nation on his shoulders and Luke Metcalf won't shy away from carrying the weight.

Metcalf batted the ball on for five-eighth Chanel Harris-Tavita to step twice through traffic and nab the Warriors' second try.

The Warriors took a 20-0 lead into half-time and never looked likely to be chased down.

The Warriors' Maori stars electrified after the break in Indigenous Round, with Nicoll-Klokstad touching down from a kick and Dallin Watene-Zelezniak finishing acrobatically in the right corner.

Left centre Leka Halasima crossed in the final five minutes to put the icing on the cake as the 16th-placed reigning premiers dropped a 12th game from 13 starts.

The Warriors may need to call on Luke Hanson for a second NRL game next week, given fellow halfback options Te Maire Martin (hamstring) and Tanah Boyd (knee) are both out.

Another option is to shift Nicoll-Klokstad from fullback and into the halves until Martin returns in coming weeks.

Cowboys lose to Eels after late penalty

The race for the NRL's top eight is still alive after a controversial late penalty consigned North Queensland to a 32-30 loss to Parramatta at CommBank Stadium.

With a chance to lock in a finals spot beckoning, the Cowboys' defence crumbled on Saturday night, allowing in six Eels tries.

The defining moment then came with four minutes to play, when Mitch Moses set up for a Parramatta field goal with scores locked at 30-30.

The Eels halfback eventually ran it on the last, was ankle-tapped by Heilum Luki and spilled the ball forward while falling.

But Moses reviewed the call, and the bunker found he had been collected in the head by Tom Chester while just inches above the ground.

The result means Canterbury are still alive in the race for the finals, albeit still two points behind the Cowboys and with North Queensland having a bye next week.

Manly also remain in the hunt, but would need to win their last three and have the Cowboys drop their final two games at home against Wests Tigers and Canberra.

As tough as the late penalty may have been for North Queensland, their defence remains a massive issue just weeks out from the finals.

A fortnight after leaking 82 points to the Sydney Roosters, it was poor again on Saturday night.

The tone was set when Parramatta winger Brian Kelly went 60 metres from the opening kick-off, while the Cowboys also conceded six first-half penalties.

The Eels produced an upset win over the Cowboys at Western Sydney Stadium. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Luki could also find himself in trouble with the match review committee, after being sin-binned in the opening half for a high shot on Luca Moretti.

There is no doubt North Queensland's attack has the spark to put points on, with halfback Jaxon Purdue again impressing.

He put on a long cut-out ball for a Braidon Burns try in the first half, then stepped Teancum Brown and fullback Apa Twidle for a second-half try of his own.

Reed Mahoney also starred out of dummy-half, burrowing over for the night's first try, before going short to Reuben Cotter and putting him over after the break.

The Cowboys also put on one of the tries of the year with scores locked at 24-24, with the ball going from right to left and back to the right through five passes and two kicks before Chester crossed.

Not to be outdone, Parramatta also had plenty of attacking flair.

It was big prop Junior Paulo who responded to level the scores at 30-30, with a lofted 35-metre cut-out ball in the lead-up to a Jordan Samrani try.

Moses also had three try assists and broke through the line in the lead-up to a Tallyn Da Silva penalty try.

And his off-contract halves partner Ronald Volkman again pushed his case for another deal, scoring one try and putting a grubber-kick in for a Josh Addo-Carr four-pointer.

Sharks stumble as Dolphins stay in NRL's vital top four

Cronulla have blown a huge opportunity to move back into the NRL's top four with a painful and potentially fatal 24-20 loss to lowly Canberra.

Star Sharks playmaker Braydon Trindall also suffered a dislocated shoulder as the Dolphins held on to the all-important fourth spot with three rounds remaining before the finals.

Cronulla will rue not finding a match-winner despite being camped on Canberra's line, set after set, for the final 10 minutes.

But the Sharks' mounting injury toll will be of equal concern for coach Craig Fitzgibbon, who has now watched his faltering side fumble and bumble their way to consecutive losses to sides well out of finals contention.

Trindall lasted less than 10 minutes before trudging off.

Initial reports were promising, with the shoulder quickly put back in.

But with the Sharks leading 8-0 and looking strong, Fitzgibbon opted not to risk their key playmaker any longer.

It may have been the wrong move as the Raiders wrestled back control and momentum.

Already without suspended forward enforcer Addin Fonua-Blake and injured centre Jesse Ramien, suddenly the Sharks were looking significantly understrength and vulnerable.

The afternoon had started brightly enough for Cronulla, with a Nicho Hynes penalty preceding a lovely chip-and-regather try for Trindall in the fifth minute.

But from 8-0 up, the Sharks lost their way after Trindall was forced off.

First, winger Xavier Savage steamed on to a beautiful long ball from Kaeo Weekes, then Owen Pattie wriggled his way over to suddenly put Canberra ahead 12-8 after 15 minutes.

Things were looking grim for the Sharks when winger Jed Stuart collected a double cut-out pass from Ethan Strange to stroll over and extend the Raiders' lead to 10 points.

But with their top-four hopes — and history would suggest — title prospects on the line, the Sharks regrouped with a much-needed reply from Teig Wilton off a short ball from Nicho Hynes.

The hosts should have snatched the lead after the half-time siren, only for Briton Nikora to ignore a three-on-one overlap on the right edge.

The Sharks, though, were first to score after the break when Will Kennedy swooped to score, before handing the momentum back to Canberra through a soft Joseph Tapine try under the sticks.

There was a huge moment with seven minutes remaining when video replays looked to have shown Ronaldo Mulitalo contorting his body and planting the ball down for a match-levelling try.

But The Bunker went with referee Gerard Sutton's on-field "no try" call.

The near-miss proved Cronulla's last chance as consecutive defeats to last-placed St George Illawarra and now Canberra leave the Sharks likely needing to beat Gold Coast, Parramatta and Melbourne to earn a double-chance in the play-offs.

No team has ever won the premiership in the NRL era from outside the top four.

World.title: Quick hits: Smith sets review record after horror drop, Warner jinxes Marnus
World.content:
Steve Smith reviews a decision before he's given out, Marnus Labuschagne gets desperate and then jinxed, while Josh Hazlewood provides a bright spot in an otherwise pitch-black day for Australia.

As it happened: Australia fighting to save first Test as Bangladesh claim top order wickets

Here are the quick hits from day three of the first Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

1. Marnus's desperate, ugly appeal

The ball clearly bounced before reaching Labuschagne. (Fox Cricket)

Marnus Labsuchagne is rarely shy in making an appeal.

But even he seemed a little sheepish about this one.

With Josh Hazlewood having snared the crucial early wicket of Hasan Mahmud, the Australians, already well behind in the game, were hopeful of wrapping up the Bangladeshi innings quickly.

But tailender Taijul Islam was finding some sweet timing in the middle, and was profiting with some quick, elegant runs.

In the 117th over, he creamed one straight into the ground and then into the covers, where Labuschagne made a fine diving stop.

But the inner-ring livewire came up holding the ball like he'd claimed a prize at the Easter Show.

Labuschagne made a desperate appeal early on day three. (Fox Cricket)

No-one seemed particularly convinced by the appeal, but umpire Kumar Dharmasena decided to send the decision upstairs.

And sure enough, the television replays confirmed what even Marnus surely must have known — the ball had clearly bounced between the batter and fielder.

Desperate, ugly stuff from the Australians.

2. Smith's inconceivable drop

Smith dropped a sitter in the morning session. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

In a morning of serious lows for Australia, this was surely the nadir.

Steve Smith, just one take away from becoming Test cricket's all-time leading catcher, settled underneath a Taskin top edge.

The Bangladeshi tailender took his eye of the ball as he played his pull shot, and the Australian vice-captain seemed destined to carve out another piece of history.

But the ball was in and then out of Smith's usually so-reliable hands, leaving the best since Bradman looking to the heavens for some sort of explanation.

Only a matter of balls later, it was Travis Head's turn to put one down.

Head's chance was a lot more difficult, retreating at full pelt, but it was the kind of catch we've seen him take in the past.

Australia was forced to wait until after lunch to belatedly see the back of the fighting Bangladeshi tail, which added another 24 runs after those fumbles, with the tourists taking an enormous 228-run lead into the second innings of the match.

3. Hazlewood passes 300

Hazlewood became the ninth Australian to pass 300 Test wickets on day three. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

A bright spot for the Australians in an otherwise pitch-black morning was Josh Hazlewood.

Playing his first international cricket since October last year, the big fast bowler ran in admirably all innings, looking amongst the fittest and most disciplined of his teammates as he returned figures of 6-89.

His fifth wicket of the innings, which was earnt by nicking off the excellent Mehidy, was his 300th in Test cricket.

He was the ninth Australian to reach the milestone, and after picking up the wicket of Ebadot Hossain to finish off the Bangladeshi innings, moved within nine wickets of Brett Lee on Australia's all-time leaderboard.

How high can Hazlewood get?

Well, Lee (310) is certainly in his crosshairs, as is Mitchell Johnson, who took 313 wickets during his Test career.

Then it's captain Cummins on 316 and the great DK Lillee on 355, which you'd imagine, given Hazlewood's injury record, may be a step too far.

Regardless, Hazlewood will finish his career of one of Australia's finest.

Not that that will be of any consolation to the Australian today.

4. Jake's horror homecoming

With 23 runs, Jake Weatherald was Australia's second-highest run scorer in the first innings, an accolade that carries as much credibility as being the English bowler with the best economy rate during the last Ashes.

But through almost all of his 37-ball, 56-minute stay at the crease, he looked skittish and nervous and wholly unsuited to opening the batting at Test level.

It made his second innings all the more crucial personally, even without accounting for the perilous situation Australia found themselves in, over 200 runs in arrears.

How disappointing then, that Weatherald seemingly learned nothing from his first-innings failure, playing with an angled bat outside off with minimal foot movement to be dismissed bowled off the inside edge by Hasan Mahmud.

The ball was too close to play a cut to, he still attempted it and was on his way.

The dismissal raises more uncomfortable questions for Australia's selectors, about whether they stick or twist ahead of a very busy 12 months.

5. Smith reviews before being given out

Smith surely set a new record for the fastest review on day three. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Steve Smith might have got away with one in the first innings, admitting that he hit the ball on its way through to Litton Das.

He got away with that one, but he was going to make doubly sure that he wouldn't be dismissed when a similar event happened when he was on just three runs in the second innings.

The ball beat the outside edge from a superb Ebadot delivery, and umpire Kumar Dharmasena wasted no time in raising the finger after hearing an edge.

Not quick enough for Smith though, who was shaking his head and reviewing before the umpire even put his finger up.

Dharmasena did nod at Smith, in his defence, but even so, it was an odd and extraordinarily self-consciously performative action.

It was not necessarily a surprise that Smith, never one to go willingly from the middle, was so quick to review, but he was proven to be vindicated, the sound coming from hitting the ground with his bat.

6. Warner puts the mockers on 'the Marnus of old'

Labuschagne departed after prematurely glowing praise from a former teammate in the commentary box. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

One of the Australians in desperate need of a big score, Marnus Labuschagne began his innings like he was cripplingly aware of just that, scratchy and anxious, struggling for any sort of rhythm.

But things were slowly improving, with the idiosyncratic first drop playing a few nice drives through the covers and finding some stability in his stance.

On commentary for Fox Cricket, David Warner was glowing in his praise for Labuschagne.

Even at the time, it felt like the former Australia opener was both jumping the gun and tempting fate.

“He’s confident in his game, he’s hitting the ball well ... now he’s in, he looks like the Marnus of old," Warner said while comparing images of Labuschagne's stance early in his innings against footage from after he had found some form.

"He’s confident, he’s got his whole rhythm back. And it’s exciting to see, and I’m happy for him.

" I really hope he goes on with it, and he'll be able to go back today and say 'I feel good, what was it?' And hopefully he can identify that. "

Labuschagne added just one more run after Warner's glowing review, being promptly yorked by spinner Taijul, the Australian playing all around a straight one and departing for 31.

World.title: Wallaby 1,000 has 'dream come true' as Australia thrash Japan
World.content:
Massimo De Lutiis has enjoyed a dream debut for Australia, as the 1,000th Wallaby scored a try in his country's commanding 56-17 win over Japan in the second Test.

De Lutiis came on in the 50th minute of the Test match in Townsville with the match delicately poised at 21-17, the half-time score.

But the introduction of the hulking 22-year-old began the start of Australia's dominance in the Test match, as fellow prop Angus Bell scored the first of five second-half tries.

De Lutiis, with the descendants of the very first Wallaby Patrick Carew in attendance, scored minutes later to send his teammates, and the crowd, into a frenzy.

"One thousand is awesome. But just to be a Wallaby in general is crazy to me. It's a dream come true," De Lutiis told the Nine Network post-match.

"When I scored, I was just over the moon. I couldn't believe it."

After a difficult first half, the Wallabies improved in attack and defence to earn the win. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Despite the impressive scoreline, the Wallabies were tested in the opening 50 minutes, with the Japanese taking the lead late in the first half.

At three tries apiece after 40 minutes, the Brave Blossoms had every right to believe a maiden win over the Wallabies was there for the taking.

But Australia showed the polish which eluded them in the first half, and the first Test in Osaka last weekend.

New coach Les Kiss, in his second match in charge, provided the right team talk at half-time to wrestle momentum from Japan.

"We got challenged by Les [Kiss] at half-time," captain Harry Wilson told the Nine Network.

"A team like Japan, if you're not up for it, they really make you pay.

"I was really proud of the group in the second half. We stepped it up and put on a great performance."

The win is Australia's third in a row, the first time the Wallabies have strung together a trio of triumphs since 2024.

The challenge for Australia gets harder, with two Tests in Argentina followed by one Test against South Africa, and two Bledisloe Cup matches against the All Blacks.

Relive all the action from the second Test between Australia and Japan in the blog below.

World.title: Last-ditch spoil leads to historic second Hawks-Pies draw this season
World.content:
Hawthorn and Collingwood have created VFL/AFL history with a second draw this season after another nail-biting finish.

Hawks forward Dylan Moore had a shot after the siren to win the game, but saw his kick fall short as both sides settled for a 13.14 (92) draw at the MCG.

It is the first time in league history that two teams have had both their matches with each other end in draws inside the same home and away season.

In Saturday night's other match, Melbourne ran out 20.12 (132) to 8.8 (56) winners over Port Adelaide at the Adelaide Oval.

Despite the win, Melbourne faces a nervous wait to see whether forward Jacob van Rooyen is suspended after his swinging arm left Port Adelaide defender Aliir Aliir concussed in a marking contest.

Earlier on Saturday, St Kilda kept its wildcard hopes alive with a convincing 14.10 (94) to 6.9 (45) win at the MCG.

Geelong came back from a 38-point deficit to defeat North Melbourne 19.11 (125) to 17.8 (110) at Docklands Stadium as the Kangaroos lost Harry Sheezel to a cheek injury.

Elsewhere, Brisbane kicked away in the second half to claim a 14.11 (95) to 6.17 (53) win over Gold Coast in the latest edition of the Q-Clash at the Gabba.

In Saturday's AFLW action, reigning premiers North Melbourne recorded a 15.10 (100) to 3.9 (27) win over Geelong at Docklands Stadium as Jasmine Garner and Ash Riddell recorded 35 disposals apiece.

At Princes Park, Richmond claimed a 6.10 (46) to 4.4 (28) win over Collingwood as Monique Conti recorded 26 disposals and a goal.

In Saturday's AFLW finale, the Western Bulldogs were too good for Gold Coast, running out 6.4 (40) to 1.8 (14) winners at Carrara Stadium.

World.title: Cyclist, 19, dies during Volta a Portugal after collision with vehicle
World.content:
A 19-year-old British cyclist has been killed in an accident during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

Welsh rider Finlay Tarling died after "a collision between the cyclist and a light goods vehicle", Major Tiago Machado of the National Republican Guard said in a statement.

An investigation is underway, according to local authorities.

Tarling, the younger brother of Netcompany-Ineos rider Josh, had raced for Great Britain on the road and track.

He was competing for the NSN Development Team when the incident occurred on the 166.8-kilometre route from Melgaco to Fafe.

Riders are seen in Fafe, Portugal, reacting to the news that Finlay Tarling had died. (Getty Images: Miguel Lemos/NurPhoto)

In a statement, NSN said the team was heartbroken to announce Tarling's passing.

"Fin was a much-loved member of our team but most importantly, he was a son, a brother, and a friend to so many. He will be deeply missed.

"Our deepest condolences go out to Fin's parents Michael and Dawn, his brother Josh, and everyone who was lucky enough to call Fin a friend."

The intrinsic failings and risks of cycling laid bare with another premature death Cycling has lost another rider due to a downhill crash, with teenager Muriel Furrer killed on a descent at the World Championships in Zurich. So where does the responsibility lie?

In a post on X, the race organisers and the Portuguese Cycling Federation also expressed their "most heartfelt condolences to the family of Finlay Tarling, to his team-mates, to the NSN Development Team, and to all his friends and loved ones".

It added that the racing was stopped and the scheduled podium ceremony would not take place as a sign of "respect and mourning".

Portuguese president António José Seguro said that Tarling's death had "plunged the peloton, the tournament and the host nation into mourning".

British Cycling's performance director Stephen Park added: "All of us at British Cycling are heartbroken to learn of the tragic passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal.

"Fin was a talented rider with a fantastic future ahead of him, a loyal teammate and an all-round brilliant young man.

"Our deepest sympathies are with his parents and brother, Josh, at this tragic time."

World.title: Australia fighting to save first Test as Bangladesh claim top order wickets
World.content:
Australia has closed day three of the first Test against Bangladesh on 4-161, still 67 runs behind the tourists on another chastening day in Darwin.

Alex Carey (19) and Cameron Green (43) are the not out batters, combining for a valuable 39-run partnership late in the day that will prove crucial for Australia's chances of saving, or perhaps even winning the Test.

Australia will back itself to make Bangladesh bat again but, on an increasingly placid pitch, will have to bat very well to set a challenging target to the tourists, a scenario almost inconceivable for supporters of the world's number one side prior to the match getting underway.

With Bangladesh resuming on 6-351, Australia once again struggled to make inroads, extending their already gruelling labours in the field.

Josh Hazlewood thought he had made the breakthrough when umpire Richard Illingworth fired out Mehidy Hasan LBW, only for the DRS to show the ball was missing the leg stump.

The veteran quick was frustrated then, but soon was celebrating when Hasan Mahmud was trapped bang in front to depart for 14.

Hazlewood became the ninth Australian to pass 300 Test wickets on day three. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Hazlewood then claimed another, having Taijul Islam caught sharply by Cam Green, whose self-preservation instincts came to the fore to stop the ball flying into his face at gully.

If those two wickets had Australia thinking they'd soon be batting, the discipline of the Bangladeshi batters made sure they had to stay out even longer, coupled with a shocking drop from Steve Smith.

Taskin Ahmed top edged a pull shot out to Smith, who settled under the ball and let it through his finger tips.

A few balls later, Travis Head dropped a far harder chance, racing around from close to the wicket as Bangladesh reached 8-417 at lunch.

Smith dropped a sitter in the morning session. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

The mounting frustration eased somewhat by two more Hazlewood wickets, as he claimed Mehidy Hasan Miraz and Ebadot Hossain, both caught behind, to secure a 14th Test five-fa and his 300th Test wicket, becoming the ninth Australian to reach that particular milestone.

Australia needed a good start, but under-pressure home-town favourite Jake Weatherald departed second over for a duck, chopping on after playing with an angled bat to Hasan Mahmud.

Failing to learn from his first innings dismissal and that of his opening partner, Travis Head followed in near identical fashion to leave Australia 2-37 and in desperate trouble.

Marnus Labuschagne and Steve Smith came to the crease and both survived big Bangladeshi appeals, with Smith forced to review a caught behind decision when he was on three, the replay showing that he hit the ground with his bat instead of the ball.

Labuschagne departed after prematurely glowing praise from a former teammate in the commentary box. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

That pair looked set, with Labuschagne seemingly playing with am encouragingly positive intent that was desperately lacking in his first innings effort.

However, the Queenslander was next to depart, playing all around a Taijul Islam fuller ball and yorking himself against the spinner to be out for 31.

Smith and Cameron Green rebuilt with a patient and untroubled 49-run partnership on an increasingly docile pitch, right up until Smith flat-batted a return catch to Bangladesh's other spinner, Mehidy Hasan for 44.

Australia still trailed by over 100 runs at that stage, with Alex Carey joining Green, who incredibly survived an inside edge that clipped his leg stump without dislodging the bail early in the evening session.

They batted out the remainder of the day without too much alarm, but know they will have to fight just as hard to save this Test match over the next two days.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog below.

World.title: Bezos consortium enters 'definitive agreement' to buy Liverpool stake
World.content:
A consortium containing Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin is buying a minority stake in Premier League club Liverpool, the English soccer giant says.

Club owner Fenway Sports Group (FSG) said in a statement it entered into a "definitive agreement" for the sale to 1892 Holdings.

The investor group is led by Amit Bhatia, who is married to a daughter of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, and has taken a stake of more than 30 per cent in the 20-time English champion. The deal reportedly values Liverpool at around $US6 billion ($8.4 billion).

Boston-based FSG paid $US400 million to take over Liverpool in 2010 and also owns the Boston Red Sox. FSG said in July that it had been approached by the Bhatia-led consortium regarding a "strategic minority investment" in the club.

Eduardo Saverin is part of the investment group with Jeff Bezos. (Getty Images: Sam Barnes/Sportsfile)

"As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special," FSG president Mike Gordon said in the statement.

It marks the first foray into soccer by Bezos, who, according to Forbes, is the fourth-richest person in the world with a net worth of about $US280 billion. He founded Amazon in 1994 and has been executive chairman since 2021.

Saverin is a Brazilian businessman worth about $US36 billion, according to Forbes.

Bhatia, a British-Indian entrepreneur, was the co-owner of second-tier English team Queens Park Rangers for 18 years before stepping down recently.

Amit Bhatia during his time as the chairman of Queens Park Rangers. (Getty Images: Steven Paston/PA Images)

"We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club's continued success for years to come," Bhatia said in the statement.

Under the leadership of FSG and its principal owner John Henry, Liverpool ended a 30-year wait to be English champion in 2020 and added another Premier League title last year. That tied Manchester United on 20 English top-flight league championships.

The club was European champion for a sixth time — a record for an English team — in 2019.

The Premier League is one of the biggest competitions in sports, with its teams now largely owned by oil-rich Gulf states or private equity.

Liverpool sack manager Arne Slot after underwhelming season The Dutchman won the Premier League title in his first season, but failed to live up to expectations the following year as Liverpool finished fifth.

Liverpool now has three of the richest people in the world as minority owners.

That does not mean, however, that the club can simply start spending recklessly in the transfer market on new players.

That is because the Premier League has financial rules in place to protect the competitive balance of the competition and ensure the financial sustainability of clubs.

In broad terms, a club's on-pitch spending is related to 85 per cent of its "football-related revenue and net profit/loss from player sales," the Premier League says.

Instead, the difference will come in how Liverpool — already one of the top teams in world soccer — is marketed more around the world under Bezos and Saverin, especially.

The deal is likely to bring more commercial revenue into the club, thereby improving its profits.

Tech.title: Have a laugh at AI’s expense by roleplaying as a chatbot
Tech.content:
Your AI Slop Bores Me is brilliant in its simplicity. There are two tabs: human and LARP as an AI. On one side you enter a request. On the other, you submit an answer. But the important thing is that there’s a human on both sides of the equation. Prompts can request a response as text or image, and then whoever is roleplaying as the AI gets 150 seconds to respond.

Just like a real LLM, Your AI Slop Bores Me works on a sort of token system. Requests cost credits, and to earn credits you have to jump onto the AI side and answer some of your own. You can also just wait as you get one free request every two minutes. But, as fun as it is to drop a question or an image request into the chatbox and see what comes back, the real joy is in pretending to be a chatbot. Sure, there are way too many people asking for drawings of obscure anime characters that are nearly impossible to pull off with the bare-bones MS-Paint-like tool in two-and-a-half minutes. But that’s part of the fun, trying to work within the extreme limitations presented while trying to maintain the illusion that you’re an AI. If a request doesn’t appeal to you, you can always skip it.

Tech.title: Don’t overlook Elektron’s budget electronic music instruments
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

When I’m asked what to buy if you want to get into making electronic music, I often recommend Elektron’s budget-minded Model:Samples and Model:Cycles grooveboxes. They don’t grab headlines the way Teenage Engineering’s gear or the Telepathic Instruments Orchid do, and even compared to the company’s higher-end and more niche musical offerings like the Digitakt, Octatrack, or Tonverk, they’re often overlooked. But as my collection has grown to include fancier and far more expensive instruments, I still find myself coming back to the Model series.

Those looking to get their first groovebox are often drawn to more familiar brand names like Korg or Roland. And lots of people on Reddit will be quick to recommend the Novation Circuit Tracks (which I personally find confusing and mediocre-sounding). This is probably also partially due to the reputation Elektron gear has for being obtuse. If you’re an established music maker and aren’t deterred by a complicated workflow, you’re probably going to pick up a more powerful Elektron box, like the Digitone or Syntakt. That leaves the Models lineup in a weird no man’s land, and that’s a shame.

The primary difference between the two Models instruments is that the Model:Cycles uses FM synthesis and the Model:Samples, appropriately enough, plays samples. (It is not technically a sampler, however, since it can’t record samples, and instead they have to be loaded over USB.)

Connectivity isn’t the Model:Cycles’ strong suit. Photo: Terrence O’Brien / The Verge

The Model:Cycles is built around a streamlined version of the engine found in the Digitone, one of my favorite-sounding synths of all time. This is a modern take on FM that can do the cold bells and icy pads you associate with iconic instruments like the DX7 (the iconic sound of the ’80s). But it also does modern glassy keys and aggressive turn-of-the-millennium EDM bass.

The two are more alike than not, though. They’re both six-track grooveboxes with six velocity-sensitive pads and plenty of knobs for hands-on controls, and they look almost identical. But most importantly, they feature Elektron’s legendary step sequencer without being nearly as intimidating as the company’s more expensive and notoriously complicated offerings.

The sequencer is built around what the company calls “trigs” and “locks.” Trigs are basically just events, typically triggering a note, and locks are just step-specific settings. It seems like a simple enough concept, but it makes these instruments far more capable than they might seem at first blush.





Quick jam on the Elektron Model:Cycles.(opens a new window) Quick jam on the Elektron Model:Cycles.

Six tracks isn’t a lot to work with. Once you’ve loaded up a kick, snare, and hi-hat, then you’ve only got three more tracks for bass, any melodic elements, and additional percussion. But sound locks allow you to change samples or presets on a per-step basis. That means, so long as they never play simultaneously, you can have your kick and snare share the same track, then you can put your hi-hats and other percussion on a second track, and leave the four other tracks for everything else. This is just the most obvious example of how locks expand the possibilities of what might seem rather limited on paper.

The sequencer can be treated like a simple step sequencer where you drop a four-on-the-floor kick and a snare on the backbeat. But it also grows with you as your skills improve, and you want to create more complex tracks. Trig conditions, for example, allow you to set rules that govern when certain steps are triggered, like only every third time through the loop, only when you press the fill button, or only if a previous trig condition is met. This means that you can create a huge amount of variety in a single 64-step pattern. And then you can chain several of those patterns together to create complex and evolving arrangements that just aren’t possible on most gear in this price range.

There’s plenty of hands-on controls for jamming. Photo: Terrence O’Brien / The Verge

The Models boxes are also just incredibly fun. Where Elektron’s other gear demands a lot of menu diving, the Model:Samples and Model:Cycles are immediately approachable and built for live performance. It’s easy to trigger a drum fill with the push of a button, tweak a knob to open the filter on a bass, or briefly bathe a lead melody in delay.

Control-all might be the most fun feature, which, as you might have guessed, allows you to control all the tracks simultaneously. Bury your entire track in reverb as you start cranking up the distortion and lowering the pitch of all your samples to create a mangled, chaotic breakdown. And then immediately undo it all and drop the beat again by pressing the function and pattern buttons. The Model:Samples and Model:Cycles encourage jamming in a way that frankly a lot of electronic music gear just doesn’t, and it’s an absolute blast.

Now, they’re not without their flaws. The pads are pretty mediocre. Having to load samples via USB rather than recording them directly kinda sucks. And the lack of polyphony (each sequencer track can only play one note at a time) is a bit of a bummer. But at $349, it’s hard to complain. Plus they can be snagged used for as little as $200 on Reverb or Craigslist. Frankly, they’re some of the best bargains in music hardware and a great place to start your journey into producing electronic music.

Tech.title: Switched on Pop’s Nate Sloan and Charlie Harding love fresh vegetables and guitar pedals
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

As if you needed more reason to love Carly Rae Jepsen’s “Call Me Maybe” beyond its pop perfection, it is also, according to lore, the genesis for Switched on Pop, one of the best music podcasts out there. Cohosts Nate Sloan and Charlie Harding obsessively dissect pop songs, from the theory behind their musical choices to their production techniques. If you’re a student of pop music, then this is a must-listen podcast.

Sloan is a composer and professor of musicology at USC Thornton School of Music, where he researches pop, but also jazz and even Tin Pan Alley. Harding is a songwriter, music journalist, and a professor as well. Their combined knowledge is near encyclopedic. Whether they’re talking about text painting in Justin Timberlake’s “Can’t Stop the Feeling!” or Taryn Southern’s AI experiments, the two reveal the rich tapestry of even the most simple-seeming songs.

Now, after 12 years and nearly 500 episodes, the show recently made the leap to video on Netflix, featuring guests like Aaron Dessner (The National), Trevor Horn (The Buggles, Yes), and Cypress Hill. Sloan and Harding told us about the importance of the metronome, fresh vegetables, and what seems to be a slightly problematic relationship with guitar pedals.

Switched on Pop is a production of New York Magazine’s Vulture and the Vox Media Podcast Network.

What is your most indispensable tool?

Charlie Harding: The Martin D-28 is the platonic idea of both what a guitar sounds like and, I’m ashamed to admit how much this matters to me, how a guitar looks. You’ve heard it on “Blackbird,” “Wish You Were Here,” and “Big Yellow Taxi.” I found one from 1970 sitting in an antique shop in Maine. But I’m still waiting for it to produce a timeless classic for me.

Nate Sloan: Sibelius music notation software. Whenever I’m analyzing a song, I don’t truly understand it until I transcribe its melody, harmony, and rhythm.

Which is the most underappreciated?

CH: Keyboard shortcuts and the app Rectangle save me hours of my life every year by doing the mundane task of repositioning windows on my computer. And they also make me feel like I’m mission control on some kind of spaceship.

NS: The metronome.

What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?

NS: AudioHijack for grabbing audio.

What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?

CH: This is very nitpicky, but it drives me mad. I extensively use focus modes on iOS to help keep away distractions. But I also need people in my family to be able to reach me, so they get exceptions to the focus modes. However, that means any group messaging chain with just one family member blows up my notifications when I’m presenting to a lecture hall full of songwriting students. This means I’m urgently notified every time my recently retired father catches a fish. I am happy for my dad, but I’d be more happy to find out after 5 pm when I’m off “do not disturb.” If this makes me sound like a curmudgeon, I am.

NS: I wish I could strum it like a guitar.

What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar?

NS: ProQuest Historical Newspapers.

How many tabs do you have open right now?

CH: 92… but they are nicely organized into groups that only I understand.

NS: Two. I used to have hundreds open, but it was killing my attention span, so I now make a point of constantly closing them.

Which social media platform do you use the most (if any)?

NS: Instagram, guiltily.

What is your happy place online?

CH: Browsing Sweetwater for variations of guitar pedals that I already own.

NS: Watching ukulele tutorials on YouTube.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

CH: The Dato DUO synthesizer and Dato DRUM drum machine. They are the easiest way to learn to program a synthesizer, and you can’t make a bad sound. My kids jam on them every night. It’s turned them into Brooklyn DJs, unfortunately.

NS: The iPod that I traveled around the world with in 2006.

Which was the most disappointing?

NS: The minidisc player.

What game do you have the fondest memories of?

NS: Pac-Man.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

CH: AI music slop, full stop.

NS: Wearable computing.

What is one thing you wish you had created?

CH: In 2007 I pitched my college friends on creating an app that would allow you to legally hitchhike in other people’s cars. We started a tea company instead, which was ultimately less of a liability.

NS: Autotune.

What creation are you most proud of?

CH: Switched On Pop. My wife read this and said I should add my children.

NS: Coining the term “pop drop” to describe the instrumental postchorus in a pop song.

Which are you least proud of?

CH: My wife read this and said I should say my guitar pedal collection.

NS: Getting dunked on by YouTuber Rick Beato after calling the Jonas Brothers “stupefyingly funky” in a New York Times article.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

CH: You can never have too many guitar pedals.

NS: Have a short memory.

What is your current obsession?

NS: LeBron James signing with the 76ers.

What do you do when you need to focus?

CH: Drink some tea.

NS: Step away from the computer, take a walk, and start recording a voicenote about what I’m trying to accomplish.

What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?

CH: Drink some tea.

NS: Call Charlie Harding.

When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?

CH: During routine surgery.

NS: Whenever I go to the gym.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

CH: The History of Sound by Ben Shattuck.

NS: Vinyl copy of the Jeff Parker IVTet.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

CH: My guitar pedals. And my beautiful wife.

NS: Fresh vegetables.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

CH: He is embarrassed there is a biopic about him.

NS: One man dared to overanalyze pop music, taking on BTS Army, Madonna stans, and the Little Monsters, and living to tell the tale.

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

CH:

Tech.title: I finally found a magnetic phone grip I never want to remove
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

I told myself I wouldn’t buy an OhSnap accessory for my phone. Every one I’d tested was nice, but felt overpriced and slightly flawed. After I weighed in on the $40 Snap Grip 5 last year, I wound up sticking with my $25 Syncwire instead. But OhSnap’s $50 Snap Grip Stand finally got me. To have a truly useful vertical stand and grip always attached to my phone, ready at a moment’s notice? Heck yes.

I started testing the Snap Grip Stand months ago, and soon discovered that I never took it off. So I bought my own.

It’s thin — 3.7mm, so it slips effortlessly into my pocket without making an extra indent in my pants. It’s got a double-sided magnetic ring, like the previous gen, so it not only sticks to your magnet ring phone, it can stick flat against a fridge or gym equipment or my garage cabinets. It even lets some wireless charging through.

Like the previous gen, the magnets hold my phone tightly, and the grip part is one of the most versatile I’ve tried. The clever interlocking joints can fit between two of your fingers loosely like a PopSocket, or you can put a finger through the joints for a very secure grip.

The whole disc spins freely (though still with a bit of scraping noise) to rotate to any angle you like.

But unlike the previous gen, the Stand has a stand unlike most other magnet grips on the market. The entire magnet ring is now encircled by a thinner fold-out ring on a hinged arm. Pull it down, and it effortlessly props up my phone in its normal vertical orientation. Most rival stands barely prop a phone, and even then they don’t deploy as fast. Here, there’s no need to take off the stand, or rotate it and lock a tab in place like OhSnap’s previous grips — pull out, plop phone on surface, done.

OhSnap advertises that it’s “thinner than your camera bumps,” but that depends on whether you’re using a case. It’s thin enough. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

It’s not the only stand with such a design. The $17 Gornergrat Grat 5 has a similar stand and costs far less. But I tried one and found I don’t like its elastic strap, which feels loose and thus less secure around my fingers.

OhSnap makes use of the extra vertical arm space to keep the stand from rotating when you don’t want it to: it’s got a extra vertical magnet in there to match Apple’s MagSafe pattern, as well as some grippy clear plastic material to provide friction.

And I’m happy to say the aluminum gadget doesn’t seem to have any other unwanted coatings: I wasn’t a fan of the adhesive on the Snap Grip 4, or the soft-touch coating that started to peel when I tested the Snap Grip 5. Here, it appears to be bare anodized metal that looks and feels great.

Neither of these phones (Pixel 9, Galaxy S25) has built-in magnets, but I bought magnet cases for each. Phone grips like this also come with adhesive magnet rings. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

Right now, I can only think of three things that’d make it better: a lower price, magnets in the stand’s ring (rather than the main ring) so I can use the magnets and the stand at the same time, and maybe a better way to open the grip one-handed.

I do like how Tango’s spring-loaded grip can pop open when you press it. But I tried a Tango too, and I don’t like the way that spring feels between my fingers, pushing them apart too much.

As for the lower price, at least OhSnap’s products are regularly on sale. I bought mine at Best Buy for $40 after tax.

With Spider-Man: Brand New Day behind us, and its reveal of Sadie Sink as Jean Grey, Marvel is finally ready to officially welcome the X-Men into the MCU.
